_comment: Private Pilot study guide (plan §39.4). One entry per covered FAR section or AIM paragraph, keyed by its note stem: a gist and 'why it matters' in the curator's words, key numbers as verbatim quotes the build checks against the official text (paragraph `where` is a CFR label path such as (a)(1)), traps, plain-English questions with the citations that answer them, mnemonics (training-community devices, not FAA text), ACS element codes, and the training stage. Rendered as labelled study aids — never as official text. Claude-drafted 2026-09-13; every entry stays `unreviewed` until a human has checked its wording against the text.

stages.pre-solo: Rules you need before you fly alone: what you carry, what the aircraft carries, seat belts, lights, alcohol, right of way, the pattern.
stages.solo-xc: Rules for leaving the pattern: preflight action, fuel, altitudes, airspace and its weather minimums, transponders.
stages.checkride: Rules the examiner probes on the oral: currency, medicals and BasicMed, privileges and cost sharing, inspections, inoperative equipment, special VFR, oxygen.

43.3.gist: Who is allowed to work on an aircraft. Mechanics, repairmen, repair stations and air carriers each get their own paragraph; paragraph (g) is the pilot's: a private pilot (or higher, not sport) may perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft they own or operate, as long as it is not flown under Part 121, 129 or 135. Paragraph (k) says avionics database updates done from the flight deck without tools are not maintenance at all.
43.3.why: The oral almost always asks what you may legally do to your own airplane; this is the section that grants it, and Appendix A to Part 43 is the list of what counts as preventive maintenance.

numbers.value: Private pilots may do preventive maintenance on aircraft they own or operate
numbers.quote: the holder of a pilot certificate issued under part 61 may perform preventive maintenance on any aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used under part 121, 129, or 135 of this chapter
Updates of databases in installed avionics meeting the conditions of this paragraph are not considered maintenance and may be performed by pilots

traps: The privilege is preventive maintenance only, and only on an aircraft you own or operate; a rented trainer you do not operate is not yours to service.
Doing the work is half of it: § 43.9 still requires a logbook entry before the aircraft is returned to service.

questions.q: Can I change the oil and replace a landing light bulb on the airplane I rent?
questions.a: Only if you own or operate it; § 43.3(g) lets a private pilot do preventive maintenance on an aircraft owned or operated by that pilot, and the item must be on the Part 43 Appendix A list. Then make the required maintenance record entry.

61.3.gist: What you must have on you to fly: your pilot certificate, a government photo ID and, unless BasicMed or a listed exception applies, your medical — in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, and shown on request to the FAA, NTSB, TSA or any law-enforcement officer.
61.3.why: Examiners ask what you carry, and a ramp inspection asks to see it.
traps: “Readily accessible in the aircraft” is the standard: a certificate left at home makes the flight illegal even if you are otherwise qualified.
Student pilots need a medical for airplanes; only glider and balloon students are exempt.

questions.q: What documents must I have with me to fly as a private pilot?
questions.a: Your pilot certificate, a government photo ID, and a current medical certificate (or, under BasicMed, the course certificate and exam checklist in your logbook).

61.15.gist: Drug and alcohol offenses and your certificate. A drug conviction, or an act prohibited by § 91.17 or § 91.19, is grounds for denying a certificate for up to a year and for suspending or revoking one you hold. A second motor vehicle action (DUI conviction or license action) within 3 years is the same. Every motor vehicle action must be reported in writing to the FAA security division within 60 days.
61.15.why: Examiners use this with § 61.16 and § 91.17 to test whether you know that a DUI on the road reaches your pilot certificate.

numbers.value: Denial for up to 1 year after a drug conviction
numbers.quote: Denial of an application for any certificate, rating, or authorization issued under this part for a period of up to 1 year after the date of final conviction

numbers.value: Two motor vehicle actions within 3 years
numbers.quote: a motor vehicle action occurring within 3 years of a previous motor vehicle action is grounds for

numbers.value: Report each motor vehicle action within 60 days
numbers.quote: not later than 60 days after the motor vehicle action

traps: The 60-day report is required for every motor vehicle action, not only the second one; failing to report is itself grounds for denial or revocation under (f).
A motor vehicle action includes a license suspension or a refused application, not only a conviction.

questions.q: I got a DUI last month. Does the FAA need to know?
questions.a: Yes. § 61.15(e) requires a written report to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division within 60 days of any motor vehicle action, and the medical application asks about it too.

61.16.gist: Refusing a law-enforcement alcohol test requested under § 91.17(c), or refusing to release the results to the FAA, is treated like a violation: denial of any certificate for up to a year and suspension or revocation of one you hold.
61.16.why: It closes the loophole a pilot might hope for: declining the test is not safer than failing it.

numbers.value: Denial for up to 1 year after a refusal
numbers.quote: for a period of up to 1 year after the date of that refusal

questions.q: What happens if I refuse a breath test after a flight?
questions.a: Under § 61.16 the refusal itself is grounds for denial of a certificate for up to a year and for suspension or revocation of any certificate you hold.

61.23.gist: A private pilot needs at least a third-class medical (or BasicMed); the class you must hold depends on the privileges you exercise, and how long it lasts depends on the class and your age on the exam date (the table in paragraph (d)).
61.23.why: The class-and-duration table is a favourite written question; the BasicMed 24-month course and 48-month exam cycle is a favourite oral one.

numbers.value: Third class for private pilot privileges
numbers.quote: at least a third-class medical certificate
during the 24 calendar months
during the 48 calendar months

traps: Duration runs in calendar months from the exam date, to the end of the month: under 40 at the exam, a third class lasts 60 calendar months; 40 or over, 24 (the § 61.23(d) table).

questions.q: How long is my third-class medical good for?
questions.a: 60 calendar months if you were under 40 on the exam date, 24 calendar months if you were 40 or over — per the table in § 61.23(d).

questions.q: Can I fly as a private pilot on BasicMed?
questions.a: Yes, within § 61.113(i): no more than 6 passengers in an aircraft with at most 7 seats and 12,500 lb, below 18,000 ft MSL and 250 knots, with the medical course every 24 months and a physician's exam every 48.

61.31.gist: When a rating alone is not enough. Large and turbojet aircraft need a type rating. Complex, high-performance (more than 200 horsepower), pressurized (service ceiling above 25,000 ft MSL) and tailwheel airplanes each need training and a one-time logbook endorsement before you act as PIC. Paragraph (d)(2) is how a student pilot flies solo: training plus a solo endorsement instead of a rating, and (m)(2)(ii) exempts student pilots from the rating limitations.
61.31.why: The oral asks what extra endorsements you would need to fly a given airplane, and the answer is always in this section.

numbers.quote: an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower

numbers.value: Pressurized means a ceiling above 25,000 ft MSL
numbers.quote: above 25,000 feet MSL

numbers.value: Operate without a type rating for up to 60 days on an authorization
numbers.quote: for up to 60 days

traps: The complex and high-performance endorsements are separate; a 180 hp retractable needs the complex endorsement, a fixed-gear 230 hp airplane needs the high-performance one.
The endorsements are one-time and never expire, unlike the flight review or the solo endorsements of § 61.87.

questions.q: What do I need to fly a 300 hp fixed-gear airplane as PIC?
questions.a: A high-performance endorsement under § 61.31(f): ground and flight training in a high-performance airplane and a one-time logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor.

questions.q: Why can a student pilot fly an airplane without holding any rating?
questions.a: § 61.31(d)(2) allows a person who has received the required training and a solo endorsement to serve as PIC, and (m)(2)(ii) exempts the holder of a student pilot certificate from the rating limitations.

mnemonics: CHiPT: Complex, High-performance, Pressurized, Tailwheel each need an endorsement.

61.51.gist: What goes in your logbook and what you may log. You must record the training and experience used for a certificate, rating, flight review or recency, with date, time, route, aircraft, and conditions of flight. Solo time means you were the sole occupant. A private pilot logs PIC when sole manipulator of an aircraft they are rated in; a student logs PIC only when sole occupant with a solo endorsement and in training. You must show your certificate, medical and logbook on request, and a student must carry the logbook and student certificate on every solo cross-country.
61.51.why: Your logbook is the evidence for every requirement in Part 61, and the examiner reads it before the oral begins.

numbers.quote: a pilot may log as solo flight time only that flight time when the pilot is the sole occupant of the aircraft

numbers.value: PIC when sole manipulator and rated
numbers.quote: when the pilot is the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which the pilot is rated

numbers.value: Student PIC time: sole occupant, solo endorsement, in training
numbers.quote: Has a solo flight endorsement as required under § 61.87 of this part

numbers.value: Solo cross-country: carry logbook and student certificate
numbers.quote: A student pilot must carry the following items in the aircraft on all solo cross-country flights

traps: A student pilot's solo time is also PIC time, but a private pilot flying with an instructor logs PIC only when rated in the aircraft and the sole manipulator.
Simulated instrument time in flight requires the safety pilot's name in the logbook.

questions.q: What must I have in the airplane on a solo cross-country as a student?
questions.a: Your pilot logbook with the instructor endorsements, your student pilot certificate, and any other record § 61.51 requires, plus the documents § 61.3 always requires.

questions.q: As a student, when can I log PIC time?
questions.a: Only when you are the sole occupant, hold a current solo endorsement under § 61.87, and are training for a certificate or rating.

61.53.gist: Do not fly when you are not medically fit. A medical-certificate holder may not act as PIC or required crew while knowing of a condition that would fail the medical standards, or while taking medication or treatment that would. Under BasicMed or when no medical is required, the standard is knowing of any condition that would make you unable to operate safely.
61.53.why: It turns the IMSAFE self-check from good advice into a regulation, and it is the rule behind every 'you have a cold, can you fly?' oral question.

numbers.value: Grounded while you know of a disqualifying condition
numbers.quote: Knows or has reason to know of any medical condition that would make the person unable to meet the requirements for the medical certificate necessary for the pilot operation

numbers.value: BasicMed standard: unable to operate safely
numbers.quote: unable to operate the aircraft in a safe manner

traps: A valid medical certificate in your pocket does not make you legal today; the rule is about what you know right now.
Medication counts even when the condition itself would be fine.

questions.q: My medical is current but I started a new prescription yesterday. May I fly?
questions.a: Not if the medication or the condition would keep you from meeting the medical standards; § 61.53(a)(2) prohibits acting as PIC while taking such medication. Check with an AME first.

61.56.gist: A flight review every 24 calendar months: at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training with an authorized instructor, covering the Part 91 rules and whatever maneuvers the instructor decides, ending in a logbook endorsement. A practical test or proficiency check in that window counts instead.
61.56.why: Being certificated is not the same as being legal to act as PIC; this is the first thing an examiner checks in your logbook.

numbers.quote: a minimum of 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training
since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which that pilot acts as pilot in command

traps: Calendar months: a review on 10 March 2026 is good through 31 March 2028, not through 10 March.
Passing your checkride restarts the clock (§ 61.56(d)).

questions.q: How often do I need a flight review, and what is in it?
questions.a: Every 24 calendar months: at least an hour of ground and an hour of flight with an authorized instructor, plus a logbook endorsement.

61.57.gist: Recency to carry passengers: three takeoffs and three landings in the preceding 90 days as sole manipulator in the same category, class and type; at night (1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise) they must be to a full stop, made in that window.
61.57.why: The examiner's favourite currency question, and the rule you will actually apply every month.

numbers.value: 3 takeoffs and 3 landings in the preceding 90 days
numbers.quote: at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days

numbers.value: Night window: 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
numbers.quote: beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise

numbers.value: Night: three full-stop landings in that window
numbers.quote: three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop

traps: Night currency uses the sunset/sunrise window, not Part 1's civil-twilight definition of night (§ 1.1) and not the position-light rule (§ 91.209).
Currency is only about carrying passengers: you may fly alone to regain it (§ 61.57(a)(2)).

questions.q: Can I take a friend up tonight?
questions.a: Only if you have made three takeoffs and three full-stop landings between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise in the preceding 90 days, in the same category and class.

questions.q: My last landing was 95 days ago. Can I fly?
questions.a: Alone, yes; with passengers, not until you have made three takeoffs and landings (§ 61.57(a)).

61.103.gist: Eligibility for the private pilot certificate: at least 17 (16 for glider or balloon); read, speak, write and understand English; a logbook endorsement for the knowledge test, then pass it; flight training and an endorsement for the practical test; the aeronautical experience of § 61.109; pass the practical test; and hold a student, sport or recreational pilot certificate.
61.103.why: The examiner checks these items against your logbook and application before the checkride can even start.

numbers.quote: Be at least 17 years of age for a rating in other than a glider or balloon
Be at least 16 years of age for a rating in a glider or balloon

traps: The knowledge-test endorsement and the practical-test endorsement are two separate endorsements from an authorized instructor.
You may take the knowledge test before you are 17; the age limit applies to the certificate itself.

questions.q: What are the eligibility requirements for a private pilot certificate?
questions.a: Be 17 (16 for glider or balloon), be proficient in English, receive the ground and flight training endorsements, pass the knowledge and practical tests, meet the § 61.109 experience, and hold a student, sport or recreational certificate.

61.109.gist: The hours for the airplane single-engine private certificate: at least 40 total, including 20 of flight training and 10 solo. The training must include 3 hours cross-country, 3 hours at night with a cross-country over 100 nm and 10 full-stop takeoffs and landings, 3 hours by reference to instruments, and 3 hours of checkride preparation within the preceding 2 calendar months. The solo time must include 5 hours cross-country, one 150 nm cross-country with full-stop landings at three points and one leg over 50 nm, and three full-stop takeoffs and landings at a towered airport. Simulators may credit 2.5 hours, and an approved Part 142 course needs only 35 hours.
61.109.why: This is the checklist your instructor and the examiner tick off in your logbook; every number on it is a knowledge-test question.

numbers.quote: at least 40 hours of flight time that includes at least 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor and 10 hours of solo flight training
One cross-country flight of over 100 nautical miles total distance
10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop

numbers.value: 3 hours of test preparation within 2 calendar months
numbers.quote: within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test
5 hours of solo cross-country time

numbers.value: 150 nm solo cross-country, three points, one leg over 50 nm
numbers.quote: One solo cross country flight of 150 nautical miles total distance, with full-stop landings at three points, and one segment of the flight consisting of a straight-line distance of more than 50 nautical miles

numbers.value: Three full-stop landings at a towered airport
numbers.quote: Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport with an operating control tower
a maximum of 2.5 hours of training in a full flight simulator or flight training device
need only have a total of 35 hours of aeronautical experience

traps: The 150 nm solo cross-country needs full-stop landings at three points and one straight-line leg of more than 50 nm; a 150 nm out-and-back with one stop does not count.
The 3 hours of checkride preparation are counted in calendar months, so training on the first of the month may age out sooner than you expect.
The night cross-country must be over 100 nm total distance, and it is dual, not solo.

questions.q: What are the minimum hours for a private pilot airplane single-engine?
questions.a: 40 total with 20 dual and 10 solo, including 3 cross-country dual, 3 night dual (100 nm cross-country and 10 full-stop landings), 3 instrument, 3 of test prep in the preceding 2 calendar months, 5 solo cross-country including the 150 nm flight, and three full-stop landings at a towered airport.

mnemonics: Threes and tens: 3 XC, 3 night, 3 instrument, 3 prep; 10 solo, 10 night landings.

61.113.gist: What a private pilot may not do: act as PIC for compensation or hire, or carry passengers or property for hire — with listed exceptions: flights incidental to a business, sharing pro rata expenses with passengers, charity events under § 91.146, search and location, and flying under BasicMed within the paragraph (i) limits.
61.113.why: Every cost-sharing scenario on the oral comes back to paragraph (c), and the BasicMed limits are numbers you must know.

numbers.value: Pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees only
numbers.quote: pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees

numbers.value: BasicMed aircraft: at most 7 seats, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers
numbers.quote: not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers
more than 18,000 feet above mean sea level
exceeding 250 knots

traps: Pro rata means you pay at least your own equal share; you may never pay less, and only fuel, oil, airport expenditures and rental fees may be shared.
A logbook hour you did not pay for can itself be “compensation”; when in doubt, treat it as compensation.

questions.q: Can my passengers chip in for the flight?
questions.a: Yes, but only their pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees, and you must pay at least your own share (§ 61.113(c)).

68.3.gist: What the BasicMed medical education course must cover (self-assessment, warning signs, medications, the prohibition on flying with a medical deficiency, the physician checklist) and what it produces: a certificate of completion you keep in your logbook, a driver-record release, and the signed statement acknowledging § 61.53.
68.3.why: If you plan to fly under BasicMed, the examiner will ask what documents prove it; this section names them.

numbers.value: Course certificate kept in the logbook
numbers.quote: A certification of completion of the medical education course, which shall be retained in the individual's logbook and made available upon request

traps: The course is retaken every 24 calendar months and the physician exam every 48 months; the two clocks run separately.

questions.q: What must I carry or keep to show I am flying under BasicMed?
questions.a: The course completion certificate stays in your logbook and must be shown on request; the physician-signed checklist is kept too. You also need a U.S. driver's license and must have held a medical after July 14, 2006.

91.3.gist: The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft; in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action the PIC may deviate from any Part 91 rule to the extent the emergency requires, and must send a written report only if the Administrator asks for one.
91.3.why: Every emergency scenario on the oral ends here: you decide, you deviate as far as needed, and you report only on request.
traps: The written report is on request only — nothing is filed automatically.
Deviation authority is limited to what the emergency requires, not a blanket licence.

questions.q: May I break a rule in an emergency?
questions.a: Yes — any rule of Part 91, to the extent the emergency requires immediate action; a written report is due only if the FAA requests it.

91.7.gist: Two sentences that carry a lot of weight: no one may operate a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy, and the PIC is responsible for deciding whether it is in condition for safe flight and must discontinue the flight when an unairworthy condition occurs.
91.7.why: The preflight inspection and every inoperative-equipment question come back to this rule: the decision is yours, not the mechanic's.

numbers.value: PIC decides whether the aircraft is safe for flight
numbers.quote: The pilot in command of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight

traps: Airworthy has two parts: conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation. A fresh annual does not settle the second part today.

questions.q: Who decides whether the airplane is airworthy before a flight?
questions.a: The pilot in command, under § 91.7(b), and the PIC must discontinue the flight if an unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural condition occurs.

91.9.gist: Fly within the operating limitations in the approved flight manual, markings and placards, and carry a current approved flight manual (or the approved manual material, markings and placards for older aircraft) in the aircraft. The aircraft must also be identified under Part 45.
91.9.why: It is why the POH lives in the airplane and why a missing placard is an airworthiness issue.

numbers.value: Current approved flight manual on board
numbers.quote: unless there is available in the aircraft a current, approved Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual

traps: The flight manual must be the one approved for that aircraft by serial number, not a generic copy for the type.

questions.q: Does the POH have to be in the airplane?
questions.a: Yes. § 91.9(b) requires a current, approved flight manual (or the approved manual material, markings and placards) to be available in the aircraft.

91.17.gist: No crewmember within 8 hours of drinking, while under the influence, with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater, or while using any drug that affects safety; and, except in an emergency, no carrying a passenger who appears intoxicated.
91.17.why: The 8-hour and 0.04 figures are asked on the written, and the passenger rule surprises people on the oral.

numbers.quote: Within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage
alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater

traps: 8 hours is the regulatory floor; “under the influence” applies at any hour, and the AIM recommends more (AIM 8-1-1).

questions.q: How long after drinking may I fly?
questions.a: At least 8 hours, and never while still under the influence or at 0.04 or more.

91.19.gist: No one may operate a civil aircraft in the United States knowing that narcotic drugs, marijuana or depressant or stimulant drugs are on board, unless the carriage is authorized by law.
91.19.why: It pairs with § 61.15: a violation is grounds for losing your certificate, and 'I did not know' is the only defense the text allows.

numbers.quote: with knowledge that narcotic drugs, marihuana, and depressant or stimulant drugs or substances as defined in Federal or State statutes are carried in the aircraft

traps: State legalization does not help: the rule looks to Federal or State statutes and a violation still reaches your certificate under § 61.15(b).

questions.q: A passenger wants to bring marijuana that is legal in our state. Can I fly them?
questions.a: No. § 91.19 prohibits operating with knowledge that marijuana is aboard unless authorized by statute, and § 61.15(b) makes a violation grounds for suspension or revocation.

91.21.gist: Portable electronic devices may not be operated on air-carrier aircraft or on any aircraft under IFR, except voice recorders, hearing aids, pacemakers, electric shavers, and any device the operator has determined will not interfere with navigation or communication. For other aircraft that determination can be made by the PIC.
91.21.why: It answers whether your tablet or phone is legal in the cockpit: on a VFR flight the PIC decides.

numbers.value: The rule applies to IFR flights and air carriers
numbers.quote: Any other aircraft while it is operated under IFR

numbers.value: PIC makes the interference determination for other aircraft
numbers.quote: the determination may be made by the pilot in command or other operator of the aircraft

questions.q: Can I use my phone or tablet in the airplane?
questions.a: On a VFR Part 91 flight § 91.21 does not restrict you at all. Under IFR the device must be one of the exceptions or one the PIC has determined will not interfere with the aircraft's navigation or communication systems.

91.103.gist: Before every flight the PIC must become familiar with all available information: for flights away from the airport or under IFR, weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives and any known ATC delays; for every flight, runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data.
91.103.why: This is the regulatory backbone of the whole cross-country planning Task, and the phrase “all available information” is what the FAA enforces.
traps: The list is a minimum; the opening sentence makes everything relevant to the flight your responsibility.

questions.q: What must I check before a cross-country?
questions.a: Weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives, known ATC delays, runway lengths and takeoff/landing performance — all available information.

mnemonics: NWKRAFT: NOTAMs, Weather, Known ATC delays, Runway lengths, Alternates, Fuel, Takeoff and landing distances.

91.105.gist: Required flight crewmembers stay at their station during takeoff, landing and en route with the safety belt fastened, and keep the shoulder harness fastened for takeoff and landing if the seat has one and it does not prevent them doing their duties.
91.105.why: The examiner will note whether you put your own shoulder harness on before takeoff; § 91.107 covers the passengers, this section covers you.

numbers.quote: Keep the safety belt fastened while at the crewmember station

numbers.value: Shoulder harness for takeoff and landing
numbers.quote: during takeoff and landing, keep his or her shoulder harness fastened

questions.q: When must the pilot wear the shoulder harness?
questions.a: During takeoff and landing, if the seat has one and it does not interfere with required duties; the safety belt stays fastened the whole time at the station.

91.107.gist: The PIC must brief everyone on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and shoulder harness, notify them to fasten before surface movement, takeoff and landing, and everyone must occupy an approved seat with the belt fastened at those times; a child under two may be held.
91.107.why: Passenger briefing is a Flight Deck Management element and the first thing the examiner watches you do.

numbers.quote: has not reached his or her second birthday

questions.q: When must seat belts be fastened?
questions.a: During movement on the surface, takeoff and landing; the PIC must brief on their use and then notify passengers to fasten them.

91.113.gist: See and avoid always applies. Converging: the aircraft on the right has the right of way, but balloons, gliders, airships and aircraft towing or refueling rank above powered aircraft; head-on, both alter course right; the overtaken aircraft has the right of way; aircraft landing or on final have it over others, and the lower of two approaching aircraft — but neither may abuse it.
91.113.why: Right-of-way scenarios are guaranteed on the written and come up in every traffic-pattern discussion.
traps: An aircraft in distress has the right of way over everything (§ 91.113(c)).
The lower aircraft on approach has the right of way but may not cut in front of one on final or overtake it.

questions.q: Two airplanes converge at the same altitude. Who yields?
questions.a: The one that sees the other on its right yields: the aircraft to the other's right has the right of way.

questions.q: An aircraft is overtaking me. Who moves?
questions.a: The overtaking aircraft alters course to the right and passes well clear; the aircraft being overtaken has the right of way.

mnemonics: Ranking, least maneuverable first: Balloon, Glider, Airship, Towing or refueling, then powered aircraft.

91.115.gist: Right-of-way on the water: keep clear of vessels and do not impede them. On crossing courses the craft to the other's right has the right-of-way, head-on both alter course to the right, and the craft being overtaken has the right-of-way.
91.115.why: Seaplane pilots live by it; for everyone else it is the knowledge-test companion to § 91.113 with one twist, the vessel rules.

numbers.value: Crossing: the one on the right has the right-of-way
numbers.quote: the aircraft or vessel to the other's right has the right-of-way

questions.q: On the water, who gives way when a seaplane and a boat are converging?
questions.a: The one that has the other on its right has the right-of-way; the other gives way. Head-on, both turn right, and anything being overtaken has the right-of-way.

91.117.gist: Speed limits: 250 knots indicated below 10,000 ft MSL; 200 knots at or below 2,500 ft AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of a Class C or D area; 200 knots beneath a Class B area or in a VFR corridor through it.
91.117.why: Three numbers, three places; the written asks all of them.

numbers.quote: below 10,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots

numbers.value: Class C/D: 200 knots within 4 NM, at or below 2,500 ft AGL
numbers.quote: at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots

numbers.value: Under Class B or in a VFR corridor: 200 knots
numbers.quote: at an indicated airspeed of more than 200 knots

questions.q: What is the speed limit under a Class B shelf?
questions.a: 200 knots indicated.

91.119.gist: Minimum safe altitudes: always high enough to make an emergency landing without undue hazard if the engine fails; over congested areas 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a 2,000 ft radius; elsewhere 500 ft above the surface, or over open water and sparsely populated areas no closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure.
91.119.why: Three altitudes, three situations; the written asks them and the examiner asks which applies to your ground-reference maneuvers.

numbers.value: Congested area: 1,000 ft above obstacles within 2,000 ft
numbers.quote: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet
500 feet above the surface

numbers.value: Open water or sparse: 500 ft from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure
numbers.quote: closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure

traps: “Except when necessary for takeoff or landing” is the only blanket exception.
The engine-failure rule in paragraph (a) applies everywhere, on top of the numbers.

questions.q: How low may I fly over a town?
questions.a: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius — and never below an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard.

91.121.gist: What to set in the altimeter: below 18,000 ft MSL, the current reported setting of a station along the route within 100 nm, or an appropriate available station, or without a radio the departure airport elevation; at or above 18,000 ft MSL, 29.92. The tables give the lowest usable flight level for low pressure.
91.121.why: It is the regulation behind the altimeter-setting question in every cross-country oral and the 29.92 rule at Class A.

numbers.quote: within 100 nautical miles of the aircraft
At or above 18,000 feet MSL

traps: Without a radio you set field elevation before departure; you do not guess a setting in flight.

questions.q: Where do I get my altimeter setting on a cross-country?
questions.a: From a station along the route within 100 nm of the aircraft; if there is none, from an appropriate available station. At or above 18,000 ft MSL everyone sets 29.92.

91.123.gist: Once you have a clearance you may not deviate from it unless you get an amended clearance, an emergency exists, or you are responding to a TCAS resolution advisory. Except in an emergency, you may not operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised. If you deviate you must notify ATC as soon as possible, and if ATC gave you priority in an emergency you must file a detailed report within 48 hours if asked. Never act on a clearance issued to another aircraft.
91.123.why: It is the rule the examiner cites when asking what you do if you cannot comply with a clearance, and the source of the 48-hour report.

numbers.value: Tell ATC of any deviation as soon as possible
numbers.quote: shall notify ATC of that deviation as soon as possible

numbers.value: Report within 48 hours if ATC asks
numbers.quote: shall submit a detailed report of that emergency within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility, if requested by ATC

traps: The 48-hour report is only when requested by ATC; the notification of the deviation itself is always required, as soon as possible.
Reading back a clearance is not accepting it blindly: if you cannot comply safely, say 'unable' and get an amended clearance.

questions.q: Tower tells me to extend downwind into a cloud. What do I do?
questions.a: You may not enter the cloud under VFR, so tell the controller 'unable' and request an amended instruction. § 91.123(b) allows deviation from an instruction only in an emergency, so ask first rather than deviate.

questions.q: When must I file a written report after an emergency?
questions.a: Under § 91.123(d), within 48 hours to the ATC facility manager, if ATC requests it because you were given priority. Under § 91.3(c) the Administrator may also request a report after a rule deviation.

91.125.gist: The light-gun signals are the regulation, not just an AIM table. The section is a single sentence pointing to its table: steady green, flashing green, steady red, flashing red, flashing white, and alternating red and green each have a fixed meaning on the ground and in flight.
91.125.why: The examiner will ask you the signals from memory, and a radio failure in the pattern is when you will need them.
traps: The same color means different things on the ground and in the air: steady red on the ground is stop, in flight it is give way and continue circling.
Flashing white applies only on the ground (return to starting point); there is no in-flight meaning.

questions.q: What does a flashing red light from the tower mean in flight?
questions.a: Airport unsafe, do not land. On the ground it means taxi clear of the runway in use.

questions.q: How do I acknowledge a light signal?
questions.a: By day, rock the wings in flight or move the ailerons or rudder on the ground; at night, blink the landing or navigation lights.

mnemonics: Green means go, red means no, white means home, red-and-green means careful.

91.126.gist: Operating at an airport in Class G airspace: approaching to land, powered fixed-wing aircraft make all turns to the left unless the airport shows light signals or markings for right traffic, and other aircraft avoid that flow. If the airport has an operating tower, keep two-way radio communications with it, established before 4 nm out and up to 2,500 ft AGL.
91.126.why: It is the legal basis for the standard left-hand traffic pattern, and § 91.127 imports it into Class E.

numbers.quote: must make all turns to the left unless the airport displays approved light signals or visual markings indicating that turns should be made to the right

numbers.value: Tower contact before 4 nm and up to 2,500 ft AGL
numbers.quote: Communications must be established prior to 4 nautical miles from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL

traps: Right traffic is shown by the segmented-circle indicators or light signals at the airport; it is not something the CTAF chatter decides.

questions.q: Which way do I turn in the pattern at a non-towered airport?
questions.a: Left, unless the airport displays approved visual markings or light signals for right traffic; look at the segmented circle and the Chart Supplement.

91.127.gist: Operating at an airport in Class E airspace: follow the § 91.126 rules (left traffic unless indicated) and any Part 93 traffic pattern, and if the airport has an operating tower keep two-way radio communications from 4 nm and 2,500 ft AGL inward.
91.127.why: Most non-towered airports you will use sit under Class E, so this is the section that actually applies to your pattern work.

numbers.value: Tower contact before 4 nm and up to 2,500 ft AGL
numbers.quote: Communications must be established prior to 4 nautical miles from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL

questions.q: Do the Class G pattern rules apply at my Class E airport?
questions.a: Yes. § 91.127(a) requires compliance with § 91.126 at an airport in Class E airspace, so left traffic applies unless right traffic is indicated.

91.129.gist: Class D: establish two-way radio communications with the tower before entering and maintain them inside; a clearance is required to taxi, take off or land at a towered airport; if the radio fails in flight under VFR you may land with basic VFR weather, visual contact with the tower and a light-signal clearance.
91.129.why: Every towered-airport question comes back to “communications established” and “clearance received”.

numbers.value: Two-way communications before entry, maintained inside
numbers.quote: prior to entering that airspace and thereafter maintain those communications while within that airspace

numbers.value: Clearance to use a runway or taxiway
numbers.quote: unless an appropriate clearance is received from ATC

traps: “Established” means the controller answered using your call sign; “aircraft calling, standby” is not established (AIM 3-2-5).

questions.q: What do I need to enter Class D?
questions.a: Two-way radio communications established with the tower before entry — they must use your call sign — and maintained inside.

91.130.gist: Class C adds to the Class D rules: two-way radio communications must be established with the facility providing ATC services before entry and maintained inside, and the aircraft must have a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out.
91.130.why: The equipment difference between Class C and D is a standard written question.

numbers.value: Two-way communications before entry, maintained inside
numbers.quote: prior to entering that airspace and thereafter maintain those communications while within that airspace
equipped with the applicable equipment specified in § 91.215, and after January 1, 2020, § 91.225

questions.q: What does Class C require that Class D does not?
questions.a: A Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out; both require two-way communications established before entry.

91.131.gist: Class B: an ATC clearance is required before entry; the PIC must hold at least a private pilot certificate (or be a student, recreational or sport pilot with the required training and endorsement, except at the airports listed in appendix D section 4); the aircraft needs a two-way radio, a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out.
91.131.why: “Cleared into the Class Bravo” is the phrase the examiner wants; the student-pilot exception is a favourite written question.

numbers.quote: must receive an ATC clearance

numbers.value: At least a private pilot certificate (or an endorsed student)
numbers.quote: holds at least a private pilot certificate

questions.q: Can a student pilot fly into Class B?
questions.a: Only with the § 61.95 training and endorsement for that specific Class B, and never at the appendix D section 4 airports.

91.133.gist: You may not fly in a restricted area contrary to its restrictions, or in a prohibited area at all, without the permission of the using or controlling agency.
91.133.why: It is the one-line rule behind the sectional's blue-hatched areas; the AIM explains how to find out whether a restricted area is active.

numbers.value: Permission comes from the using or controlling agency
numbers.quote: unless that person has the permission of the using or controlling agency, as appropriate

traps: A restricted area that is not active may be flown through, but only the controlling agency or FSS can tell you it is cold; the chart's published times are a starting point, not permission.

questions.q: Can I fly through a restricted area?
questions.a: Only when it is not active or with permission of the using or controlling agency; contact the controlling agency listed on the chart. Prohibited areas are closed regardless.

91.135.gist: Class A airspace (18,000 ft MSL to FL600) is IFR only: an ATC clearance before entry, two-way radio with ATC, and a transponder and ADS-B Out. Deviations are possible only by ATC authorization.
91.135.why: It is why VFR cruising altitudes stop at 17,500 and why a VFR-only pilot never enters Class A.

numbers.quote: must conduct that operation under instrument flight rules (IFR)
Operations may be conducted only under an ATC clearance received prior to entering the airspace

questions.q: Can I fly VFR at 18,500 ft on a clear day?
questions.a: No. Class A begins at 18,000 ft MSL and § 91.135 requires IFR with an ATC clearance there.

91.137.gist: Temporary flight restrictions for disasters and hazards. A NOTAM designates the area for one of three reasons: protect people from a surface hazard, provide a safe environment for relief aircraft, or prevent sightseeing congestion over an event. Who may enter depends on which paragraph the NOTAM cites; for a sightseeing TFR, flights to or from an airport inside the area and IFR flights may continue.
91.137.why: TFRs are the number-one way a well-meaning student violates airspace; this section tells you what each type permits.

numbers.value: (a)(1): protect persons and property from a surface hazard
numbers.quote: Protect persons and property on the surface or in the air from a hazard associated with an incident on the surface
Prevent an unsafe congestion of sightseeing and other aircraft above an incident or event which may generate a high degree of public interest

traps: Under an (a)(1) hazard TFR only aircraft participating in the relief effort under the on-scene official may enter; the exceptions for IFR or transiting flights apply to (a)(2) and (a)(3) only.

questions.q: A wildfire TFR sits between me and my destination airport, which is inside it. Can I land there?
questions.a: Depends on the NOTAM's paragraph. Under (a)(2) or (a)(3) an operation directly to or from an airport within the area is allowed with notification to the facility named in the NOTAM; under (a)(1) it is not.

91.141.gist: No flight over or near an area the President, Vice President or other public figures are visiting, contrary to the restrictions the FAA publishes by NOTAM.
91.141.why: Presidential TFRs are large, move with the schedule, and are enforced; the NOTAM is the only place their shape is published.

numbers.quote: the President, the Vice President, or other public figures contrary to the restrictions established by the Administrator and published in a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM)

questions.q: How do I find out about a VIP TFR?
questions.a: Check the FDC NOTAMs in your briefing; § 91.141 restrictions exist only as published NOTAMs, so no briefing means no way to know.

91.145.gist: TFRs for aerial demonstrations and major sporting events (airshows, the Super Bowl, the Indy 500 and similar). The FAA publishes a NOTAM at least 30 days ahead when it can; the restricted airspace is normally limited to a 3 nm radius for sporting events, and no one may operate inside it except as the NOTAM allows or with ATC or waiver authorization.
91.145.why: Stadium and airshow TFRs are the ones most likely to sit on top of a training airport on a weekend.

numbers.value: NOTAM at least 30 days in advance
numbers.quote: will be issued at least 30 days in advance of an aerial demonstration or a major sporting event
The restricted airspace will normally be limited to a 3 nautical mile

questions.q: Is there a TFR over a big game even if the stadium is not on the chart?
questions.a: Yes when the FAA issues one under § 91.145; it is published by NOTAM, normally about a 3 nm radius, so check the TFR list in your briefing.

91.151.gist: Day VFR: enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then for at least 30 minutes at normal cruise; at night, at least 45 minutes.
91.151.why: Two numbers the written asks directly and the examiner applies to your flight plan.

numbers.quote: at least 30 minutes
at least 45 minutes

traps: These are the legal minimums to begin the flight, computed considering wind and forecast weather; personal reserves should be larger.

questions.q: How much fuel must I have for a VFR flight?
questions.a: Enough to reach the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes at normal cruise by day, 45 minutes at night.

91.153.gist: What a VFR flight plan must contain: aircraft identification, type, PIC name and address, departure point and time, route, cruising altitude and true airspeed, first intended landing point and ETE, fuel on board in hours, persons aboard, and anything else ATC needs. Once activated, you must notify an FSS or ATC when you cancel or complete the flight.
91.153.why: It is the regulation behind closing your flight plan; the AIM adds that search and rescue starts 30 minutes after your ETA.

numbers.quote: The amount of fuel on board (in hours)
upon canceling or completing the flight under the flight plan, shall notify an FAA Flight Service Station or ATC facility

traps: The tower does not close your VFR flight plan for you; landing at a towered airport does not satisfy paragraph (b).

questions.q: Who closes my VFR flight plan?
questions.a: You do, with Flight Service or any ATC facility that can relay it, as soon as you land or cancel; if you do not, search and rescue begins half an hour after your ETA.

91.155.gist: Basic VFR weather minimums by airspace: 3 statute miles and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds in Classes C, D and E below 10,000 ft; Class B is 3 miles clear of clouds; Class G by day below 1,200 ft AGL is 1 mile clear of clouds; at or above 10,000 ft MSL it is 5 miles and 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 mile horizontal. Plus: no VFR beneath a ceiling below 1,000 ft in a surface area, and 3 miles ground visibility to take off, land or enter the pattern there.
91.155.why: The table is the single most-tested piece of the FAR on the private written, and paragraphs (c) and (d) are the oral's follow-up.

numbers.value: 3 SM in Classes B, C, D and E below 10,000 ft
numbers.quote: 3 statute miles
2,000 feet horizontal

numbers.value: 5 SM at or above 10,000 ft MSL
numbers.quote: 5 statute miles

numbers.value: At or above 10,000 ft MSL: 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
numbers.quote: 1 statute mile horizontal

numbers.value: Surface area: ceiling at least 1,000 ft
numbers.quote: when the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet

numbers.value: Surface area: 3 SM ground visibility to take off, land or enter the pattern
numbers.quote: ground visibility at that airport is at least 3 statute miles

traps: Class G at night below 1,200 ft AGL jumps to 3 miles and 500/1,000/2,000 — night Class G is treated like Class E.
“Clear of clouds” in Class B is not a distance: you may not enter them.

questions.q: What are the VFR minimums in Class E below 10,000 feet?
questions.a: 3 statute miles visibility; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontal from clouds.

questions.q: The ceiling is 800 feet at a Class D airport. Can I fly VFR there?
questions.a: Not beneath the ceiling within the surface area — it must be at least 1,000 feet — unless you obtain a special VFR clearance.

mnemonics: 3-152: 3 miles, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal — the everyday minimums.

91.157.gist: Special VFR lets you operate in a surface area below basic VFR minimums with an ATC clearance, clear of clouds, with at least 1 statute mile flight visibility (and 1 mile ground visibility to take off or land); between sunrise and sunset unless you are instrument rated and the aircraft is equipped for IFR.
91.157.why: The examiner's follow-up to any weather-minimums question, and the way home when the field goes below basic VFR.

numbers.quote: flight visibility is at least 1 statute mile

numbers.value: 1 SM ground visibility to take off or land
numbers.quote: ground visibility is at least 1 statute mile

numbers.value: Only below 10,000 ft MSL within the surface area
numbers.quote: below 10,000 feet MSL

traps: You must ask for it — ATC will not offer special VFR.
Some Class B and C surface areas prohibit fixed-wing special VFR (Part 91 appendix D, section 3).

questions.q: Visibility is 2 miles at my Class D airport. Can I depart VFR?
questions.a: Only with a special VFR clearance: at least 1 mile visibility, clear of clouds, and by day unless you are instrument rated and equipped.

91.159.gist: VFR cruising altitudes apply in level flight more than 3,000 ft above the surface: on a magnetic course of 0° through 179° fly an odd thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 ft; on 180° through 359° fly an even thousand plus 500 ft.
91.159.why: Asked on every written; applied on every cross-country.

numbers.quote: more than 3,000 feet above the surface
any odd thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet
any even thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet

traps: Magnetic course, not heading — a wind-correction angle does not change your altitude.
Below 3,000 ft AGL the rule does not apply at all.

questions.q: I am on a course of 090 at cruise. What altitudes are legal?
questions.a: Odd thousands plus 500 — 3,500, 5,500, 7,500 — once you are more than 3,000 feet above the surface.

mnemonics: East is odd.

91.203.gist: The paperwork that must be in the airplane: an appropriate and current airworthiness certificate, displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance where it is legible, and an effective U.S. registration certificate (or the temporary alternatives the section lists). A fuel tank in the cabin needs a Form 337 aboard.
91.203.why: It is the A and R of the ARROW checklist; § 91.9 supplies the O (operating limitations) and Part 23 or the POH the W (weight and balance).

numbers.quote: An appropriate and current airworthiness certificate

numbers.value: Displayed and legible at the entrance
numbers.quote: displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so that it is legible to passengers or crew

traps: The registration expires; check the expiration date on the certificate, not just that it exists.
A photocopy of the airworthiness certificate does not satisfy the display requirement.

questions.q: What documents must be aboard the airplane?
questions.a: Airworthiness certificate (displayed), registration, the operating limitations of § 91.9, and weight and balance data; remember ARROW.

mnemonics: ARROW: Airworthiness, Registration, Radio license (international only), Operating limitations, Weight and balance.

91.205.gist: The instruments and equipment that must be installed and operable: paragraph (b) for day VFR (airspeed, altimeter, compass, tachometer, oil pressure and temperature gauges, fuel gauges, gear indicator, belts and harnesses, ELT and more), paragraph (c) adds for night VFR position lights, an anticollision light system, an adequate electrical source, spare fuses and a landing light if for hire; paragraph (d) is the IFR list. Anything inoperative goes through § 91.213.
91.205.why: The examiner will hand you a scenario with something broken and ask whether the flight is legal; this list is the answer key.

numbers.value: Night: spare fuses — one set, or three of each kind
numbers.quote: One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required

numbers.value: Safety belt for every occupant 2 or older
numbers.quote: each occupant 2 years of age or older

questions.q: What extra equipment does night VFR require?
questions.a: Position lights, an anticollision light system, an adequate source of electrical energy, spare fuses, and a landing light if the flight is for hire.

mnemonics: ATOMATOFLAMES for day and FLAPS for night are the classic memory aids; the rule's list is what counts.

91.207.gist: Most U.S. airplanes must carry an operable automatic ELT; batteries are replaced after more than 1 cumulative hour of use or at 50 percent of their useful life, the ELT is inspected within 12 calendar months, and exemptions include training flights within 50 NM of the departure airport and up to 90 days with the ELT removed for repair.
91.207.why: Four numbers the written and the oral both like, and a real preflight item.

numbers.value: Battery: more than 1 cumulative hour of use
numbers.quote: more than 1 cumulative hour
50 percent of their useful life
within 12 calendar months after the last inspection
50-nautical mile radius

numbers.value: Removed for repair: at most 90 days
numbers.quote: more than 90 days after the ELT is initially removed

questions.q: When must the ELT battery be replaced?
questions.a: After more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired.

91.209.gist: From sunset to sunrise an aircraft must show lighted position lights, and an aircraft equipped with anticollision lights must have them on at all times unless the PIC decides safety requires them off.
91.209.why: This is one of the three “nights” — a classic oral question that trips people who only know the currency rule.

numbers.quote: from sunset to sunrise

traps: Three different nights: position lights from sunset to sunrise (here), logging night time from the end of evening civil twilight (§ 1.1), and night passenger currency from 1 hour after sunset (§ 61.57(b)).

questions.q: When do I need position lights on?
questions.a: From sunset to sunrise.

91.211.gist: Supplemental oxygen by cabin pressure altitude: the required crew must use it above 12,500 ft MSL for any part of the flight over 30 minutes, at all times above 14,000 ft, and every occupant must be provided with it above 15,000 ft.
91.211.why: Three altitudes the written asks and the examiner connects to hypoxia.

numbers.quote: above 12,500 feet (MSL) up to and including 14,000 feet (MSL)
more than 30 minutes duration

numbers.value: Above 14,000 ft: crew at all times
numbers.quote: above 14,000 feet (MSL)

numbers.value: Above 15,000 ft: every occupant provided with oxygen
numbers.quote: above 15,000 feet (MSL)

questions.q: When must I use oxygen?
questions.a: As required crew: above 12,500 ft MSL after 30 minutes and at all times above 14,000; above 15,000 every occupant must be provided with it.

91.213.gist: Flying with inoperative equipment: without an MEL, a small non-turbine airplane may fly if the item is not required by the day-VFR type certification list, the aircraft's equipment list or KOEL, § 91.205 or any other rule for that kind of flight, or an AD; it is removed, or deactivated and placarded “Inoperative”, with maintenance recorded; and a pilot or mechanic determines it is no hazard.
91.213.why: The airworthiness scenario on every checkride: something is broken — can you go?
traps: A placard alone is not enough — the item must also be removed or deactivated, and deactivation that is maintenance must be recorded under Part 43.
If the item is required for the kind of flight you intend (night, IFR), you stay on the ground or get a special flight permit (§ 91.213(e)).

questions.q: The fuel gauge for one tank is dead. Can I fly?
questions.a: No — a fuel gauge for each tank is required by § 91.205(b), so it must be repaired or the flight needs a special flight permit.

questions.q: What must happen before I fly with a broken item under § 91.213(d)?
questions.a: Confirm it is not required, remove or deactivate it, placard it Inoperative, record the maintenance, and have a pilot or mechanic determine it is no hazard.

91.215.gist: A Mode C transponder is required in Class A, B and C airspace, within the 30 NM Mode C veil of Class B primary airports from the surface to 10,000 ft, above Class B and C to 10,000 ft, and at and above 10,000 ft MSL except within 2,500 ft of the surface; when installed and operable it must be on and replying in all controlled airspace. ADS-B Out (§ 91.225) covers the same footprint.
91.215.why: The Mode C veil and the 10,000-foot rule are exam staples; the examiner also asks where your transponder must be on.

numbers.value: Mode C veil: 30 NM, surface to 10,000 ft MSL
numbers.quote: within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in appendix D, section 1 of this part from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL

numbers.value: At and above 10,000 ft MSL, except within 2,500 ft of the surface
numbers.quote: at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface

numbers.value: Deviation for no transponder: request 1 hour ahead
numbers.quote: at least one hour before the proposed operation

questions.q: Where do I need a Mode C transponder?
questions.a: Class A, B and C; the 30 NM Mode C veil below 10,000 ft; above Class B and C to 10,000 ft; and at or above 10,000 ft MSL outside 2,500 ft AGL — ADS-B Out has the same footprint under § 91.225.

91.225.gist: Where ADS-B Out is required: Class A; Class B and C; within 30 nm of the Appendix D airports (the Mode C veil) from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL; above the ceiling of Class B or C up to 10,000 ft; Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL except at or below 2,500 ft AGL; and over the Gulf at and above 3,000 ft MSL out to 12 nm. Aircraft without an engine-driven electrical system are exempt from some of it. Equipped aircraft transmit at all times; an unequipped aircraft must request an ATC deviation at least an hour ahead.
91.225.why: The airspace list is identical to the § 91.215 transponder list, and the examiner will ask how you would get into Class C without ADS-B.

numbers.quote: Class B and Class C airspace areas

numbers.value: Mode C veil: 30 nm, surface to 10,000 ft MSL
numbers.quote: within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in appendix D, section 1 to this part from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL

numbers.value: Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL, except at or below 2,500 ft AGL
numbers.quote: at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface

numbers.value: Unequipped: request a deviation 1 hour ahead
numbers.quote: the request must be made at least 1 hour before the proposed operation

traps: Class D airspace is not on the list; you can fly into a Class D airport without ADS-B unless it sits inside a Mode C veil.
Below the floor of a Class B shelf you are still inside the 30 nm veil if the primary airport is in Appendix D.

questions.q: Where do I need ADS-B Out?
questions.a: Everywhere a transponder is required: Class A, B and C, within the 30 nm Mode C veil, above B or C to 10,000 ft, Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL (except within 2,500 ft of the ground), and the Gulf of Mexico above 3,000 ft MSL.

91.403.gist: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy, including compliance with airworthiness directives (Part 39), and maintenance may only be done as Part 43 and this subpart prescribe.
91.403.why: It is where the examiner's 'who is responsible for ADs?' question comes from: the owner or operator, and as PIC you confirm it before flight.

numbers.value: Owner or operator is primarily responsible, including ADs
numbers.quote: The owner or operator of an aircraft is primarily responsible for maintaining that aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with part 39 of this chapter

questions.q: Who is responsible for complying with airworthiness directives?
questions.a: The owner or operator under § 91.403(a). The PIC is still responsible under § 91.7 for determining the aircraft is safe for flight, which includes checking that ADs are complied with.

91.405.gist: Owner and operator duties: have the required inspections done and discrepancies repaired between them, make sure maintenance personnel record the return to service, have inoperative equipment permitted by § 91.213(d) repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection, and make sure inoperative instruments and equipment are placarded.
91.405.why: It closes the loop on § 91.213: inoperative equipment does not get to stay inoperative forever.

numbers.quote: shall ensure that a placard has been installed as required by § 43.11 of this chapter

questions.q: How long can an inoperative instrument stay deferred under § 91.213(d)?
questions.a: Until the next required inspection: § 91.405(c) requires it to be repaired, replaced, removed or inspected then, and it must be placarded meanwhile.

91.407.gist: After maintenance the aircraft may not be operated until it is approved for return to service by an authorized person and the record entry is made. If the work may have appreciably changed the flight characteristics, no one other than crew may be carried until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies it and logs a satisfactory operational check, unless ground tests prove the check unnecessary.
91.407.why: It is the reason a private pilot, not a student, does the test flight after an engine change, and why the logbook entry matters before the first flight.

numbers.value: Test flight needs at least a private pilot
numbers.quote: an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies the aircraft

questions.q: The shop just replaced the propeller. Can I take my passenger up right away?
questions.a: Not until the aircraft is approved for return to service with a record entry, and if the change may have altered flight characteristics, a private pilot or higher must first fly an operational check and log it.

91.409.gist: An annual inspection within the preceding 12 calendar months is required before any operation; an aircraft carrying persons for hire, or used to give flight instruction for hire, also needs a 100-hour inspection, which may be exceeded by up to 10 hours to reach a place where it can be done.
91.409.why: The AVIATE list is on every oral, and the 10-hour overrun is the detail examiners probe.

numbers.value: Annual: within the preceding 12 calendar months
numbers.quote: within the preceding 12 calendar months

numbers.value: 100-hour: for hire, or instruction for hire
numbers.quote: within the preceding 100 hours of time in service

numbers.value: 100-hour overrun: at most 10 hours, to reach the shop
numbers.quote: not more than 10 hours while en route

traps: The overrun hours count against the next 100-hour interval.
An annual can stand in for a 100-hour; a 100-hour never stands in for an annual.

questions.q: Does a rental airplane need a 100-hour inspection?
questions.a: If it carries persons for hire or is used for flight instruction for hire, yes; otherwise the annual alone is required.

mnemonics: AVIATE: Annual; VOR check (30 days, IFR only); 100-hour (if for hire); Altimeter and pitot-static (24 months, IFR); Transponder (24 months); ELT (12 months).

91.411.gist: For IFR in controlled airspace, the static system, each altimeter and the automatic altitude-reporting system must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months, and again after the static system is opened or the encoder worked on.
91.411.why: The 24-month altimeter check is on the AV1ATE inspection list even though it is only required for IFR; the examiner will ask which inspections are VFR-required and which are not.

numbers.quote: Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected

traps: This inspection is required only for IFR operations; a VFR-only airplane can legally skip it, but its encoder is still governed by § 91.413.

questions.q: Is the altimeter and static check required for a VFR-only airplane?
questions.a: No. § 91.411 applies to IFR operations in controlled airspace. The transponder test of § 91.413 does apply whenever the transponder is used.

91.413.gist: Any ATC transponder you use must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months, and re-tested after any installation or maintenance that could introduce a data error. Only a rated repair station, a continuous-airworthiness program holder or the manufacturer may do it.
91.413.why: It is on the inspection list for every airplane with a transponder, VFR or IFR.

numbers.quote: within the preceding 24 calendar months, the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected

questions.q: What inspections does my airplane need?
questions.a: Annual (every 12 calendar months), 100-hour if used for hire, transponder every 24 calendar months, altimeter and static every 24 calendar months for IFR, ELT every 12 calendar months, plus airworthiness directives.

mnemonics: AV1ATE: Annual, VOR (IFR, 30 days), 100-hour, Altimeter (24 months), Transponder (24 months), ELT (12 months).

91.417.gist: Maintenance records the owner or operator must keep: records of maintenance, preventive maintenance, alterations and inspections (description, date, signature and certificate number), plus the running status records (total time, life-limited parts, overhaul times, inspection status, AD status with method of compliance, and Form 337s). The first set is kept for a year or until the work is repeated; the status records stay with the aircraft when sold. Records must be available to the FAA and NTSB.
91.417.why: These are the logbooks you review before the checkride to prove the airplane is airworthy, and the AD paragraph is what the examiner wants you to find.

numbers.value: AD status with method of compliance
numbers.quote: The current status of applicable airworthiness directives (AD) including, for each, the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date

numbers.value: Work records kept 1 year or until repeated
numbers.quote: for 1 year after the work is performed

numbers.value: Status records transfer with the aircraft
numbers.quote: shall be retained and transferred with the aircraft at the time the aircraft is sold

questions.q: How do I verify the annual and ADs are done before a checkride?
questions.a: Read the maintenance records § 91.417 requires: the inspection entries with date and signature, and the AD status list showing each AD's method of compliance and when recurring action is next due.

1-1-2.gist: The NDB is a low or medium frequency beacon (190 to 535 kHz) that an ADF receiver can home on or take bearings from. It gives no course guidance of its own, only a bearing to the station, and it is vulnerable to lightning, precipitation static and, at night, interference from distant stations.
1-1-2.why: Few trainers still carry an ADF, but NDBs remain on the sectional and on the knowledge test, and the failure modes explain why they are being retired.

numbers.quote: These facilities normally operate in a frequency band of 190 to 535 kilohertz (kHz)

traps: Noisy or missing identification usually means the bearing is unreliable too; the AIM says nearly all disturbances that affect the bearing also affect the ident.

questions.q: What is an NDB and how do you use it?
questions.a: A low or medium frequency beacon you receive with an ADF; the needle points to the station so you can home on it or plot a bearing. It is subject to interference from thunderstorms and, at night, distant stations.

1-1-3.gist: The VOR: 108.0 to 117.95 MHz, line-of-sight, course accuracy of about plus or minus 1 degree, identified only by its Morse code or recorded voice ident. Propeller RPM can make the needle wander up to 6 degrees. The VOR Minimum Operational Network keeps enough stations that a MON airport with a non-GPS approach is always within 100 nm and VOR coverage is continuous at 5,000 ft AGL.
1-1-3.why: VOR navigation is a checkride task, and the identification rule is the one examiners ask first: you have not tuned a VOR until you have heard its ident.

numbers.quote: VORs operate within the 108.0 to 117.95 MHz frequency band

numbers.value: Identify by Morse code or voice ident only
numbers.quote: The only positive method of identifying a VOR is by its Morse Code identification or by the recorded automatic voice identification

numbers.value: Course accuracy about plus or minus 1 degree
numbers.quote: generally plus or minus 1 degree
a MON airport (equipped with legacy ILS or VOR approaches) will be within 100 nautical miles

traps: Hearing a Flight Service voice on the VOR frequency is not identification; many FSSs transmit over several VORs with different names.
A VOR without an ident is out of service even if the needle looks alive.

questions.q: How do you confirm you are receiving the right VOR?
questions.a: Listen for its Morse code identification or the recorded voice ident ending in the word VOR. Voice transmissions from Flight Service do not count.

questions.q: What is the VOR MON?
questions.a: The Minimum Operational Network of VORs retained so that during a GPS outage you can navigate VOR to VOR at 5,000 ft AGL and reach a MON airport with an ILS or VOR approach within 100 nm.

1-1-4.gist: How to check a VOR receiver: a VOT test signal reads 0 degrees FROM or 180 TO; ground checkpoints allow plus or minus 4 degrees, airborne checkpoints and airway checks plus or minus 6, and two independent receivers checked against each other may differ by 4 degrees. Checkpoint and VOT locations are in the Chart Supplement, and the check is required before IFR flight by § 91.171.
1-1-4.why: The tolerances are a knowledge-test staple, and the VOT is the easiest thing to check on a taxi-out at a big airport.

numbers.quote: Should an error in excess of plus or minus 4 degrees be indicated through use of a ground check, or plus or minus 6 degrees using the airborne check
The maximum permissible variations between the two indicated bearings is 4 degrees

numbers.value: Airway check point: more than 20 nm from the VOR
numbers.quote: preferably more than 20 NM from the VOR ground facility

traps: The VOT reads 0 FROM or 180 TO regardless of where you are on the airport; a different reading is receiver error, not position.

questions.q: What should the VOR indicate when tuned to a VOT?
questions.a: With the needle centered, 0 degrees with a FROM indication or 180 degrees with a TO indication; an error over 4 degrees means the receiver may not be used for IFR until corrected.

mnemonics: VOT: 0 FROM, 180 TO. Ground 4, air 6, dual 4.

1-1-7.gist: DME measures the round-trip time of paired pulses between aircraft and ground station and shows slant-range distance, not horizontal distance. It is line-of-sight, usable to 199 nm with accuracy of a half mile or 3 percent, and it is paired with the VOR or localizer frequency so you tune one and get both.
1-1-7.why: Slant range is the trap: directly over the station at 6,000 ft the DME reads about 1 nm.

numbers.quote: Reliable signals may be received at distances up to 199 NM at line-of-sight altitude with an accuracy of better than 1/2 mile or 3 percent of the distance, whichever is greater
Distance information received from DME equipment is SLANT RANGE distance and not actual horizontal distance

questions.q: Why does the DME never read zero over the station?
questions.a: Because it measures slant range; over the station it reads roughly your altitude above it in nautical miles (6,000 ft is about 1 nm).

1-1-8.gist: Standard service volumes tell you how far from a NAVAID the signal is protected: Terminal class out to 25 nm from 1,000 to 12,000 ft above the transmitter, Low class 40 nm up to 18,000 ft, High class 40, 100 or 130 nm depending on altitude, plus the newer VOR Low and VOR High classes that extend to 70 nm for the MON. NDB ranges are by class: compass locator 15, MH 25, H 50, HH 75 nm at any altitude. The cone directly above a NAVAID is unusable.
1-1-8.why: Range questions on the knowledge test and 'why did the VOR flag at 40 miles?' on your cross-country both come from this table.

numbers.quote: From 1,000 feet ATH up to and including 12,000 feet ATH at radial distances out to 25 NM.
From 1,000 feet ATH up to and including 18,000 feet ATH at radial distances out to 40 NM.

numbers.value: NDB range does not change with altitude
numbers.quote: The distance (radius) is the same at all altitudes for each class.

numbers.value: Cone of confusion above the station
numbers.quote: A conical area directly above the NAVAID is generally not usable for navigation.

traps: Altitudes in the table are above the transmitter height, not MSL or AGL at your position.
Service volume restrictions are published first by NOTAM, then in the Chart Supplement; the chart symbol alone does not tell you.

questions.q: How far can I rely on a low-altitude VOR?
questions.a: 40 nm between 1,000 and 18,000 ft above the transmitter, unless a NOTAM or the Chart Supplement lists a restriction; the newer VOR Low class reaches 70 nm above 5,000 ft.

1-1-13.gist: Pilots are asked to report NAVAID malfunctions and GPS anomalies (interference, jamming, spoofing) promptly: switch to another navigation source, tell ATC if you need an amended clearance, and file a detailed report with the time, location, aircraft and equipment. GPS anomalies inside a known testing NOTAM area need not be reported in detail unless something unexpected happens.
1-1-13.why: GPS interference events are increasingly common; knowing to cross-check and to report is an ACS risk element.

numbers.quote: Pilots encountering navigation error events should transition to another source of navigation and request amended clearances from ATC as necessary.

questions.q: My GPS position suddenly jumps 10 miles. What do I do?
questions.a: Treat it as unreliable: navigate by another source (VOR, pilotage), tell ATC if you are receiving services, and report the anomaly afterward through the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form.

1-1-17.gist: GPS for pilots: the constellation is designed so at least five satellites are visible, four are needed for a 3D position, and RAIM needs five (or four plus baro-aiding) to detect a bad satellite. For VFR the AIM's cautions are the point: VFR and hand-held receivers have no RAIM alerting, databases need not be current for VFR but should be, antenna placement matters, and you must not rely on GPS alone. VFR waypoints are five-letter names starting with VP, not for use with ATC and not allowed on IFR flight plans. The IFR half covers approved equipment, database and approach requirements.
1-1-17.why: The examiner will ask what your tablet GPS cannot do; the answer is RAIM and integrity, and the AIM says so in plain words.

numbers.quote: A minimum of four satellites is necessary for receivers to establish an accurate three-dimensional position.

numbers.value: RAIM needs 5 satellites, or 4 with baro-aiding
numbers.quote: RAIM requires a minimum of 5 satellites, or 4 satellites and barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding), to detect an integrity anomaly.

numbers.value: VFR and hand-held units have no RAIM alerting
numbers.quote: VFR GPS panel mount receivers and hand-held units have no RAIM alerting capability.

numbers.value: No database currency requirement for VFR
numbers.quote: there is no requirement for databases to be updated for VFR navigation

numbers.value: Do not rely on GPS alone
numbers.quote: Do not solely rely on GPS for VFR navigation.

numbers.value: VFR waypoints are not for IFR flight plans
numbers.quote: VFR waypoints may not be used on IFR flight plans.

traps: An outdated database around Class B or a TFR can show airspace that has moved; verify waypoints against a current chart.
Do not fly a mountain pass from VFR waypoint to VFR waypoint; the points mark entries, not a path.

questions.q: What is RAIM and why does my VFR GPS not have it?
questions.a: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring lets the receiver detect a bad satellite using extra satellites in view. VFR and hand-held units do not alert on its loss, so you must cross-check position with other navigation.

questions.q: Can I file a VFR waypoint in my route?
questions.a: Yes, on a VFR flight plan the five-letter VP identifier may be used; VFR waypoints are not accepted on IFR flight plans and are not used in ATC communications.

1-1-18.gist: WAAS augments GPS with ground reference stations and a geostationary correction signal, improving accuracy, integrity and availability enough for approaches with vertical guidance (LPV as low as 200 ft and a half mile). A WAAS receiver does not need other navigation equipment for the route, and WAAS NOTAMs use the words MAY NOT BE AVBL to warn of degraded vertical guidance.
1-1-18.why: You will see LPV on approach plates and WAAS in every modern GPS; this is the background the oral may touch on.

numbers.value: WAAS improves accuracy, integrity and availability
numbers.quote: The FAA developed the WAAS to improve the accuracy, integrity and availability of GPS signals.

numbers.value: LPV as low as 200 ft and 1/2 mile
