numbers.quote: LPV minima may have a decision altitude as low as 200 feet height above touchdown with visibility minimums as low as 1/2 mile

numbers.value: No other route equipment required with WAAS
numbers.quote: installation of WAAS avionics does not require the aircraft to have other equipment appropriate to the route to be flown

questions.q: What does WAAS add to GPS?
questions.a: Corrections and integrity monitoring broadcast from geostationary satellites, giving accuracy and integrity good enough for vertically guided approaches and removing the need for a backup navigation receiver on the route.

2-1-4.gist: Runway edge lights come in high, medium and low intensity. They are white, except that on instrument runways the last 2,000 ft or half the runway (whichever is less) is yellow as a caution zone. The lights at the runway end show red to the departing aircraft and green outward to the landing aircraft as the threshold.
2-1-4.why: Night landing and taxi questions start here: what color tells you the runway is ending.

numbers.value: Yellow caution zone: last 2,000 ft or half the runway
numbers.quote: The runway edge lights are white, except on instrument runways yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway length, whichever is less, to form a caution zone for landings.

numbers.value: Red end lights, green threshold lights
numbers.quote: The lights marking the ends of the runway emit red light toward the runway to indicate the end of runway to a departing aircraft and emit green outward from the runway end to indicate the threshold to landing aircraft.

questions.q: What color are runway edge lights, and what does yellow mean?
questions.a: White; on an instrument runway the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less, turns yellow to warn that the runway is about to end.

2-1-5.gist: Lights set into the runway pavement: centerline lights every 50 ft that are white, then alternate red and white in the last 3,000 ft, then all red in the last 1,000; touchdown zone lights; lead-off and lead-on taxiway lights alternating green and yellow at the runway boundary; and land-and-hold-short lights, a row of pulsing white lights at the hold-short point when LAHSO is in effect.
2-1-5.why: These are precision-runway features you may only meet at larger airports, but the color sequence is a knowledge-test item.

numbers.value: Centerline lights every 50 ft, white until the last 3,000 ft
numbers.quote: They are located along the runway centerline and are spaced at 50-foot intervals. When viewed from the landing threshold, the runway centerline lights are white until the last 3,000 feet of the runway.

numbers.value: LAHSO lights: pulsing white at the hold-short point
numbers.quote: Land and hold short lights consist of a row of pulsing white lights installed across the runway at the hold short point.

questions.q: What do alternating red and white centerline lights mean?
questions.a: You are in the last 3,000 ft of the runway; when they turn all red, 1,000 ft remain.

2-1-6.gist: Runway Status Lights are automatic red lights driven by surveillance: Runway Entrance Lights at the hold line mean the runway is unsafe to enter or cross, and Takeoff Hold Lights in the runway mean it is unsafe to take off. Never cross illuminated red lights; if they conflict with your clearance, stop and ask ATC. When they go out, that is not a clearance.
2-1-6.why: They are installed at busy airports and the AIM is explicit that a pilot must stop for them even with a clearance in hand.

numbers.quote: Never cross over illuminated red lights.

numbers.value: Lights going out is not a clearance
numbers.quote: Do not proceed when lights have extinguished without an ATC clearance. RWSL verifies an ATC clearance; it does not substitute for an ATC clearance.

questions.q: Tower cleared me to cross but the red in-pavement lights are on. What do I do?
questions.a: Stop at the hold line, tell the tower you are holding because of the runway status lights, and get the clearance re-confirmed before moving.

2-1-8.gist: At airports without a tower or after hours, the runway and approach lights can be turned on from the air by keying the microphone on the published frequency (usually the CTAF): 7 clicks within 5 seconds for highest intensity, 5 for medium, 3 for lowest, and the lights stay on for 15 minutes. All radio-controlled systems at one airport share the same frequency, so keying 7 first then stepping down is the recommended technique.
2-1-8.why: A night arrival at a non-towered airport depends on it; the click counts are a knowledge-test question.

numbers.value: Lights are keyed with the microphone
numbers.quote: Radio control of lighting is available at selected airports to provide airborne control of lights by keying the aircraft's microphone.

traps: Key 7 times first even if you want low intensity, so the system is on, then key 5 or 3; keying 3 times into a dark system may leave you with nothing.
The 15-minute timer restarts each time you key, so re-key on short final if you have been in the pattern a while.

questions.q: How do I turn on the runway lights at night at a non-towered airport?
questions.a: Key the mic on the frequency listed in the Chart Supplement (usually the CTAF) 7 times within 5 seconds for high intensity, 5 for medium, 3 for low; they stay on for 15 minutes.

mnemonics: 7-5-3 in 5 seconds, 15 minutes on.

2-1-9.gist: Airport beacons flash 24 to 30 times a minute (30 to 45 for heliports). White and green is a lighted land airport, white and yellow a water airport, green-yellow-white a heliport, and a military airport shows two quick white flashes between the greens. In a Class B, C, D or E surface area a beacon running during the day often means the weather is below VFR, but do not rely on it alone.
2-1-9.why: Identifying an airport at night by its beacon and reading the daytime beacon as an IFR hint are both oral questions.

numbers.value: 24 to 30 flashes per minute for airports
numbers.quote: 24 to 30 per minute for beacons marking airports, landmarks, and points on Federal airways.
White and Green- Lighted land airport.
White and Yellow- Lighted water airport.
Military airport beacons flash alternately white and green, but are differentiated from civil beacons by dualpeaked (two quick) white flashes between the green flashes.

numbers.value: Daytime beacon: often visibility below 3 miles or ceiling below 1,000 ft
numbers.quote: operation of the airport beacon during the hours of daylight often indicates that the ground visibility is less than 3 miles and/or the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet

traps: The daytime beacon is a hint, not a report; some beacons run all day and the weather may still be VFR. Get the ATIS or AWOS.

questions.q: The beacon is on at noon at a Class D airport. What does that tell me?
questions.a: Often that ground visibility is below 3 miles and/or the ceiling is below 1,000 ft, so you would need a special VFR or IFR clearance; confirm with the weather broadcast rather than relying on the beacon.

mnemonics: Green land, yellow water, military double-flash.

2-1-10.gist: Taxiway lights by color: blue edge lights, green centerline lights, yellow clearance bars at holding positions, flashing yellow runway guard lights at runway intersections, and red stop bars that you never cross even with a clearance until they are turned off.
2-1-10.why: Blue-versus-green at night and the stop bar rule are standard night-operations questions.

numbers.quote: These fixtures emit blue light.
Taxiway centerline lights are steady burning and emit green light.

numbers.value: Runway guard lights: flashing yellow at the hold position
numbers.quote: Runway guard lights consist of either a pair of elevated flashing yellow lights installed on either side of the taxiway, or a row of in-pavement yellow lights installed across the entire taxiway, at the runway holding position marking.

numbers.value: Never cross a lit red stop bar
numbers.quote: Pilots should never cross a red illuminated stop bar, even if an ATC clearance has been given to proceed onto or across the runway.

questions.q: What do flashing yellow lights on either side of the taxiway mean?
questions.a: Runway guard lights: you are at a runway holding position. Stop unless you have a clearance to enter or cross.

2-2-1.gist: An aeronautical light beacon is a flashing white or colored light that marks an airport, heliport, landmark, a Federal airway point in mountainous terrain, or an obstruction; the color combination tells you which.
2-2-1.why: It is the general definition behind the airport beacon colors of 2-1-9.

numbers.quote: An aeronautical light beacon is a visual NAVAID displaying flashes of white and/or colored light to indicate the location of an airport, a heliport, a landmark, a certain point of a Federal airway in mountainous terrain, or an obstruction.

questions.q: How do I tell an airport beacon from an obstruction beacon at night?
questions.a: By color: airports flash white with green or yellow, obstructions are red (or high-intensity white by day).

2-2-3.gist: Obstructions are marked with flashing red beacons (20 to 40 flashes a minute) and steady red lights at night, with orange and white paint by day; medium- or high-intensity white strobes may replace paint and red lights; and catenary lighting marks high-voltage lines across rivers and gorges.
2-2-3.why: Knowing that red or white strobes mean an obstruction, and that wires may be lit in sequence, is a night cross-country safety item.

numbers.value: Red beacons flash 20 to 40 per minute
numbers.quote: Flashing aviation red beacons (20 to 40 flashes per minute) and steady burning aviation red lights during nighttime operation.
Aviation orange and white paint is always required for daytime marking on structures exceeding 500 feet (153m) AGL.

questions.q: What do sequential flashing white lights across a river mean?
questions.a: Catenary lighting: high-voltage transmission wires span the gap between the lit structures. Stay well above.

2-3-3.gist: Runway markings: visual, non-precision and precision runways carry progressively more elements. The runway number is the magnetic azimuth to the nearest 10 degrees; the aiming point bars sit about 1,000 ft from the threshold; touchdown zone bars count 500 ft increments; threshold stripes reflect runway width. A displaced threshold's pavement may be used for taxi, takeoff, and landing from the opposite direction, but not for landing on; chevrons mark pavement unusable for anything.
2-3-3.why: Displaced thresholds and chevrons are the markings most often asked about on the oral and the ones that catch pilots on a short field.

numbers.value: Runway number: magnetic azimuth to the nearest tenth
numbers.quote: The runway number is the whole number nearest one‐tenth the magnetic azimuth of the centerline of the runway, measured clockwise from the magnetic north.

numbers.value: Aiming point about 1,000 ft from the threshold
numbers.quote: approximately 1,000 feet from the landing threshold

numbers.value: Displaced threshold: taxi, take off, land from the other end
numbers.quote: The portion of runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction and landings from the opposite direction.
Chevrons. These markings are used to show pavement areas aligned with the runway that are unusable for landing, takeoff, and taxiing.

traps: White arrows lead to a displaced threshold and you may roll out onto them after landing from the other direction; yellow chevrons are never to be used.
The Chart Supplement runway length includes a displaced threshold; landing distance available does not.

questions.q: Can I use the pavement before a displaced threshold?
questions.a: For taxiing and takeoff yes, and for the rollout when landing the opposite direction; you may not touch down before the displaced threshold.

2-3-4.gist: Taxiway markings are yellow: a single continuous centerline, an enhanced centerline of dashes on both sides for 150 ft before a runway holding position, a continuous double yellow edge line you must not cross, a dashed double yellow edge line you may cross onto usable pavement, and surface-painted signs and geographic position markings at some airports.
2-3-4.why: The enhanced centerline is the runway-incursion warning painted under your nose; knowing what it means is an ACS risk item.

numbers.quote: The taxiway centerline is a single continuous yellow line, 6 inches (15 cm) to 12 inches (30 cm) in width.

numbers.value: Enhanced centerline runs 150 ft before the hold line
numbers.quote: The taxiway centerlines are enhanced for a maximum of 150 feet prior to a runway holding position marking.

numbers.value: Continuous double yellow edge: pavement not for aircraft
numbers.quote: These consist of a continuous double yellow line, with each line being at least 6 inches (15 cm) in width spaced 6 inches (15 cm) apart.

traps: Staying on the centerline does not guarantee wingtip clearance; the AIM says so explicitly.

questions.q: What do yellow dashes on both sides of the taxiway centerline mean?
questions.a: Enhanced centerline: a runway holding position marking is within 150 ft, so slow down, look for the hold-short line and the red sign, and be ready to stop.

2-3-5.gist: Holding position markings: four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, across the taxiway; the solid lines are on the side where you hold, and you must stop so no part of the aircraft crosses the marking unless cleared. Markings on runways are for LAHSO and taxi. ILS critical-area markings are a yellow ladder of two solid lines with rungs. A single dashed line across a taxiway is a taxiway-to-taxiway hold point, used only when ATC says hold short of that taxiway.
2-3-5.why: The hold-short line is the single most important marking on the airport; every runway-incursion question comes back to it.

numbers.value: Two solid, two dashed; solid on the holding side
numbers.quote: They consist of four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, spaced six or twelve inches apart, and extending across the width of the taxiway or runway. The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft must hold.

numbers.value: ILS critical area: two solid lines with rungs
numbers.quote: Holding position markings for ILS critical areas consist of two yellow solid lines spaced two feet apart connected by pairs of solid lines spaced ten feet apart

traps: Coming off the runway you cross the dashed side first; you are not clear of the runway until the whole aircraft is past the solid lines.
At a non-towered airport you still hold at the marking until you have checked final and announced; the marking defines the runway safety area either way.

questions.q: Which side of the hold-short line do I stop on?
questions.a: The side with the solid lines. You may cross when the dashed lines are toward you (leaving the runway) but you must be entirely past the solid lines to be clear.

mnemonics: Solid side, stay; dashed side, dash through.

2-3-7.gist: Six kinds of airport signs: mandatory instruction, location, direction, destination, information, and runway distance remaining. Each has its own colors and the following paragraphs describe them.
2-3-7.why: It is the index to the sign colors the examiner will show you on an airport diagram or a photo.

numbers.quote: There are six types of signs installed on airfields: mandatory instruction signs, location signs, direction signs, destination signs, information signs, and runway distance remaining signs.

questions.q: What are the colors of the main airport signs?
questions.a: Mandatory: white on red. Location: yellow on black. Direction and destination: black on yellow. Runway distance remaining: white numerals on black.

mnemonics: Red is a stop sign, black is where you are, yellow is where to go.

2-3-8.gist: Mandatory instruction signs are white on red: runway holding position signs (the numbers are arranged so the runway threshold on the left is the left number, e.g. 15-33), runway approach-area holding signs, ILS critical area signs, and the no-entry sign. They mark where you must stop without clearance.
2-3-8.why: Reading 15-33 correctly tells you which way each runway's threshold lies, which is what the examiner is testing when they show you the sign.

numbers.quote: These signs have a red background with a white inscription

numbers.value: 15-33: threshold 15 to the left, 33 to the right
numbers.quote: For example, “15-33” indicates that the threshold for Runway 15 is to the left and the threshold for Runway 33 is to the right.

traps: A sign with only one runway number means you are at the beginning of that takeoff runway, not that the other direction does not exist.

questions.q: What does a red sign reading 15-33 tell me?
questions.a: You are at the holding position for runway 15-33; the threshold of runway 15 is to your left and that of 33 to your right. Hold short unless cleared.

2-3-9.gist: Location signs are yellow on black and tell you which taxiway or runway you are on. Two related boundary signs face the runway: the runway boundary sign (yellow with the hold-line graphic) and the ILS critical area boundary sign; when you can read them you are clear of the runway or the critical area.
2-3-9.why: The black sign answers 'where am I?' and the yellow boundary sign answers 'am I clear?', both questions the tower may ask you.

numbers.quote: This sign has a black background with a yellow inscription and yellow border

numbers.value: Runway boundary sign: yellow with hold-line graphic
numbers.quote: This sign has a yellow background with a black inscription with a graphic depicting the pavement holding position marking

questions.q: How do I know I am clear of the runway after landing?
questions.a: When the whole aircraft is past the hold-short marking; the yellow runway boundary sign facing you shows that line. Then call ground as instructed.

2-3-10.gist: Direction signs are black on yellow with an arrow for each intersecting taxiway, normally placed on the left before the intersection and arranged clockwise from the first taxiway on your left, with the location sign in the middle separating left turns from straight-ahead and right turns.
2-3-10.why: Taxi-diagram reading is a checkride task, and the clockwise arrangement is what lets you predict which arrow you need.

numbers.quote: Direction signs have a yellow background with a black inscription.

numbers.value: Normally on the left before the intersection
numbers.quote: Direction signs are normally located on the left prior to the intersection.

numbers.value: Arranged clockwise from the pilot's left
numbers.quote: The taxiway designations and their associated arrows on the sign are arranged clockwise starting from the first taxiway on the pilot's left.

questions.q: I see a sign array reading B with a left arrow, A, and C with a right arrow. Where am I?
questions.a: On taxiway A (the black location sign in the middle); B is to the left and C to the right at the coming intersection.

3-1-1.gist: The airspace taxonomy in one paragraph: two categories (regulatory, meaning Classes A through E plus restricted and prohibited areas; and nonregulatory, meaning MOAs, warning areas, alert areas, controlled firing areas and national security areas) and four types: controlled, uncontrolled, special use and other.
3-1-1.why: The oral on airspace usually opens with 'what kinds of airspace are there?' and this is the FAA's own answer.

numbers.quote: Regulatory (Class A, B, C, D and E airspace areas, restricted and prohibited areas); and
Nonregulatory (military operations areas [MOA], warning areas, alert areas, controlled firing areas [CFA], and national security areas [NSA]).

questions.q: What are the categories and types of airspace?
questions.a: Regulatory and nonregulatory categories; controlled, uncontrolled, special use and other types. Restricted and prohibited areas are regulatory special use; MOAs, warning, alert, CFAs and NSAs are nonregulatory.

3-1-3.gist: When two airspace designations overlap, the rules of the more restrictive one apply, and the AIM ranks them: A over B over C over D over E over G.
3-1-3.why: It answers what to do where a Class D surface area sits under a Class B shelf or an E surface area extension.

numbers.quote: When overlapping airspace designations apply to the same airspace, the operating rules associated with the more restrictive airspace designation apply.

questions.q: A Class D airport lies under a Class B shelf that starts at 3,000 ft. Which rules apply at 2,000 ft?
questions.a: Class D, because Class B does not reach down there; wherever the two actually overlap, the more restrictive (Class B) rules apply.

3-1-4.gist: The AIM's copy of the basic VFR weather minimums table from § 91.155, with two reminders: student pilots also have their own limits in § 61.89, and VFR beneath a ceiling below 1,000 ft in a surface area is prohibited without special VFR.
3-1-4.why: The table version here is the one most pilots memorize from; the regulation itself is in § 91.155.

numbers.value: Student pilots have their own limits
numbers.quote: Student pilots must comply with 14 CFR section 61.89(a) (6) and (7).

numbers.value: Class G day, at or below 1,200 ft AGL: 1 statute mile, clear of clouds
numbers.quote: 1,200 feet or less above the surface (regardless of MSL altitude).

traps: The Class G row is split by height above the surface, not MSL; 1,200 ft AGL is the line even on a mountain.

questions.q: What are the VFR minimums in Class G at night below 1,200 ft AGL?
questions.a: 3 statute miles and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal, unless the § 91.155(b) traffic-pattern exception applies.

3-1-5.gist: VFR cruising altitudes above 3,000 ft AGL and below 18,000 ft MSL: magnetic course 0 to 179 degrees, odd thousands plus 500; 180 to 359, even thousands plus 500. Above 18,000 the same pattern applies to flight levels, but that is Class A and IFR.
3-1-5.why: The examiner will ask for a cruising altitude on your planned route; it must fit this table.

numbers.value: Applies above 3,000 ft AGL and below 18,000 ft MSL
numbers.quote: And you are more than 3,000 feet above the surface but below 18,000 feet MSL, fly:
Odd thousands MSL, plus 500 feet
Even thousands MSL, plus 500 feet

traps: It is magnetic course, not heading; a strong crosswind does not change your altitude.
Below 3,000 ft AGL the rule does not apply, but a sensible altitude still does.

questions.q: My magnetic course is 090. What cruising altitudes may I use?
questions.a: Odd thousands plus 500 ft: 3,500, 5,500, 7,500 and so on, when more than 3,000 ft above the surface.

mnemonics: East is odd: 0 to 179 fly odd thousands plus 500 (NEodd SWeven).

3-2-1.gist: Controlled airspace basics: ATC service is provided to IFR flights and to VFR flights according to the class. It is the pilot's responsibility to meet the clearance or communication requirement before entering Class B, C or D, even while receiving radar advisories. Traffic advisories are workload permitting; safety alerts are mandatory. Ultralights, unmanned balloons and parachute jumps need authorization in the controlled classes.
3-2-1.why: The 'responsibility stays with the pilot' sentence is why a flight-following handoff is not a clearance into Class B.

numbers.value: You must meet the entry requirement yourself
numbers.quote: It is the responsibility of the pilot to ensure that ATC clearance or radio communication requirements are met prior to entry into Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace.
Safety Alerts are mandatory services and are provided to ALL aircraft.
Traffic advisories will be provided to all aircraft as the controller's work situation permits.

traps: Being on flight following with approach does not clear you into Class B; you need the words 'cleared into the Class Bravo'.

questions.q: I am talking to approach on flight following. Can I enter the Class B ahead?
questions.a: Not until you hear an explicit Class B clearance; the AIM makes the pilot responsible for meeting entry requirements even while receiving radar advisories.

3-2-2.gist: Class A: from 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL600, including the airspace over the waters out to 12 nm; IFR only unless otherwise authorized; not charted.
3-2-2.why: It is the ceiling on VFR flight and the reason the VFR cruising altitude table stops at 17,500.

numbers.value: 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL600
numbers.quote: Generally, that airspace from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600
Class A airspace is not specifically charted.

questions.q: Where is Class A airspace and how is it shown on the chart?
questions.a: From 18,000 ft MSL to FL600 over the 48 states and Alaska and out to 12 nm offshore; it is not charted because it is everywhere at those altitudes.

3-2-3.gist: Class B surrounds the busiest airports, typically from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL in tailored layers; an ATC clearance is required to enter, VFR aircraft receive separation inside, cloud clearance is simply clear of clouds, and the 30 NM Mode C veil surrounds the primary airport.
3-2-3.why: Knowing what a clearance sounds like keeps you out of the most expensive airspace violation there is.

numbers.quote: from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL
within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in Appendix D

questions.q: How do I know I am cleared into Class B?
questions.a: Only when ATC says “cleared into the Class Bravo airspace”; radar contact or a squawk code is not a clearance.

3-2-4.gist: Class C is usually a 5 NM core from the surface and a 10 NM shelf from about 1,200 ft, both up to 4,000 ft above the airport, with a 20 NM outer area where services continue but participation is voluntary; two-way communications (your call sign used) before entry, transponder and ADS-B Out required.
3-2-4.why: The dimensions and the “standby” rule are both tested.

numbers.value: Surface to 4,000 ft above the airport
numbers.quote: from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation
5 NM radius core surface area
10 NM radius shelf area
20 NM from the primary Class C airspace airport

questions.q: The controller says “aircraft calling, standby”. May I enter Class C?
questions.a: No — communications are established only when the controller uses your call sign; “[call sign], standby” is enough, “aircraft calling, standby” is not.

3-2-5.gist: Class D surrounds towered airports, usually from the surface to 2,500 ft above field elevation; two-way communications before entry (your call sign used), no separation services for VFR, and when a part-time tower closes the area reverts to Class E or Class G as the Chart Supplement states.
3-2-5.why: The part-time tower question is a favourite: what airspace is it at night?

numbers.value: Surface to 2,500 ft above the airport
numbers.quote: from the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation

questions.q: The tower closes at night. What is the airspace then?
questions.a: It reverts to Class E or Class G as the Chart Supplement's airport entry states — check it before you go.

3-2-6.gist: Class E is controlled airspace with no communication or clearance requirement for VFR: transition areas begin at 700 ft AGL (magenta vignette) or 1,200 ft AGL (blue vignette) around airports with instrument procedures, Class E otherwise starts at 14,500 ft MSL, and Federal airways are Class E from 1,200 ft AGL up to 18,000 ft.
3-2-6.why: The vignette colours are the chart-reading question every written asks.

numbers.value: Transition areas: 700 ft AGL (magenta) or 1,200 ft AGL (blue)
numbers.quote: 700 feet AGL (shown as magenta vignette on sectional charts) or 1,200 feet AGL (blue vignette)
extending upward from 14,500 feet MSL to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL

numbers.value: Federal airways: 1,200 ft AGL to 18,000 ft MSL
numbers.quote: extend upward from 1,200 feet AGL to, but not including,18,000 feet MSL

questions.q: Do I need to talk to anyone to fly through Class E?
questions.a: No — VFR in Class E below 10,000 ft has no communication or equipment requirement; only the weather minimums change.

3-4-1.gist: Special use airspace confines hazardous activities or limits nonparticipating aircraft. Prohibited and restricted areas are regulatory (Part 73); warning areas, MOAs, alert areas, controlled firing areas and national security areas are not. Permanent SUA is charted with hours, altitudes and controlling agency; CFAs, temporary MOAs and temporary restricted areas are not charted.
3-4-1.why: The sectional legend for SUA and the 'is it active?' question both start here.

numbers.quote: Prohibited and restricted areas are regulatory special use airspace and are established in 14 CFR part 73 through the rulemaking process.
Warning areas, MOAs, alert areas, CFAs, and national security areas (NSA) are nonregulatory special use airspace.

numbers.value: Not charted: CFAs, temporary MOAs, temporary restricted areas
numbers.quote: SUA areas are depicted on aeronautical charts, except for controlled firing areas (CFA), temporary military operations areas (MOA), and temporary restricted areas.

traps: Temporary MOAs and restricted areas are only in the Domestic Notices and NOTAMs; a clean chart is not proof that none exist on your route.

questions.q: What special use airspace is not shown on the sectional?
questions.a: Controlled firing areas, temporary MOAs and temporary restricted areas. Check the Domestic Notices and NOTAMs for the temporary ones.

3-4-2.gist: Prohibited areas are established for national security or welfare and flight inside them is prohibited; they are published in the Federal Register and charted.
3-4-2.why: There are only a handful (P-40 at Camp David, P-56 in Washington) but they are absolute.

numbers.quote: Prohibited areas contain airspace of defined dimensions identified by an area on the surface of the earth within which the flight of aircraft is prohibited.

questions.q: Can ATC clear me through a prohibited area?
questions.a: No. § 91.133 allows entry only with permission of the using agency, and for a prohibited area that is in practice never given to a transiting VFR flight.

3-4-3.gist: Restricted areas contain invisible hazards such as artillery, aerial gunnery or guided missiles; flight is subject to restrictions rather than prohibited outright. When a joint-use area is not active and released to the FAA, ATC will let IFR aircraft through; VFR pilots must find out the status from the controlling agency or FSS. Permanent restricted areas are charted; temporary ones are not.
3-4-3.why: Every cross-country near a military range raises the same oral question: how do you know whether R-XXXX is hot?

numbers.quote: Restricted areas denote the existence of unusual, often invisible, hazards to aircraft such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery, or guided missiles.

numbers.value: Temporary restricted areas are not charted
numbers.quote: Temporary restricted areas are not charted.

questions.q: How do I find out whether a restricted area is active?
questions.a: Check the times on the chart and the NOTAMs, then ask the controlling agency (listed on the chart margin) or Flight Service; when it is not active you may fly through under § 91.133.

3-4-4.gist: A warning area begins 3 nm off the coast and contains activity hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft, over domestic or international waters. Its purpose is to warn; there is no legal bar to entry, but the hazard is the same as a restricted area.
3-4-4.why: The knowledge test likes the 3 nm number and the 'may be over international waters' point.

numbers.quote: A warning area is airspace of defined dimensions, extending from three nautical miles outward from the coast of the U.S., that contains activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft.

questions.q: What is the difference between a warning area and a restricted area?
questions.a: Both hold hazardous activity, but a warning area is offshore, often in international airspace where the FAA cannot regulate, so it warns rather than restricts.

3-4-5.gist: MOAs separate military training (air combat, intercepts, aerobatics, low-altitude tactics) from IFR traffic. VFR flight is permitted but the AIM says exercise extreme caution, get the real-time status from an FSS within 100 miles, and contact the controlling agency for advisories before entering an active MOA. Permanent MOAs are charted; temporary ones are not.
3-4-5.why: MOAs cover huge areas of the western U.S.; you will cross one, and the examiner wants to hear the FSS and controlling-agency calls.

numbers.quote: Pilots operating under VFR should exercise extreme caution while flying within a MOA when military activity is being conducted.

numbers.value: Contact the controlling agency before entering
numbers.quote: Prior to entering an active MOA, pilots should contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories.
Temporary MOAs are not charted.

traps: Military aircraft in an active MOA may exceed 250 knots below 10,000 ft and do aerobatics; see-and-avoid is much harder.

questions.q: Do I need a clearance to fly VFR through a MOA?
questions.a: No, but check its status with Flight Service, contact the controlling agency for advisories if it is active, and keep a sharp lookout.

3-4-6.gist: Alert areas mark a high volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity. Everyone flies under the regular rules there and both participants and transiting aircraft share collision-avoidance responsibility.
3-4-6.why: It is the least restrictive SUA; the test asks what it means and whether you need permission (you do not).

numbers.value: High volume of training or unusual activity
numbers.quote: Alert areas are depicted on aeronautical charts to inform nonparticipating pilots of areas that may contain a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity.

questions.q: What is an alert area?
questions.a: Charted airspace with lots of training or unusual activity; no permission is needed, but all pilots there are equally responsible for collision avoidance.

3-4-7.gist: Controlled firing areas contain hazardous activity that is suspended the moment spotters, radar or lookouts detect an approaching aircraft, which is why they are not charted.
3-4-7.why: The 'not charted, because they stop for you' fact is a classic knowledge-test item.

numbers.quote: There is no need to chart CFAs since they do not cause a nonparticipating aircraft to change its flight path.

questions.q: Why are controlled firing areas not on the chart?
questions.a: Because the firing is suspended as soon as an aircraft is seen approaching, so the area never requires a pilot to change course.

3-4-8.gist: National security areas surround sensitive ground facilities; pilots are asked to avoid them voluntarily, and when needed flight through them can be prohibited by NOTAM under § 99.7.
3-4-8.why: The distinction between 'requested to avoid' and 'prohibited by NOTAM' is what the examiner is after.

numbers.quote: Pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying through the depicted NSA.

questions.q: Is it legal to fly through a national security area?
questions.a: Normally yes, though you are asked to avoid it; when a § 99.7 NOTAM prohibits flight there it becomes mandatory.

3-5-2.gist: Military training routes carry high-speed low-level training: generally below 10,000 ft MSL at more than 250 knots. IR routes are flown IFR, VR routes VFR with at least 5 miles visibility and a 3,000 ft ceiling. Four-digit routes have no segment above 1,500 ft AGL; three-digit routes do. You are not prohibited from an MTR, but call an FSS within 100 nm for the activity schedule and be vigilant; route width can be several miles either side of the line.
3-5-2.why: The thin grey lines on the sectional hide fast jets; reading the route number tells you how low they will be.

numbers.quote: Generally, MTRs are established below 10,000 feet MSL for operations at speeds in excess of 250 knots.

numbers.value: Four digits: nothing above 1,500 ft AGL
numbers.quote: MTRs with no segment above 1,500 feet AGL must be identified by four number characters; e.g., IR1206, VR1207.

numbers.value: Three digits: some segment above 1,500 ft AGL
numbers.quote: MTRs that include one or more segments above 1,500 feet AGL must be identified by three number characters; e.g., IR206, VR207.
Nonparticipating aircraft are not prohibited from flying within an MTR or SMAR; however, extreme vigilance should be exercised when conducting flight through or near these routes.

questions.q: What does VR1207 on the chart tell me?
questions.a: A VFR military training route flown entirely at or below 1,500 ft AGL (four digits) at high speed; call Flight Service for its schedule and cross it with care.

mnemonics: Four digits fly low (all below 1,500 AGL); three digits climb.

3-5-3.gist: The AIM's operational explanation of temporary flight restrictions: who requests them, which rule each type cites (§ 91.137 hazards, § 91.138 Hawaii, § 91.141 VIPs, § 91.143 space operations), that hazard TFRs are normally 3 nm and 2,000 ft, that incidents inside Class B, C or D are handled by existing procedures, and how the NOTAM text is formatted.
3-5-3.why: It turns the regulation into what you will actually read in a TFR NOTAM and how big the area usually is.

numbers.value: Typical hazard TFR: 2,000 ft AGL and 3 nm radius
numbers.quote: The amount of airspace needed to protect persons and property or provide a safe environment for rescue/relief aircraft operations is normally limited to within 2,000 feet above the surface and within a 3-nautical-mile radius.

numbers.value: Inside Class B, C or D existing procedures are used
numbers.quote: Incidents occurring within Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace will normally be handled through existing procedures and should not require the issuance of a temporary flight restrictions NOTAM.

questions.q: How big is a typical disaster TFR?
questions.a: Normally a 3 nm radius up to 2,000 ft above the surface, but the NOTAM defines the actual area, altitudes and coordination facility.

3-5-6.gist: A TRSA is not regulatory airspace: the primary airport is Class D, the rest overlies Class E, and participation in TRSA radar service is voluntary. It is charted with a solid black line and segment altitudes, with the Class D core in blue dashes.
3-5-6.why: TRSAs confuse students because they look like Class C on the chart but carry no entry requirement beyond the Class D core.

numbers.quote: TRSAs were never controlled airspace from a regulatory standpoint because the establishment of TRSAs was never subject to the rulemaking process
However, participation is voluntary on the part of the pilot.

numbers.value: Charted with a solid black line
numbers.quote: TRSAs are depicted on VFR sectional and terminal area charts with a solid black line and altitudes for each segment. The Class D portion is charted with a blue segmented line.

questions.q: Do I have to talk to approach to fly through a TRSA?
questions.a: No; participation is voluntary, though encouraged. You must still establish communications with the tower to enter the Class D core.

3-5-7.gist: Special air traffic rules areas and special flight rules areas are Part 93 airspace with their own rules; anyone operating to, from or within one must follow them unless ATC authorizes otherwise, and SFRAs are charted on sectionals, terminal area and helicopter route charts.
3-5-7.why: The Hudson River, Grand Canyon and Washington DC areas are Part 93; the examiner wants you to know they exist and where the rules live.

numbers.quote: Each person operating an aircraft to, from, or within airspace designated as a SATR area or SFRA must adhere to the special air traffic rules set forth in 14 CFR part 93, as applicable, unless otherwise authorized or required by ATC.

questions.q: Where are the rules for a special flight rules area?
questions.a: In 14 CFR Part 93 for that area, charted on the sectional and terminal area chart, with procedures on the FAA Safety website.

3-5-8.gist: The Washington DC SFRA and inner Flight Restricted Zone: comply with § 93.339, complete the § 91.161 special awareness training before flying within 60 nm of the DCA VOR, and watch for § 99.7 security NOTAMs.
3-5-8.why: Any pilot flying in the mid-Atlantic must have the DC SFRA course certificate; the FRZ is effectively closed to general aviation.

numbers.quote: A pilot conducting any type of flight operation in the Washington, DC, SFRA/FRZ must comply with the requirements in:

questions.q: What do I need before flying near Washington, DC?
questions.a: The § 91.161 special awareness training (a free online course) for flight within 60 nm of the DCA VOR, a flight plan and discrete squawk to enter the SFRA under § 93.339, and a check of the § 99.7 NOTAMs.

4-1-1.gist: Air Route Traffic Control Centers exist primarily for IFR aircraft in controlled airspace during the en route phase; VFR flight following from Center is a workload-permitting extra.
4-1-1.why: It explains who you are talking to when approach hands you off to 'Center' on a long cross-country.

numbers.quote: Centers are established primarily to provide air traffic service to aircraft operating on IFR flight plans within controlled airspace, and principally during the en route phase of flight.

questions.q: Can I get flight following from Center?
questions.a: Yes when workload permits; Center's primary job is IFR en route traffic, so VFR advisories may be refused or terminated when they are busy.

4-1-2.gist: Control towers provide a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of traffic on and around the airport, and where delegated they separate IFR aircraft in the terminal area.
4-1-2.why: It is the one-line definition behind every tower interaction in your training.

numbers.quote: Towers have been established to provide for a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of traffic on and in the vicinity of an airport.

questions.q: What does the control tower actually do for VFR traffic?
questions.a: Sequences and separates traffic on the runways and in the pattern, issues taxi, takeoff and landing clearances, and passes traffic information; it does not provide radar separation to VFR aircraft unless it has that delegation.

4-1-3.gist: Flight Service Stations provide pilot briefings, flight plan processing, en route advisories, search and rescue services and help for lost aircraft and emergencies; they relay clearances, process NOTAMs and broadcast weather. In Alaska some also take observations and give airport advisories.
4-1-3.why: When the examiner asks who you would call when lost or to open a flight plan, this is the answer.

numbers.quote: Flight Service Stations (FSSs) are air traffic facilities that provide pilot briefings, flight plan processing, en route flight advisories, search and rescue services, and assistance to lost aircraft and aircraft in emergency situations.

questions.q: What services does Flight Service offer a VFR pilot?
questions.a: Weather briefings, filing, opening and closing flight plans, en route weather and NOTAM updates, search and rescue alerting, and help if you are lost or in trouble, on 122.2 or the frequencies on the chart.

4-1-9.gist: Operating at an airport without an operating control tower: use the CTAF (a UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS or tower frequency listed in the Chart Supplement), use the airport's correct name, and self-announce. Inbound: monitor and report from 10 miles out, entering downwind, base and final, and leaving the runway. Outbound: report before taxiing and before taxiing onto the runway, and monitor until 10 miles out. Where there is no tower, FSS or UNICOM, self-announce on MULTICOM 122.9.
4-1-9.why: Non-towered radio work is a checkride task and the 10-mile, downwind, base, final, clear-of-runway sequence is what the examiner listens for.

numbers.quote: The acronym CTAF which stands for Common Traffic Advisory Frequency, is synonymous with this program.

numbers.value: MULTICOM 122.9 when there is no tower, FSS or UNICOM
numbers.quote: Self‐announce on MULTICOM frequency 122.9.

numbers.value: Inbound calls: 10 miles, downwind, base, final, leaving the runway
numbers.quote: 10 miles out. Entering downwind, base, and final. Leaving the runway.

numbers.value: Outbound calls: before taxiing and before taking the runway
numbers.quote: Before taxiing and before taxiing on the runway for departure.
Pilots of inbound traffic should monitor and communicate as appropriate on the designated CTAF from 10 miles to landing.

traps: Say the airport name at the start and end of every call; the same CTAF is shared by several airports within radio range.
A UNICOM operator's advisory is not a clearance and may be wrong; look at the windsock.

questions.q: What radio calls do I make arriving at a non-towered airport?
questions.a: On the CTAF: about 10 miles out with position, altitude and intentions; entering downwind; turning base; turning final; and when clear of the runway, each starting and ending with the airport name.

4-1-11.gist: The FCC frequency plan: 122.700, 122.725, 122.800, 122.975, 123.000, 123.050 and 123.075 for UNICOM at airports without a tower; 122.900 MULTICOM where there is no tower, FSS or UNICOM; 122.950 UNICOM at towered airports; 122.750 for fixed-wing air-to-air; 123.300 and 123.500 for flight instruction, gliders and balloons.
4-1-11.why: The knowledge test asks which frequency is MULTICOM and which is air-to-air.

numbers.quote: (MULTICOM FREQUENCY) Activities of a temporary, seasonal, emergency nature or search and rescue, as well as, airports with no tower, FSS, or UNICOM.
Airports with a control tower or FSS on airport.

questions.q: Which frequency do two airplanes use to talk to each other?
questions.a: 122.750 for private fixed-wing air-to-air; 123.025 is the helicopter air-to-air frequency.

4-1-13.gist: ATIS is a continuous recorded broadcast of routine airport information (weather, runways in use, approaches, NOTAMs) identified by a phonetic letter. Tell the controller on initial contact that you have the current letter so the information need not be repeated. Ceiling and visibility are omitted when the ceiling is above 5,000 ft and visibility more than 5 miles. Saying 'have numbers' means only wind, runway and altimeter, never the ATIS.
4-1-13.why: The examiner will expect 'with information Bravo' on your first call and may ask what a missing ceiling on the ATIS means.

numbers.quote: ATIS is the continuous broadcast of recorded noncontrol information in selected high activity terminal areas.

numbers.value: Ceiling and visibility omitted above 5,000 ft and 5 miles
numbers.quote: The ceiling/sky condition, visibility, and obstructions to vision may be omitted from the ATIS broadcast if the ceiling is above 5,000 feet and the visibility is more than 5 miles.
Pilots should notify controllers on initial contact that they have received the ATIS broadcast by repeating the alphabetical code word appended to the broadcast.
It does not indicate receipt of the ATIS broadcast and should never be used for this purpose.

questions.q: The ATIS gives wind and altimeter but no ceiling or visibility. Why?
questions.a: Because the ceiling is above 5,000 ft and visibility more than 5 miles; the AIM allows those items to be omitted then.

4-1-15.gist: Radar traffic information service ('flight following'): the controller points out targets that may conflict, by clock position, distance, direction of travel and type and altitude if known. Clock position is based on your track, so with a crab the traffic appears offset. It is entirely at the controller's discretion, does not include vectors away from traffic unless you ask, and never relieves you of see-and-avoid. Monitor the frequency continuously and, when you no longer want the service, tell the controller before switching and squawk 1200.
4-1-15.why: The examiner asks how to request, use and terminate flight following, and what a clock call really means.

numbers.quote: This service is not intended to relieve the pilot of the responsibility for continual vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft.
Azimuth from the aircraft in terms of the 12 hour clock, or

numbers.value: Ending the service: tell ATC, then squawk 1200
numbers.quote: advise the controller before changing frequencies and then change your transponder code to 1200

traps: The clock position is relative to your ground track, not your heading; crabbing 20 degrees right puts 12 o'clock traffic at about 11 o'clock out the window.
Uncorrected Mode C altitude in a traffic call is 'indicated' and may be wrong; look above and below the reported altitude.

questions.q: How do I request and end VFR flight following?
questions.a: Call the approach control or Center on the chart frequency with type, position, altitude and destination and request VFR traffic advisories; when done, tell the controller you are terminating and squawk 1200.

4-1-16.gist: A safety alert is issued when the controller sees an aircraft under their control in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft: a terrain or obstruction alert (often from Minimum Safe Altitude Warning on Mode C) or an aircraft conflict alert with a suggested heading or altitude. VFR aircraft with Mode C can request MSAW monitoring.
4-1-16.why: It is the one mandatory ATC service for VFR aircraft and the source of the 'low altitude alert, check your altitude immediately' call.

numbers.value: When a safety alert is issued
numbers.quote: A safety alert will be issued to pilots of aircraft being controlled by ATC if the controller is aware the aircraft is at an altitude which, in the controller's judgment, places the aircraft in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft.
Pilots operating VFR may request MSAW monitoring if their aircraft are equipped with Mode C transponders.

questions.q: What should I do when ATC says 'low altitude alert'?
questions.a: Check your altitude and position immediately, climb if in doubt, and tell the controller what you are doing; the alert is advisory but it means the controller thinks you are too low for the terrain ahead.

4-1-17.gist: Radar-equipped facilities can give VFR aircraft vectors when you can communicate, are in radar coverage and are identified. The vectors are advisory: flying safely and legally stays with the pilot, so keep the controller told of the weather you are in and ahead so you are not vectored into IMC. Vectors may be started by the controller with your concurrence, under a published program, or when needed for safety.
4-1-17.why: The 'a vector is not permission to bust a cloud' point is what the examiner is testing when they ask about accepting a heading.

numbers.value: A vector does not authorize a violation
numbers.quote: Pilots should clearly understand that authorization to proceed in accordance with such radar navigational assistance does not constitute authorization for the pilot to violate CFRs.

numbers.value: Keep ATC told about the weather
numbers.quote: pilots should keep controllers advised of the weather conditions in which they are operating and along the course ahead

questions.q: Approach assigns a heading that will take me into a cloud. What do I do?
questions.a: Tell them 'unable, VFR' and the reason; a vector to a VFR aircraft is advisory and never authorizes you to violate the cloud clearance rules.

4-1-18.gist: Terminal radar services for VFR aircraft come in tiers: basic radar service (safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring and, at some airports, sequencing); TRSA service (separation and sequencing, voluntary, decline with 'negative TRSA service'); Class C service (separation between IFR and VFR plus sequencing to the primary airport); and Class B service (separation of all aircraft). Contact approach about 25 miles out where sequencing is provided. None of it relieves you of see-and-avoid, wake avoidance, terrain clearance or VFR weather minimums, and the Class B clearance and Class C contact requirements stand even when radar is down.
4-1-18.why: It is the difference between flight following, a TRSA and Class C in one place, which is exactly how the oral tends to ask it.

numbers.value: Contact approach about 25 miles out for sequencing
numbers.quote: Pilots of arriving VFR aircraft should initiate radio contact on the publicized frequency with approach control when approximately 25 miles from the airport at which sequencing services are being provided.
Class C Service. This service provides, in addition to basic radar service, approved separation between IFR and VFR aircraft, and sequencing of VFR arrivals to the primary airport.

numbers.value: TRSA separation: 500 ft vertical, visual or target resolution
numbers.quote: 500 feet vertical separation.

numbers.value: Radar out does not cancel entry requirements
numbers.quote: The absence of ATC radar does not negate the requirement of an ATC clearance to enter Class B airspace or two way radio contact with ATC to enter Class C airspace.

traps: Being told to follow another aircraft does not let you act on any clearance issued to that aircraft.
In a TRSA, ATC may assign an altitude that does not match the VFR hemispheric rule; go back to a legal altitude when told to resume appropriate VFR altitudes.

questions.q: What does Class C service give me that flight following does not?
questions.a: Approved separation between you and IFR traffic and sequencing to the primary airport; basic radar service only gives advisories, safety alerts and limited vectors.

4-1-20.gist: Squawk 1200 for VFR with altitude reporting on; the transponder and ADS-B Out stay on from pushback to parking, ident only when asked, never squawk 7777, and avoid passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700 when changing codes.
4-1-20.why: The emergency codes are on every written; the ground-operation rule is a common oral question.

numbers.quote: Code 1200
Code 7777

questions.q: What do I squawk VFR, and what are the emergency codes?
questions.a: 1200; 7500 for hijack, 7600 for radio failure, 7700 for an emergency.

4-2-1.gist: The single most important thing in radio communication is understanding: acknowledge every ATC transmission with your call sign, be brief but tell the controller what you want, and use the Pilot/Controller Glossary phraseology rather than jargon or CB slang.
4-2-1.why: Radio competence is graded on the checkride and this paragraph is the standard the examiner uses.

numbers.quote: It is essential, therefore, that pilots acknowledge each radio communication with ATC by using the appropriate aircraft call sign.
Jargon, chatter, and “CB” slang have no place in ATC communications.

questions.q: What must every reply to ATC include?
questions.a: Your call sign, plus a readback of the key items (runway, hold-short, altitude, heading); the point is that both of you know exactly what was said.

4-2-2.gist: Radio technique: listen before you transmit, think before you key, hold the mic close and pause after keying, wait a few seconds before calling again, watch for a stuck mic, and remember VHF is line of sight so altitude extends range.
4-2-2.why: It is the fix for most early radio problems: stepping on people, half-words and calling the same facility three times.

numbers.quote: Think before keying your transmitter.
When you release the button, wait a few seconds before calling again.
Remember that higher altitudes increase the range of VHF “line of sight” communications.

questions.q: Why can I hear Flight Service but not reach them?
questions.a: Remote outlets do not always receive on every frequency they transmit on, and VHF is line of sight; climb or use a frequency listed above the FSS box on the chart.

4-2-3.gist: Initial contact format: the facility you are calling, your full aircraft identification, your position if on the airport surface, your request if short, and 'over' if needed; add position, altitude and the ATIS letter when reception is good. Acknowledge every frequency change and make it as soon as possible unless told to change at a time, fix or altitude. 'Change to my frequency' means the same controller and an abbreviated call.
4-2-3.why: The examiner listens to your first call to ground; this is the template.

numbers.value: Start with who you are calling
numbers.quote: Name of the facility being called;
Your full aircraft identification as filed in the flight plan or as discussed in paragraph 4-2-4, Aircraft Call Signs;
When advised by ATC to change frequencies, acknowledge the instruction.

numbers.value: Change frequency as soon as possible
numbers.quote: When instructed by ATC to change frequencies, select the new frequency as soon as possible unless instructed to make the change at a specific time, fix, or altitude.

questions.q: What is the correct format for an initial call to ground control?
questions.a: 'Columbia Ground, Cessna Three One Six Zero Foxtrot, south ramp, ready to taxi with information Delta, VFR to Memphis': facility, full call sign, position, request, ATIS.

mnemonics: Who you are calling, who you are, where you are, what you want.

4-2-4.gist: Call signs: never abbreviate on initial contact or when similar call signs are on frequency; ATC may shorten yours to the last three characters and then you may too. Civil aircraft state the type or manufacturer and the registration without the N; air taxis without authorized call signs prefix 'Tango'; MEDEVAC is for urgent medical priority only; and student pilots should say 'student pilot' on initial contact with each facility to get extra help.
4-2-4.why: The 'student pilot' identification is a gift the AIM offers you and the examiner may ask whether you know it.

numbers.quote: Call signs should never be abbreviated on an initial contact or at any time when other aircraft call signs have similar numbers/sounds or identical letters/number

numbers.value: Drop the N when you state the type
numbers.quote: When the aircraft manufacturer's name or model is stated, the prefix “N” is dropped; e.g., Aztec Two Four Six Four Alpha.
student pilots need only identify themselves as a student pilot during their initial call to an FAA radio facility
Dayton tower, Fleetwing One Two Three Four, student pilot.

questions.q: Should I tell the tower I am a student pilot?
questions.a: Yes; the AIM recommends identifying yourself as a student pilot on initial contact with each facility so controllers can give extra assistance and slower instructions.

4-2-7.gist: The ICAO phonetic alphabet (Alfa through Zulu) is used when conditions make plain letters hard to copy, and pilots should use it when identifying their aircraft on initial contact and whenever similar call signs are on frequency.
4-2-7.why: You must be fluent in it before the first solo radio call.

numbers.value: Use it for your call sign
numbers.quote: Pilots should use the phonetic alphabet when identifying their aircraft during initial contact with air traffic control

questions.q: How do I say N1234F on the radio?
questions.a: Cessna One Two Three Four Foxtrot on initial contact; after ATC abbreviates it, Cessna Three Four Foxtrot.

4-2-8.gist: Speaking numbers: round hundreds and thousands up to 9,900 are spoken as words ('four thousand five hundred'); above 9,900 the digits before 'thousand' are separated ('one zero thousand'); airways as 'Victor Twelve'; all other numbers digit by digit; and a frequency's decimal is 'point'.
4-2-8.why: The examiner listens for 'one zero thousand five hundred', not 'ten five'.

numbers.quote: 4,500 four thousand five hundred
10,000 one zero thousand
122.1 one two two point one

questions.q: How do I say 13,500 feet and 118.7?
questions.a: 'One three thousand five hundred' and 'one one eight point seven'.

4-2-9.gist: Altitudes below 18,000 ft are spoken as the separate digits of the thousands plus the hundreds ('one two thousand five hundred'); at and above 18,000 say 'flight level' and the digits ('flight level one niner zero').
4-2-9.why: It is the phraseology you use in every position report and altitude readback.

numbers.quote: 12,500 one two thousand five hundred
190 Flight Level One Niner Zero

questions.q: How do I read back 'maintain 4,500'?
questions.a: 'Maintain four thousand five hundred, Cessna Three Four Foxtrot'.

4-2-13.gist: Radio failure at a towered airport. Receiver out: stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you have the traffic flow, then tell the tower your type, position, altitude and intentions and ask for light signals. Transmitter out: same, then join the pattern, monitor tower, and watch for light signals, acknowledging by rocking wings by day or blinking the landing light at night. Both out: join the pattern and watch the tower. Departing with a dead radio: phone the tower for authorization.
4-2-13.why: Combined with the light-gun table it is the complete answer to 'your radio dies in the pattern, what now?'

numbers.value: Stay outside or above the Class D until you know the flow
numbers.quote: remain outside or above the Class D surface area until the direction and flow of traffic has been determined

numbers.value: Call the tower at 3 to 5 miles
numbers.quote: When you are approximately 3 to 5 miles from the airport, advise the tower of your position and join the airport traffic pattern.

numbers.value: Acknowledge by day by rocking wings
numbers.quote: During hours of daylight, acknowledge tower transmissions or light signals by rocking your wings.

traps: With only the receiver dead you still transmit in the blind: the tower may hear you even though you cannot hear them.
A dead radio before taxi is not an emergency; the AIM's answer is a telephone call to the tower, not a departure on light signals you never asked for.

questions.q: My transmitter fails 10 miles from a Class D airport. What do I do?
questions.a: Squawk 7600 if able, stay outside the Class D until you see the traffic flow, enter the pattern, monitor the tower frequency and watch for light signals, acknowledging with a wing rock by day or the landing light at night.

4-2-14.gist: Talking to Flight Service in flight: 122.2 is the common en route frequency for most FSSs, with other frequencies listed on the chart; state the frequency you are using and your location on the initial call so the specialist knows which transmitter to answer on.
4-2-14.why: It is how you update a flight plan or get weather en route without a data link.

numbers.quote: 122.2 MHz is assigned to the majority of FSSs as a common en route simplex frequency

numbers.value: State frequency and location on callup
numbers.quote: In order to expedite communications, state the frequency being used and the aircraft location during initial callup.

questions.q: How do I call Flight Service in flight?
questions.a: On 122.2 or the frequency printed above the FSS box on the chart: 'Dayton Radio, Cessna One Two Three Four Five on one two two point two, over Springfield VOR'.

4-3-1.gist: Why airport operations get their own section: congestion, climbing and descending traffic, cockpit distraction and marginal weather all pile up near the airport, so the AIM asks for extra alertness there and lays out the rules and practices that follow.
4-3-1.why: It frames the whole of Section 4-3, which the checkride's airport-operations tasks are built on.

numbers.quote: Pilots must be particularly alert when operating in the vicinity of an airport.

questions.q: Why are most midair collisions near airports?
questions.a: Traffic converges there, aircraft are climbing and descending through each other's altitudes, and pilots are busy with checklists and radios; the AIM says be particularly alert in the vicinity of an airport.

4-3-2.gist: At a towered airport keep two-way radio contact with the tower inside the Class B, C or D surface area, calling about 15 miles out. Fixed-wing aircraft circle to the left unless the tower says otherwise. The standard pattern legs are departure, upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final; the departure climb continues to at least a half mile past the runway end and within 300 ft of pattern altitude. Tower radar displays are for the controller's efficiency, and suggested headings from the tower are advisory.
4-3-2.why: Pattern terminology and the 15-mile call are what the examiner expects on the way home from the practice area.

numbers.quote: Initial callup should be made about 15 miles from the airport.

numbers.value: Circle to the left unless told otherwise
numbers.quote: If not otherwise authorized or directed by the tower, pilots of fixed-wing aircraft approaching to land must circle the airport to the left.

numbers.value: Departure leg: half mile past the runway, within 300 ft of pattern altitude
numbers.quote: The departure climb continues until reaching a point at least 1/2 mile beyond the departure end of the runway and within 300 feet of the traffic pattern altitude.
Base leg. A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its approach end and extending from the downwind leg to the intersection of the extended runway centerline.

traps: A tower's 'suggested heading' is not a radar vector; you remain responsible for see-and-avoid and for staying VFR.

questions.q: When should I turn crosswind after takeoff?
questions.a: The AIM's departure leg runs to at least a half mile beyond the runway end and to within 300 ft of pattern altitude before the crosswind turn, unless the tower directs otherwise.

4-3-3.gist: The standard traffic pattern: enter in level flight abeam midfield at pattern altitude (1,000 ft AGL for propeller aircraft unless the Chart Supplement says otherwise), all turns left unless RP is charted, turn crosswind beyond the departure end within 300 ft of pattern altitude, complete the turn to final at least 1/4 mile out, depart straight out or with a 45° turn beyond the departure end.
4-3-3.why: Pattern entry, altitudes and turn direction are asked on the written and demonstrated on every flight.

numbers.quote: 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL)

numbers.value: Large and turbine: 1,500 ft AGL or 500 above the pattern
numbers.quote: not less than 1,500 feet AGL or 500 feet above the established pattern altitude

numbers.value: Turn final at least 1/4 mile out
numbers.quote: Complete turn to final at least 1/4 mile from the runway

numbers.value: Turn crosswind within 300 ft of pattern altitude
numbers.quote: within 300 feet of pattern altitude

questions.q: What altitude is the traffic pattern?
questions.a: 1,000 feet AGL for propeller aircraft unless the Chart Supplement publishes another; large and turbine aircraft fly 1,500 feet AGL.

4-3-4.gist: At a non-towered airport the segmented circle shows the pattern: the wind sock or tee gives wind, a tetrahedron (small end into the landing direction) gives landing direction, landing strip indicators show runway alignment and traffic pattern indicators show which runways use right traffic. Turns are to the left unless an indicator says right. When two aircraft are approaching to land, the lower one has the right-of-way but may not cut in front of one on final.
4-3-4.why: The examiner will show you a segmented circle diagram and ask which runway and which direction of traffic it calls for.

numbers.value: Wind cone: large end into the wind
numbers.quote: The large end of the wind cone/wind sock points into the wind as does the large end (cross bar) of the wind tee.

numbers.value: Tetrahedron: small end points to the landing direction
numbers.quote: The small end of the tetrahedron points in the direction of landing.

numbers.value: Left turns unless the indicator shows right
numbers.quote: When approaching for landing, all turns must be made to the left unless a traffic pattern indicator indicates that turns should be made to the right.

numbers.value: Lower aircraft has the right-of-way, but no cutting in
numbers.quote: However, the pilot operating at the lower altitude should not take advantage of another aircraft, which is on final approach to land, by cutting in front of, or overtaking that aircraft.

traps: The tetrahedron may be set by wind or locked by the airport; the AIM warns not to use it for anything but landing direction.

questions.q: How do I read the traffic pattern indicators in the segmented circle?
questions.a: Mentally enlarge the L-shaped indicator for your runway: the long leg is the final approach, the short leg is the base leg, so it shows whether base is flown from the left or right.

4-3-5.gist: Controllers sequence traffic on what they observe and what you tell them; an unexpected maneuver (a 360 on final, an unannounced go-around, an early turn) breaks the sequence and causes incidents. Fly what you said you would, and if you must change, say so first.
4-3-5.why: It is the AIM's reason for the checkride emphasis on telling the tower before you do something different.

numbers.value: ATC plans on your expected maneuvers
numbers.quote: These adjustments can only be based on observed traffic, accurate pilot reports, and anticipated aircraft maneuvers.

questions.q: The tower asked me to extend downwind and I would rather do a 360. May I?
questions.a: Not without asking; the tower sequenced the traffic on the extended downwind, and an unexpected 360 can put you nose to nose with the following aircraft.

4-3-6.gist: Runways are numbered by the magnetic azimuth to the nearest 10 degrees, and the tower's wind is magnetic in knots. ATC assigns the runway most aligned with a wind of 5 knots or more, otherwise the calm-wind runway, unless a runway use program applies; you may request another runway. Declared distances (TORA, TODA, ASDA, LDA) are what the airport operator says is available for takeoff, accelerate-stop and landing, and may be shorter than the pavement.
4-3-6.why: Runway numbers and the calm-wind rule are knowledge-test items; declared distances are how a short-field performance question turns into a legality question.

numbers.value: Runway numbers are the nearest 10 degrees magnetic
numbers.quote: Runways are identified by numbers that indicate the nearest 10-degree increment of the azimuth of the runway centerline.
ATC will assign the runway/s most nearly aligned with the wind when 5 knots or more, or the “calm wind” runway when less than 5 knots unless:
Landing Distance Available (LDA) - The runway length declared available and suitable for a landing airplane.

pilots must use the declared distances determined by the airport operator and not attempt to independently calculate declared distances by adding those elements to the reported physical length of the runway

questions.q: What runway number goes with a magnetic azimuth of 087?
questions.a: Runway 9; runways are numbered to the nearest 10 degrees of magnetic azimuth with the trailing zero dropped.

4-3-7.gist: Airports may have wind shear and microburst detection (LLWAS, TDWR, WSP, ITWS) whose alerts controllers relay: for LLWAS as airport wind followed by a boundary wind, and for the newer systems as a microburst or wind shear alert with the expected airspeed loss and location on final.
4-3-7.why: If you ever hear 'microburst alert, 40 knot loss, 3 mile final' you should know what it means before it is said.

numbers.quote: Wind shear alert, airport wind 230 at 8, south boundary wind 170 at 20.
Runway 17 arrival microburst alert, 40 knot loss 3 mile final.

questions.q: Tower says 'wind shear alert, airport wind 230 at 8, south boundary wind 170 at 20'. What does it mean?
questions.a: The LLWAS sensors disagree: the airport center reads one wind and the south boundary another, so expect a wind change on approach from the south. Consider delaying or going around.

4-3-11.gist: Land and hold short operations: ATC may clear you to land and hold short of an intersecting runway, taxiway or point. You may accept only if you can stop within the published Available Landing Distance, you must read back the hold-short instruction, and the PIC may decline. LAHSO needs at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 miles visibility, and the AIM says student pilots and pilots unfamiliar with LAHSO should not participate.
4-3-11.why: The examiner may ask whether you must accept a LAHSO clearance; the AIM's answer for a student is no.

numbers.quote: Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate in the program.
The pilot-in-command has the final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short clearance.
Pilots should read back their LAHSO clearance and include the words, “HOLD SHORT OF (RUNWAY/TAXIWAY/OR POINT)” in their acknowledgment of all LAHSO clearances.
Pilots should only receive a LAHSO clearance when there is a minimum ceiling of 1,000 feet and 3 statute miles visibility.

traps: Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance binds you like any other clearance; if a go-around becomes necessary, keep clear of the crossing traffic and tell the tower.

questions.q: Tower says 'cleared to land runway 27, hold short of runway 36'. Must I accept?
questions.a: No. As a student you should decline ('unable, request full length'); a private pilot may accept only after confirming the available landing distance is enough, and must read back the hold-short.

4-3-13.gist: The tower light-gun signals: steady green (cleared for takeoff / cleared to land), flashing green (cleared to taxi / return for landing), steady red (stop / give way and continue circling), flashing red (taxi clear of the runway / airport unsafe, do not land), flashing white (return to starting point on the airport), alternating red and green (exercise extreme caution). Acknowledge by day by moving the ailerons or rudder, at night by blinking the landing or navigation lights. At night, turn on a landing light to get the tower's attention.
4-3-13.why: You must know the table cold; § 91.125 makes it regulatory and the examiner will quiz it.

numbers.quote: Cleared to land
Return for landing (to be followed by steady green at the proper time)
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Airport unsafe, do not land
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return to starting point on airport
Exercise extreme caution
During daylight hours, acknowledge tower transmissions or light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder. At night, acknowledge by blinking the landing or navigation lights.

traps: Flashing green in flight means return for landing, not cleared to land; wait for the steady green.
The tower can only approve or disapprove what it thinks you intend; it cannot explain, so make your intentions obvious.

questions.q: What does a steady red light mean on the ground and in the air?
questions.a: On the ground: stop. In the air: give way to other aircraft and continue circling.

mnemonics: Steady = do it now; flashing = get ready or get out; white = go home; red-green = watch out.

4-3-14.gist: Departing a towered airport: call ground or clearance delivery before starting engines for taxi and clearance information, stay on ground during taxi and run-up, then switch to tower when ready for takeoff. Ground frequencies are mostly 121.6 to 121.9, so the controller may say 'ground point seven'; if in doubt about a frequency, ask.
4-3-14.why: It is the sequence of frequencies you will use on every departure from a towered field.

numbers.quote: The majority of ground control frequencies are in the 121.6-121.9 MHz bandwidth.
If the ground control frequency is in the 121 MHz bandwidth the controller may omit the numbers preceding the decimal point; e.g., 121.7, “CONTACT GROUND POINT SEVEN.”

questions.q: The tower says 'contact ground point niner'. What frequency is that?
questions.a: 121.9; ground control frequencies are almost all 121.6 to 121.9 so the controller may drop the 121.

4-3-18.gist: Taxiing at a towered airport: get approval before moving onto the movement area, state your position when you call, and get a clearance before taxiing on a runway, taking off or landing. Every runway crossing needs an explicit clearance and ATC never says 'cleared' for taxi. Read back the runway assignment, any clearance to enter a runway, and any hold-short or line-up-and-wait instruction. Ask for progressive taxi if unsure. A taxi clearance does not relieve you of avoiding other aircraft.
4-3-18.why: The runway-crossing and readback rules are the heart of the ACS runway-incursion risk items.

numbers.value: Approval before entering the movement area
numbers.quote: General. Approval must be obtained prior to moving an aircraft or vehicle onto the movement area during the hours an Airport Traffic Control Tower is in operation.

numbers.value: Explicit clearance for every runway crossing
numbers.quote: A clearance must be obtained prior to crossing any runway. ATC will issue an explicit clearance for all runway crossings.

numbers.value: ATC does not say 'cleared' for taxi
numbers.quote: In order to preclude misunderstandings in radio communications, ATC will not use the word “cleared” in conjunction with authorization for aircraft to taxi.

numbers.value: Read back: runway, runway entry, hold short or line up and wait
numbers.quote: Any instruction to hold short of a specific runway or line up and wait.

If the pilot is unfamiliar with the airport or for any reason confusion exists as to the correct taxi routing, a request may be made for progressive taxi instructions which include step-by-step routing directions.

traps: 'Runway 27, taxi via Alpha' does not let you enter or cross runway 27 anywhere along the way; you stop at its hold line until cleared for takeoff.
A taxi instruction to a point that crosses a runway includes the crossing clearance only if the controller says so.

questions.q: What must I read back from a taxi instruction?
questions.a: The assigned runway, any clearance to enter a specific runway, and any instruction to hold short or line up and wait; controllers must get a readback of hold-short instructions.

questions.q: Ground says 'runway 9, taxi via Bravo, cross runway 4'. Can I cross runway 4?
questions.a: Yes, because the crossing was explicitly cleared; without those words you would stop at the runway 4 hold line.

4-3-19.gist: In low visibility the tower may not be able to see you, so tell the controller at the first sign of difficulty or disorientation, use extreme caution taxiing toward the sun, and keep all attention on taxiing: checklists and non-essential radio calls wait until the aircraft is stopped with the brakes set.
4-3-19.why: 'Stop and set the brakes before the checklist' is a habit the examiner watches for on the taxi out.

numbers.quote: Checklists and nonessential communication should be withheld until the aircraft is stopped and the brakes set.

questions.q: I lose track of where I am on the airport in fog. What should I do?
questions.a: Stop, tell ground control immediately and ask for progressive taxi instructions; never guess your way across a runway.

4-3-20.gist: Standard taxi routes are pre-defined, published routes some airports use; you may request one by name if you know it, and requesting one means you are familiar with it. An STR instruction never includes a runway crossing and gives no right of way, and you may decline it or ask for full taxi instructions.
4-3-20.why: Big airports are starting to use them and the examiner may ask what an STR is.

numbers.quote: An STR instruction does not constitute nor imply a clearance to cross a runway.

numbers.value: Requesting one means you know it
numbers.quote: By requesting an STR, a pilot acknowledges full familiarity with the STR.

questions.q: Ground assigns a standard taxi route I have never seen. What do I do?
