questions.a: Ask for clarification or decline it and request detailed taxi instructions; an STR still requires an explicit clearance to cross any runway.

4-3-21.gist: After landing, exit at the first available taxiway or as instructed, without stopping or reversing on the runway. You are clear of the runway only when every part of the aircraft is past the hold-short markings, so taxi beyond them even if that means entering another taxiway. Then change to ground when told and get a taxi clearance; a taxi-to-parking clearance never authorizes entering or crossing a runway.
4-3-21.why: 'Clear of the runway' has a precise definition here, and controllers and examiners use it.

numbers.value: Clear means past the hold-short markings
numbers.quote: An aircraft is considered clear of the runway when all parts of the aircraft are past the runway edge and there are no restrictions to its continued movement beyond the runway holding position markings.
Exit the runway without delay at the first available taxiway or on a taxiway as instructed by ATC.

numbers.value: Parking clearance is not a runway clearance
numbers.quote: Ground control will issue taxi clearance to parking. That clearance does not authorize the aircraft to “enter” or “cross” any runways.

traps: Do not switch to ground on your own after landing; the tower will tell you when, after resolving conflicts on the taxiway you are about to enter.

questions.q: When am I clear of the runway after landing?
questions.a: When the whole aircraft, tail included, is past the runway hold-short markings on the taxiway you exited onto; stopping with the tail over the line is still on the runway.

4-3-24.gist: Aircraft lights: position lights are required from sunset to sunrise on the surface and in flight, and anti-collision lights whenever the aircraft operates, day or night, unless the PIC judges them a hazard. Operation Lights On encourages landing lights for takeoff and below 10,000 ft near airports. Turn on nav, beacon and strobes before taxi (strobes off if they blind others), all exterior lights when crossing or entering any runway, and landing lights when cleared for takeoff.
4-3-24.why: The lighting choreography is an ACS airport-operations item and the sunset-to-sunrise rule is regulatory.

numbers.value: Position lights sunset to sunrise; anti-collision lights always
numbers.quote: Aircraft position lights are required to be lighted on aircraft operated on the surface and in flight from sunset to sunrise. In addition, aircraft equipped with an anti-collision light system are required to operate that light system during all types of operations (day and night).

numbers.value: Landing lights below 10,000 ft near airports
numbers.quote: Pilots are further encouraged to turn on their landing lights when operating below 10,000 feet, day or night, especially when operating within 10 miles of any airport

numbers.value: All lights when on a runway
numbers.quote: At the discretion of the pilot-in-command, all exterior lights should be illuminated when taxiing on or across any runway.

numbers.value: Landing lights on with takeoff clearance
numbers.quote: Landing lights should be turned on when takeoff clearance is received or when commencing takeoff roll at an airport without an operating control tower.

questions.q: Which lights go on when, from engine start to takeoff?
questions.a: Beacon before start; nav, position and anti-collision lights before taxi; all exterior lights when crossing or entering a runway; landing lights when cleared for takeoff or starting the roll. Strobes off during taxi if they bother others.

4-3-27.gist: Many non-towered airports have ASOS or AWOS broadcasting one-minute weather, receivable within about 25 nm below 10,000 ft on the frequency in the Chart Supplement. Controllers issuing special VFR or IFR clearances there rely on you to report that weather, so state that you have the one-minute weather when you call.
4-3-27.why: A special VFR request at an uncontrolled airport depends on this: the controller often cannot see the weather you can hear.

numbers.value: One-minute weather within about 25 nm below 10,000 ft
numbers.quote: the one-minute updated airport weather should be available to you within approximately 25 NM of the airport below 10,000 feet

numbers.value: The controller relies on your report
numbers.quote: Controllers will rely on the pilot to determine the current airport weather from the ASOS/AWOS.

questions.q: How do I get a special VFR clearance into a non-towered Class E surface area?
questions.a: Listen to the ASOS or AWOS, then call the approach control or Center on the chart frequency, say you have the one-minute weather and request special VFR; you must have at least 1 mile visibility and stay clear of clouds.

4-4-6.gist: Special VFR: in a Class B, C, D or E surface area with weather below VFR you can ask for a clearance to enter, leave or operate there, traffic permitting. You must stay clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile flight visibility (and 1 mile ground visibility to take off or land); helicopters are exempt from the mile. Ask the tower, or in a Class E surface area the nearest tower, FSS or Center. No altitude is assigned because you must stay clear of clouds, and you are responsible for terrain and obstacles. Some Class B and C areas prohibit fixed-wing SVFR, and at night fixed-wing SVFR requires an instrument-rated pilot and an IFR-equipped aircraft.
4-4-6.why: The oral's 'can you get in with an 800 ft ceiling?' question is answered here together with § 91.157.

numbers.value: Clear of clouds, 1 mile flight visibility
numbers.quote: At least 1 statute mile flight visibility for operations within Class B, Class C, Class D, and Class E surface areas.

numbers.value: 1 mile ground visibility to take off or land
numbers.quote: At least 1 statute mile ground visibility if taking off or landing. If ground visibility is not reported at that airport, the flight visibility must be at least 1 statute mile.

When a control tower is located within the Class B, Class C, or Class D surface area, requests for clearances should be to the tower. In a Class E surface area, a clearance may be obtained from the nearest tower, FSS, or center.

numbers.value: Night: instrument rating and IFR equipment
numbers.quote: Special VFR operations by fixed-wing aircraft are prohibited between sunset and sunrise unless the pilot is instrument rated and the aircraft is equipped for IFR flight.
The pilot is responsible for obstacle or terrain clearance.

traps: ATC will not offer special VFR; you must request it, and 'traffic permitting' means IFR arrivals come first.
Once outside the surface area the clearance and its separation end, and you must meet the ordinary VFR minimums for the airspace you are in.

questions.q: The Class D reports 900 overcast and 2 miles. Can I depart VFR?
questions.a: Only with a special VFR clearance from the tower, which needs at least 1 mile ground visibility and lets you leave the surface area clear of clouds; a private pilot may do it by day, at night only with an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped airplane.

4-4-10.gist: Once you have a clearance you must follow it unless amended; execute it on receipt. 'Immediately' means urgency; a heading assignment means start the turn promptly. 'At pilot's discretion' lets you start a climb or descent when you like, at any rate, with level-offs, but you may not return to an altitude you have left. If emergency authority is used to deviate, tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance; if ATC gives you priority you may be asked for a report within 48 hours. The last clearance always supersedes the previous one.
4-4-10.why: It is the AIM companion to § 91.123 and the source of the 'pilot's discretion' and '48 hours' oral questions.

numbers.quote: When ATC issues a clearance or instruction, pilots are expected to execute its provisions upon receipt.

numbers.value: Pilot's discretion: no returning to a vacated altitude
numbers.quote: However, once the aircraft has vacated an altitude, it may not return to that altitude.
the pilot of such aircraft must, when requested by ATC, make a report within 48 hours of such emergency situation to the manager of that ATC facility
The guiding principle is that the last ATC clearance has precedence over the previous ATC clearance.

questions.q: What does 'descend at pilot's discretion' allow?
questions.a: Starting the descent when you choose, at any rate, with temporary level-offs, but once you leave an altitude you may not climb back to it.

4-4-15.gist: Clearing procedures and scanning: check the approach paths before taking the runway, make gentle clearing banks in climbs and descents, break up long straight-and-level periods with clearing turns, avoid descending into the pattern, be vigilant near VORs, verbalize 'clear left, clear right' during training, and raise the wing (high-wing) or lower it (low-wing) before turning. Know the scan's limits: instruments and tablets, blind spots, sun and haze, and the eye's refocus time; ADS-B In helps but does not show unequipped aircraft.
4-4-15.why: Clearing turns before every maneuver are a checkride requirement, and this is the AIM text behind them.

numbers.value: Scan the approach before taking the runway
numbers.quote: Prior to taxiing onto a runway or landing area in preparation for takeoff, pilots should scan the approach areas for possible landing traffic and execute the appropriate clearing maneuvers to provide them a clear view of the approach areas.

numbers.value: Do not descend into the pattern
numbers.quote: Entries into traffic patterns while descending create specific collision hazards and should be avoided.

numbers.value: High wing: raise the wing and look
numbers.quote: High-wing airplane. Momentarily raise the wing in the direction of the intended turn and look.

numbers.value: ADS-B In does not show everyone
numbers.quote: In certain airspace, not all aircraft will be equipped with ADS-B Out or transponders and will not be visible on your ADS-B In display.

questions.q: Why do I do clearing turns before a maneuver?
questions.a: To look into the blind spots (below and behind the wings and nose) before stalls, steep turns or slow flight; the AIM asks for clearing procedures before all turns and maneuvers.

4-5-7.gist: ADS-B basics: the aircraft broadcasts its GPS position about once a second on 978 MHz (UAT) or 1090 MHz (1090ES); ADS-B Out is required in the § 91.225 airspace and above 18,000 ft it must be 1090ES. The transmitted flight ID must match the flight plan call sign. UAT anonymous mode may be used only when not on an IFR flight plan and not requesting ATC services, with 1200 set. Keep the transponder and ADS-B on whenever operating. Unequipped aircraft may only enter ADS-B airspace with a pre-flight deviation, and if ATC issues a clearance into it you must say you are unequipped. ADS-B In traffic is for visual acquisition only, never for avoidance maneuvers.
4-5-7.why: The examiner will ask which link you have, where you may fly without it, and what to say if vectored into rule airspace unequipped.

numbers.quote: In the United States, ADS-B equipped aircraft exchange information on one of two frequencies: 978 or 1090 MHz.
In general, operators flying at 18,000 feet and above (Class A airspace) are required to have 1090ES equipment.

numbers.value: Flight ID must match the flight plan
numbers.quote: If ATC services are anticipated when either a VFR or IFR flight plan is filed, the aircraft identification (as entered in the flight plan) must be entered as the FLT ID in the ADS-B avionics.
Pilots of aircraft not equipped with ADS-B may only operate outside airspace designated as ADS-B airspace in 14 CFR §91.225.
ADS-B is intended only to assist in visual acquisition of other aircraft.

traps: An ATC-initiated clearance into ADS-B airspace is legal for an unequipped aircraft only because ATC initiated it; you may not request one except for safety of flight, and you should tell the controller you are negative ADS-B.

questions.q: Can I use a UAT (978 MHz) ADS-B Out for all my flying?
questions.a: Yes below 18,000 ft; Class A requires 1090ES. Either link satisfies § 91.225 in Class B, C, the Mode C veil and Class E above 10,000 ft.

4-5-9.gist: FIS-B is the free weather and aeronautical data broadcast over the 978 MHz UAT link within line of sight of a ground station: METARs, TAFs, NEXRAD, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, PIREPs, TFRs and NOTAMs, each with its own update interval. It does not replace a preflight briefing or in-flight updates from FSS or ATC, and the products have known latency.
4-5-9.why: Most training tablets show FIS-B; the examiner wants to know you understand its limits, especially radar age.

numbers.quote: FIS-B is a ground broadcast service provided through the ADS-B Services network over the 978 MHz UAT data link.

numbers.value: Not a substitute for a briefing
numbers.quote: FIS-B does not replace a preflight weather briefing from a source listed in paragraph 7-1-2, FAA Weather Services, or inflight updates from an FSS or ATC.

traps: FIS-B is only on 978 MHz; a 1090ES-only installation receives TIS-B traffic but no FIS-B weather.
The NEXRAD mosaic can be 15 to 20 minutes older than its time stamp; never use it to pick a path through storms.

questions.q: Can I rely on the FIS-B radar on my tablet to avoid thunderstorms?
questions.a: Only strategically, to route around an area; the mosaic is minutes old and the AIM says FIS-B must not be the sole weather source or be used for tactical avoidance.

5-1-1.gist: Preflight preparation: gather all information vital to the flight, decide whether it is safe, then file a flight plan. Self-briefing from automated sources is regulatory-compliant (see AC 91-92); if you call Flight Service, self-brief first and give them the type of flight, aircraft, departure, route, destination, altitude, ETD and ETE. Briefers must give NOTAMs in a standard briefing but not Domestic or International Notices unless asked. Use only current charts: sectionals are revised every 56 days.
5-1-1.why: It is the AIM's expansion of § 91.103 and the source of the 56-day chart cycle question.

numbers.quote: Pilots can receive a regulatory compliant briefing without contacting Flight Service.
FSSs are required to advise of pertinent NOTAMs if a standard briefing is requested, but if they are overlooked, do not hesitate to remind the specialist that you have not received NOTAM information.

In the conterminous U.S., Sectional Charts are updated every 56 days, IFR En Route Charts every 56 days, and amendments to civil IFR Approach Charts are accomplished on a 56-day cycle with a change notice volume issued on the 28-day midcycle.

questions.q: What do I tell the briefer when I call for a standard briefing?
questions.a: VFR or IFR, aircraft number or your name, aircraft type, departure airport, route, destination, altitude, ETD and ETE, so the briefing is tailored to the flight.

5-1-3.gist: The NOTAM system carries time-critical information not yet on charts. § 91.103 requires you to know it before flight. NOTAM (D) covers airports and navaids (runways, taxiways, lighting, obstructions); FDC NOTAMs are regulatory: chart and procedure amendments, TFRs, GPS and WAAS status, laser activity and special notices. Also review the ARTCC NOTAMs for the centers you cross, pointer NOTAMs, and GPS testing NOTAMs, and get destination updates en route.
5-1-3.why: 'What kinds of NOTAMs are there and where are TFRs?' is a stock oral question.

numbers.quote: Preflight. 14 CFR § 91.103, Preflight Action directs pilots to become familiar with all available information concerning a planned flight prior to departure, including NOTAMs.
Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFR) restrict entrance to a certain airspace at a certain time, however, some TFRs provide relief if ATC permission is given to enter the area when requested.
NOTAM (D) information includes taxiway closures, personnel and equipment near or crossing runways, and airport lighting aids that do not affect instrument approach criteria (i.e., VGSI).
NOTAMs may be disseminated up to 7 days before the start of activity.

questions.q: What is the difference between a NOTAM (D) and an FDC NOTAM?
questions.a: NOTAM (D)s report the status of airports and navaids (closures, lighting, obstructions); FDC NOTAMs are regulatory, covering TFRs, chart and procedure changes and GPS status.

5-1-5.gist: VFR flight plans: not required inside the continental U.S. except for DVFR into an ADIZ, but strongly recommended for search and rescue. File FAA Form 7233-4 (the international form), activate it with Flight Service by radio or electronically (towers do not), file a separate plan for each leg, and know that the proposal is held only two hours after the proposed departure time. An assumed departure time can activate it automatically but then you must update any changes.
5-1-5.why: Filing and activating a VFR flight plan is part of the cross-country planning task, and the 'towers do not activate it' point is a favorite.

numbers.value: Towers do not activate VFR flight plans
numbers.quote: Control tower personnel do not automatically activate VFR flight plans.
Within the continental U.S., a VFR flight plan is not normally required.
VFR flight plan proposals are normally retained for two hours following the proposed time of departure.
When a stopover flight is anticipated, it is recommended that a separate flight plan be filed for each leg of the flight.

questions.q: How do I open my VFR flight plan after takeoff?
questions.a: Call Flight Service on the radio (or use your app or an assumed departure time); the tower will not open it for you, and it expires two hours after the proposed departure if never activated.

5-1-12.gist: A change in flight plan includes altitude, route, destination and also speed: tell ATC when your true airspeed at cruise differs from the filed value by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater. Changes to a filed plan should be made with the original provider more than 46 minutes before departure; closer than that, through ATC or FSS.
5-1-12.why: It is a knowledge-test number (5 percent or 10 knots) and the practical answer to 'I filed for 100 knots and am doing 115'.

numbers.value: Speed change of 5 percent or 10 knots
numbers.quote: at any time the average true airspeed at cruising altitude between reporting points varies or is expected to vary from that given in the flight plan by plus or minus 5 percent, or 10 knots, whichever is greater, ATC should be advised

numbers.value: Changes more than 46 minutes before departure go to the original filer
numbers.quote: All changes to existing flight plans should be completed more than 46 minutes prior to the proposed departure time.

questions.q: When must I tell ATC my speed changed?
questions.a: When true airspeed varies from the filed value by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater.

5-1-13.gist: Filed flight plans that are never activated are deleted, usually 2 hours after the proposed departure time, so if you will be delayed 2 hours or more, revise the departure time with Flight Service or your filing service rather than over the ATC frequency.
5-1-13.why: It explains why a late departure can leave you with no flight plan and no search and rescue protection.

numbers.value: Deleted about 2 hours after the proposed departure
numbers.quote: Most centers have this parameter set so as to delete these flight plans a minimum of 2 hours after the proposed departure time or Expect Departure Clearance Time (EDCT).

questions.q: I filed for 10:00 but will not leave until 13:00. Is my flight plan still there?
questions.a: Probably not; unactivated plans are deleted about 2 hours after the proposed time. Update the departure time with Flight Service before you go.

5-1-14.gist: You are responsible for closing your VFR or DVFR flight plan with the nearest FSS or, through any ATC facility, by relay. Towers do not close them because they do not know who is on one. If the plan is not closed within a half hour after your ETA, search and rescue begins.
5-1-14.why: Closing the plan is the last item of every cross-country and the number the examiner asks is 30 minutes.

numbers.value: Search starts a half hour after ETA
numbers.quote: If you fail to report or cancel your flight plan within 1/2 hour after your ETA, search and rescue procedures are start

numbers.value: Towers do not close VFR flight plans
numbers.quote: Control towers do not automatically close VFR or DVFR flight plans since they do not know if a particular VFR aircraft is on a flight plan.

questions.q: I landed at a towered airport. Is my VFR flight plan closed?
questions.a: No. Close it yourself with Flight Service by radio, phone or app; if you forget, a search starts 30 minutes after your ETA.

5-6-13.gist: Military interception: NORAD fighters or helicopters may intercept to identify, track, inspect, divert or establish communications with an aircraft. Monitor 121.5 (guard); if intercepted, contact ATC immediately, follow the visual signals, and squawk 7700 unless told otherwise. Fighters approach from behind; if you do not comply they may fly across your path to divert you. Comply until positively released.
5-6-13.why: The ACS lists interception procedures as a knowledge element, and TFR violators meet them for real.

numbers.quote: All aircraft operating in US national airspace are highly encouraged to maintain a listening watch on VHF/UHF guard frequencies (121.5 or 243.0 MHz).

numbers.value: Call on guard with identity, position, nature of flight
numbers.quote: Attempt to establish radio communications with the intercepting aircraft or with the appropriate air traffic control facility by making a general call on guard frequencies (121.5 or 243.0 MHz), giving the identity, position, and nature of the flight.
If transponder equipped, select Mode 3/A Code 7700 unless otherwise instructed by air traffic control.
The crew of the intercepted aircraft must continue to comply with interceptor aircraft signals and instructions until positively released.

questions.q: A fighter appears off my left wing rocking its wings. What do I do?
questions.a: Rock your wings and follow it, call on 121.5 with your identity, position and nature of flight, squawk 7700, and keep complying with its signals until released.

5-6-14.gist: The ICAO interception signals: the interceptor rocking wings (with lights flashing at night) means you have been intercepted, follow me; you respond by rocking wings and following. A climbing breakaway turn of 90 degrees or more means you may proceed. Circling the airport, lowering the gear and overflying the runway means land here; you lower the gear, follow and land. Your own signals: raising the gear and flashing landing lights over the runway means the airfield is inadequate; regular switching of lights means cannot comply; irregular flashing means in distress.
5-6-14.why: The examiner may show you the table and ask what the interceptor is telling you.

numbers.quote: You have been intercepted. Follow me.

numbers.value: Breakaway climbing turn of 90 degrees or more: you may proceed
numbers.quote: DAY or NIGHT-An abrupt break-away maneuver from the intercepted aircraft consisting of a climbing turn of 90 degrees or more without crossing the line of flight of the intercepted aircraft.

numbers.value: Gear down, overfly runway: land here
numbers.quote: Land at this aerodrome.

numbers.value: Irregular flashing of all lights: in distress
numbers.quote: DAY or NIGHT-Irregular flashing of all available lights.

questions.q: The interceptor lowers its gear and overflies a runway. What does it want?
questions.a: It is telling you to land at that airport; you lower your gear, follow it, and land if the runway is safe after overflying it.

6-1-1.gist: The PIC is directly responsible for and the final authority on the operation of the aircraft, and in an emergency requiring immediate action may deviate from any rule of Part 91 Subparts A and B to the extent required. If that authority is used to deviate from a clearance, notify ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance.
6-1-1.why: It is the AIM statement of § 91.3, the first regulation every examiner asks about.

numbers.value: Final authority; deviate to meet an emergency
numbers.quote: In an emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot-in-command may deviate from any rule in 14 CFR part 91, Subpart A, General, and Subpart B, Flight Rules, to the extent required to meet that emergency.

numbers.value: Tell ATC and get an amended clearance
numbers.quote: If the emergency authority of 14 CFR section 91.3(b) is used to deviate from the provisions of an ATC clearance, the pilot-in-command must notify ATC as soon as possible and obtain an amended clearance.

questions.q: Which rules may I break in an emergency?
questions.a: Any rule in Part 91 Subparts A and B (the general and flight rules), only to the extent the emergency requires, and you must notify ATC of any clearance deviation as soon as possible.

6-1-2.gist: An emergency is a distress or an urgency condition. Pilots declare distress (fire, structural failure) readily but hesitate over urgency; the AIM says you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you become doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else that could affect safety. Ask for help immediately: delay has cost lives.
6-1-2.why: The examiner wants to hear that you would declare early when lost or low on fuel, and this is the paragraph that says so.

numbers.quote: An emergency can be either a distress or urgency condition as defined in the Pilot/Controller Glossary.
Pilots who become apprehensive for their safety for any reason should request assistance immediately.
Delay has caused accidents and cost lives. Safety is not a luxury! Take action!

questions.q: When should I declare an emergency?
questions.a: As soon as you are doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else affecting safety: that is already an urgency condition (PAN-PAN), and distress (MAYDAY) is for immediate danger.

6-2-1.gist: Radar can help a VFR pilot in difficulty with vectors, but the guidance is advisory and does not authorize violating the rules. Many non-instrument pilots lose control in clouds, so keep the controller told of the weather; if a VFR option exists take it rather than accept a vector into IMC; if VFR is not possible, tell the controller you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition.
6-2-1.why: 'Lost, weather closing in, what do you say to ATC?' is answered here word for word.

numbers.quote: If a course of action is available which will permit flight and a safe landing in VFR weather conditions, noninstrument rated pilots should choose the VFR condition rather than requesting a vector or approach that will take them into IFR weather conditions; or

numbers.value: Otherwise say you are not instrument rated and declare distress
numbers.quote: If continued flight in VFR conditions is not possible, the noninstrument rated pilot should so advise the controller and indicating the lack of an instrument rating, declare a distress condition; or

questions.q: I am lost and the clouds are lowering. What do I tell ATC?
questions.a: Squawk 7700, say you are lost, give your last known position, altitude and fuel, tell them the weather you are in, that you are not instrument rated, and ask for vectors to VFR conditions; declare distress if VFR cannot be maintained.

6-2-2.gist: In distress or urgency, squawk 7700 with Mode C to alert the radar facility, then establish communications as soon as possible; keep squawking because you may be outside radar coverage.
6-2-2.why: 7700 is the first thing to set when things go wrong and the examiner will ask why.

numbers.quote: should squawk Mode 3/A, Code 7700/Emergency and Mode C altitude reporting and then immediately establish communications with the ATC facility
Radar facilities are equipped so that Code 7700 normally triggers an alarm or special indicator at all control positions.

questions.q: What transponder codes should I know?
questions.a: 1200 VFR, 7500 hijack, 7600 lost communications, 7700 emergency.

mnemonics: 75 taken alive, 76 need a radio fix, 77 going to heaven.

6-2-4.gist: Emergency locator transmitters are required on most GA airplanes (§ 91.207). Older units transmit on 121.5 and 243.0 MHz, which satellites stopped monitoring in 2009; 406 MHz units are digital, registered with NOAA, and detected almost instantly. Armed ELTs activate on crash forces and run at least 48 hours. Test analog units only during the first 5 minutes after the hour, for no more than three sweeps; 406 units per the manufacturer; never airborne. Monitor 121.5 before shutdown to catch an accidental activation.
6-2-4.why: ELT type, testing and the 121.5 shutdown check are questions the examiner asks during the preflight and the emergency discussion.

numbers.quote: These operating frequencies are 121.5 MHz, 243.0 MHz, and the newer 406 MHz.
As of 2009, the Cospas-Sarsat system terminated monitoring and reception of the 121.5 MHz and 243.0 MHz frequencies.
The transmitters will operate continuously for at least 48 hours over a wide temperature range.

numbers.value: Test analog ELTs in the first 5 minutes after the hour, three sweeps
numbers.quote: Analog 121.5/243 MHz ELTs should only be tested during the first 5 minutes after any hour. If operational tests must be made outside of this period, they should be coordinated with the nearest FAA Control Tower. Tests should be no longer than three audible sweeps.
Airborne tests are not authorized.

questions.q: How and when may I test the ELT?
questions.a: An analog 121.5 ELT only in the first 5 minutes after the hour for no more than three sweeps, never in flight; a 406 MHz unit per its manual. Listen on 121.5 before engine shutdown to catch an inadvertent activation.

6-2-6.gist: Search and rescue is coordinated by the Coast Guard and Air Force rescue coordination centers. A filed flight plan is the most timely indicator that you are overdue; an Air Force study found 36 hours pass before family concern starts a search when there is no plan. File to the first landing point and refile each leg, report a landing elsewhere or a delay over 30 minutes to FSS, and close the plan on arrival. Survival equipment and body signals for rescue aircraft round out the paragraph.
6-2-6.why: The 'why file a VFR flight plan' argument the examiner wants is here, with numbers.

numbers.value: A flight plan is the best overdue indicator
numbers.quote: A filed flight plan is the most timely and effective indicator that an aircraft is overdue.
since 36 hours normally pass before family concern initiates an (alert)

numbers.value: Report delays of 30 minutes or more
numbers.quote: If your ETE changes by 30 minutes or more, report a new ETA to the nearest FSS and give them your original destination.

numbers.value: File to the first landing point
numbers.quote: For maximum protection, file only to the point of first intended landing, and refile for each leg to final destination.

questions.q: Why file a VFR flight plan if it is not required?
questions.a: Because it is the fastest trigger for search and rescue: without one it typically takes 36 hours before anyone raises the alarm, and the first 24 hours matter most to an injured survivor.

6-3-1.gist: Distress and urgency communications: start with MAYDAY (distress) or PAN-PAN (urgency), preferably three times. MAYDAY has absolute priority and silences the frequency; PAN-PAN has priority over everything but distress. Call the facility you are already talking to, otherwise the one responsible for the area, and if needed use 121.5 or 243.0, which towers, radar facilities and direction-finding stations guard.
6-3-1.why: The words to say and the frequency to say them on are the emergency-communications ACS element.

numbers.value: MAYDAY for distress, PAN-PAN for urgency
numbers.quote: The initial communication, and if considered necessary, any subsequent transmissions by an aircraft in distress should begin with the signal MAYDAY, preferably repeated three times. The signal PAN-PAN should be used in the same manner for an urgency condition.
Distress communications have absolute priority over all other communications, and the word MAYDAY commands radio silence on the frequency in use.
121.5 MHz and 243.0 MHz. Both have a range generally limited to line of sight.

questions.q: What is the difference between MAYDAY and PAN-PAN?
questions.a: MAYDAY is distress (immediate danger, needs help now) and silences the frequency; PAN-PAN is urgency (safety in doubt, help wanted) and takes priority over all but distress.

6-3-2.gist: Obtaining emergency assistance: climb if possible for better radio and radar reception; keep the assigned squawk if in contact, otherwise squawk 7700; then transmit MAYDAY or PAN-PAN with the station, your identification and type, nature of the problem, weather, intentions, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, people on board and anything else useful. Then comply with instructions, do not change frequency unless necessary, and if a crash or ditching is imminent give the extra items, turn on the ELT, and stay with the aircraft afterward.
6-3-2.why: The distress message format is what the examiner wants when they say 'your engine just quit, talk to me'.

numbers.quote: Climb, if possible, for improved communications, and better radar and direction finding detection.
If unable to immediately establish communications with an air traffic facility/agency, squawk Mode A/3, Code 7700/Emergency and Mode C.
Fuel remaining in minutes.

After a crash landing, unless you have good reason to believe that you will not be located by search aircraft or ground teams, it is best to remain with your aircraft and prepare means for signaling search aircraft.

questions.q: What goes in a MAYDAY call?
questions.a: MAYDAY three times, who you are calling, your call sign and type, the nature of the problem, weather, your intentions, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, souls on board, and anything else useful.

6-3-3.gist: Ditching: success depends on sea and wind first, aircraft type second, pilot skill third. Read the swell, land parallel to the primary swell on its crest or back side (never into the face), accept more crosswind to avoid it, judge wind from the streaks on the water, and touch down at the lowest safe speed with the nose up; with no power, carry extra speed to the flare.
6-3-3.why: Over-water flight to an island or across a bay makes this a realistic emergency discussion.

numbers.quote: A successful aircraft ditching is dependent on three primary factors. In order of importance they are:

numbers.value: Avoid the face of a swell
numbers.quote: Remember one axiom- AVOID THE FACE OF A SWELL.
In ditching parallel to the swell, it makes little difference whether touchdown is on the top of the crest or in the trough.

questions.q: Which way do I land when ditching?
questions.a: Parallel to the primary swell, on the crest or its back side, choosing the direction with the most headwind component; only a strong wind justifies landing into it across the swell.

6-4-1.gist: Two-way radio failure: whether it is an emergency is the pilot's call, and § 91.3(b) allows deviation as needed. Under IFR, § 91.185 governs: in VFR conditions, or when VFR is encountered, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable; in IFR conditions fly the route assigned, vectored, expected or filed, at the highest of the assigned, minimum IFR or expected altitude for each segment, and leave the clearance limit at the expect-further-clearance time or ETA.
6-4-1.why: For a VFR pilot the takeaway is the first rule: with a dead radio in VFR, land as soon as practicable, and know the light signals.

numbers.value: The pilot decides whether it is an emergency
numbers.quote: Whether two‐way communications failure constitutes an emergency depends on the circumstances, and in any event, it is a determination made by the pilot.

numbers.value: In VFR conditions: continue VFR and land as soon as practicable
numbers.quote: VFR conditions. If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, each pilot must continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.

questions.q: My radio quits on a VFR cross-country. What do I do?
questions.a: Squawk 7600, stay VFR, land as soon as practicable at a suitable airport (a non-towered one is simplest), and at a towered airport follow the radio-failure arrival and light-signal procedures.

6-4-2.gist: If you lose two-way radio capability, set the transponder to 7600 so ATC sees it, remembering you may be outside radar coverage.
6-4-2.why: 7600 is the one code you set without being asked when the radio dies.

numbers.quote: If an aircraft with a coded radar beacon transponder experiences a loss of two‐way radio capability, the pilot should adjust the transponder to reply on Mode A/3, Code 7600.

questions.q: What code do I squawk for lost communications?
questions.a: 7600; then follow the VFR radio-failure procedures and watch for light signals at a towered airport.

7-1-1.gist: Aviation weather is a joint NOAA, NWS, FAA and DoD effort with the FAA as the meteorological authority. The NWS runs the observing network and forecasts: automated METARs and SPECIs, TAFs for over 700 airports valid 24 or 30 hours, SIGMETs and AIRMETs from the Aviation Weather Center and its Alaska and Hawaii counterparts, and the specialized centers (SPC, NHC, SWPC, WPC). The Aviation Weather Handbook, FAA-H-8083-28, describes the products.
7-1-1.why: It names the sources behind everything on aviationweather.gov and the handbook the examiner expects you to have read.

numbers.quote: Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF) are prepared by 123 NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) for over 700 airports. These forecasts are valid for 24 or 30 hours and amended as required.
Details on the products provided by the above listed offices and centers is available in FAA-H-8083-28, Aviation Weather Handbook.

questions.q: Who issues SIGMETs and AIRMETs?
questions.a: The NWS Aviation Weather Center in Kansas City for the contiguous U.S., the Alaska Aviation Weather Unit and the Honolulu forecast office for their regions.

7-1-2.gist: FAA weather services: Flight Service by phone at 1-800-WX-BRIEF or online at 1800wxbrief.com, and the automated surface observations (METAR) with human augmentation at larger airports. The SPECI table lists what triggers a special report: a wind shift of 45 degrees or more in under 15 minutes at 10 knots or more, visibility crossing 3, 2, 1, half or quarter mile, ceilings crossing 3,000, 1,500, 1,000 or 500 ft, a thunderstorm beginning or ending, tornadoes, hail, freezing precipitation, squalls, and aircraft mishaps.
7-1-2.why: Knowing what makes a SPECI is the answer to 'why is there a second report this hour?'

numbers.value: SPECI for a wind shift of 45 degrees in under 15 minutes
numbers.quote: Wind direction changes by 45° or more, in less than 15 minutes, and the wind speed is 10 kt or more throughout the wind shift.

questions.q: What is a SPECI?
questions.a: A special METAR issued off-schedule when a listed threshold is crossed: a big wind shift, visibility or ceiling passing a critical value, a thunderstorm starting or ending, hail, freezing precipitation and similar events.

7-1-3.gist: Weather information comes in three types: observations (raw sensor data), analysis (interpreted observations) and forecasts. Approved sources are the Federal Government (FAA and NWS), FAA-authorized Enhanced Weather Information Systems for certificate holders, and commercial providers who repackage or add to government products. Part 91 operators are encouraged to use FAA and NWS products, must base every decision on all available pertinent products, and should check what a third-party source actually provides.
7-1-3.why: The 'observations, analysis, forecasts' triad is an ACS knowledge element, and the examiner may ask whether your app is an approved source.

numbers.quote: Observations. Raw weather data collected by some type of sensor suite including surface and airborne observations, radar, lightning, satellite imagery, and profilers.
Forecasts. Predictions of the development and/or movement of weather phenomena based on meteorological observations and various mathematical models.
All flight-related, aviation weather decisions must be based on all available pertinent weather products.

questions.q: Is the weather in my flight-planning app an approved source?
questions.a: If it repackages FAA and NWS products without changing them it carries the same standing; if the vendor adds its own forecasts you should review their description of the service. Either way, base the decision on all available products.

7-1-4.gist: The Graphical Forecasts for Aviation website (aviationweather.gov/gfa) replaced the text area forecast: gridded clouds, ceiling and visibility, precipitation, thunderstorms, winds, turbulence and icing from 14 hours in the past to 15 hours ahead, with observation tabs for METARs, PIREPs and radar and satellite, plus static Aviation Cloud Forecast and Aviation Surface Forecast images.
7-1-4.why: The examiner will expect you to have used the GFA for your cross-country plan and to know it superseded the area forecast.

numbers.quote: can be viewed from 14 hours in the past to 15 hours in the future
explore the enhanced digital and graphical weather products designed to replace the legacy FA

questions.q: Where do I get an en route forecast for a VFR cross-country now that area forecasts are gone?
questions.a: The Graphical Forecasts for Aviation on aviationweather.gov: ceiling and visibility, clouds, precipitation, turbulence and icing grids out to 15 hours, plus the Aviation Cloud and Surface Forecast images.

7-1-5.gist: Preflight briefings from Flight Service: a Standard briefing when you have had no prior information (adverse conditions, a 'VFR flight not recommended' advisory when the briefer judges VFR doubtful, synopsis, current conditions if departing within 2 hours, en route forecast, destination forecast, winds aloft in knots and degrees true, NOTAMs, ATC delays, and on request SUA status, density altitude and RAIM); an Abbreviated briefing to update or fill gaps; and an Outlook briefing when departure is six or more hours away.
7-1-5.why: The three briefing types and the meaning of 'VFR flight not recommended' are standard knowledge-test and oral questions.

numbers.quote: Standard Briefing. You should request a Standard Briefing any time you are planning a flight and you have not received a previous briefing or have not received preliminary information through online resources.
This recommendation is advisory in nature.

numbers.value: Current conditions omitted if departure is beyond 2 hours
numbers.quote: This element will be omitted if the proposed time of departure is beyond 2 hours, unless the information is specifically requested by the pilot.

numbers.value: Winds aloft: knots and degrees true
numbers.quote: Forecast winds aloft will be provided in knots and degrees, referenced to true north.

numbers.value: Outlook briefing: six or more hours ahead
numbers.quote: Outlook Briefing. You should request an Outlook Briefing whenever your proposed time of departure is six or more hours from the time of the briefing.

traps: Winds aloft are true, not magnetic; convert before computing headings.
MOA, MTR and warning-area NOTAMs are 'on request' items; ask for them.

questions.q: What does 'VFR flight not recommended' mean legally?
questions.a: Nothing binding: it is the briefer's advisory that conditions make VFR doubtful; the go or no-go decision is still the pilot's, and ignoring it without good reason is poor judgment.

7-1-6.gist: In-flight advisories. SIGMETs (non-convective) cover severe icing, severe or extreme turbulence or clear air turbulence, dust or sand storms below 3 miles, and volcanic ash; valid 4 hours (6 for tropical cyclones and ash). Convective SIGMETs cover severe thunderstorms (winds 50 knots or more, hail 3/4 inch or more, tornadoes), embedded storms, lines, and heavy precipitation over 40 percent of at least 3,000 square miles; any convective SIGMET implies severe turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear; issued hourly at H+55 for the western, central and eastern U.S. AIRMETs (Sierra for IFR and mountain obscuration, Tango for turbulence, surface winds and wind shear, Zulu for icing and freezing level) are lower-intensity, scheduled every 6 hours. Center Weather Advisories are the ARTCC's short-term product.
7-1-6.why: Examiners ask what each advisory means for a VFR pilot; an AIRMET Sierra on your route is a red flag.

numbers.value: SIGMET valid 4 hours (6 for tropical cyclone or ash)
numbers.quote: Are unscheduled products that are valid for 4 hours; except SIGMETs associated with tropical cyclones and volcanic ash clouds are valid for 6 hours.
Severe icing not associated with thunderstorms.

numbers.value: Convective SIGMET: winds 50 knots or more
numbers.quote: Surface winds greater than or equal to 50 knots.

numbers.value: Convective SIGMET: hail 3/4 inch or more
numbers.quote: Hail at the surface greater than or equal to 3/4 inches in diameter.

numbers.value: Any convective SIGMET implies severe turbulence, icing and wind shear
numbers.quote: Any convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing, and low-level wind shear.
Bulletins are issued hourly at H+55.
AIRMETs contain details about IFR conditions, extensive mountain obscuration, turbulence, strong surface winds, icing, and freezing levels.
Are issued on a scheduled basis every 6 hours, except every 8 hours in Alaska.

questions.q: What is the difference between an AIRMET and a SIGMET?
questions.a: Both warn of en route hazards; a SIGMET is for severe phenomena affecting all aircraft (severe icing, severe turbulence, dust storms, ash, and convective SIGMETs for severe thunderstorms), while an AIRMET covers the same kinds of weather at lower intensity that matters most to VFR and light aircraft.

mnemonics: Sierra sees nothing (IFR), Tango tosses (turbulence), Zulu freezes (icing).

7-1-8.gist: When a SIGMET, convective SIGMET, AIRMET (outside the contiguous U.S.), urgent PIREP or Center Weather Advisory affects airspace within 150 miles of their area, Centers broadcast an alert once on all frequencies and tell you to contact Flight Service for details; towers and approach controls may limit their alerts to 50 miles.
7-1-8.why: It explains the 'attention all aircraft' calls you hear on Center frequency.

numbers.quote: when any part of the area described is within 150 miles of the airspace under their jurisdiction

numbers.value: Terminal facilities may limit to 50 miles
numbers.quote: Tower cab and approach control positions may opt to broadcast hazardous weather information alerts only when any part of the area described is within 50 miles of the airspace under their jurisdiction.

questions.q: Center says 'attention all aircraft, convective SIGMET two seven eastern'. What do I do?
questions.a: Note it, and if it may affect your route get the details from Flight Service or your FIS-B display; the broadcast only alerts you that the advisory exists.

7-1-9.gist: Flight Information Services put weather and aeronautical data on cockpit displays via the FAA's free FIS-B (978 MHz UAT) or commercial data links. It supplements, never replaces, voice communication with FSS and ATC; it supports strategic decisions (20 minutes or more) not tactical weather avoidance (under 3 minutes); TFR and NOTAM depictions are for awareness only; and FIS-B NOTAMs are limited to those issued within the past 30 days.
7-1-9.why: The examiner wants to hear you treat the tablet as a planning aid with latency, not as a radar.

numbers.quote: FIS should not serve as the sole source of aviation weather and other operational information.

FIS aviation weather products (for example, graphical ground-based radar precipitation depictions) are not appropriate for tactical (typical timeframe of less than 3 minutes) avoidance of severe weather such as negotiating a path through a weather hazard area.

numbers.value: NOTAMs only from the last 30 days
numbers.quote: The NOTAM-D and NOTAM-FDC products broadcast via FIS-B are limited to those issued or effective within the past 30 days.

traps: A long-standing runway closure NOTAM older than 30 days will not appear on FIS-B; you still need the preflight briefing.

questions.q: Can I skip the briefing because my tablet shows NOTAMs and weather in flight?
questions.a: No. FIS-B is a supplement: it omits NOTAMs older than 30 days, its products lag, and the AIM says it must not be the sole source; the § 91.103 briefing still happens before flight.

7-1-10.gist: Automated weather observing systems (AWOS) broadcast minute-by-minute weather on a VHF frequency or NAVAID voice, receivable to about 25 nm and 10,000 ft AGL. Levels run from AWOS-A (altimeter only) through AWOS-3 (adds visibility and ceiling) to AWOS-3P, 3PT, 3T and 4 with precipitation, lightning and runway sensors. Automated reports carry the prefix AUTO, the lowest visibility reported is 'less than one quarter', and the word 'clear' is replaced by 'no clouds below' or 'clear below' the sensor's range.
7-1-10.why: You will hear AWOS on every cross-country, and the level tells you what the broadcast cannot report.

numbers.quote: The AWOS observations will include the prefix “AUTO” to indicate that the data are derived from an automated system.
AWOS-3 provides the information provided by AWOS-2 plus cloud/ceiling data.

numbers.value: Receivable to 25 nm and 10,000 ft AGL
numbers.quote: AWOS transmissions on a discrete VHF radio frequency are engineered to be receivable to a maximum of 25 NM from the AWOS site and a maximum altitude of 10,000 feet AGL.
The word “Clear” is not used in AWOS due to limitations in the height ranges of the sensors.

questions.q: The AWOS says 'clear below one two thousand'. Is the sky clear?
questions.a: It means the ceilometer detected no clouds within its 12,000 ft range; there may be clouds above that. An AWOS-A or AV gives no cloud information at all.

7-1-12.gist: ATC radar shows precipitation intensity (light under 26 dBZ, moderate 26 to 40, heavy over 40 to 50, extreme over 50) but cannot detect turbulence, and Center's mosaic can be up to 6 minutes old. Controllers will describe weather and help you avoid it when asked: request a deviation with a heading or degrees, direction and miles, a new route, an altitude change or vectors, as early as possible with where you want to start, the extent, and where you will rejoin. IFR pilots must not deviate without a clearance except under emergency authority.
7-1-12.why: When you ask a controller 'how does the weather look ahead?' this is what they can and cannot tell you.

numbers.quote: “LIGHT” (< 26 dBZ)

numbers.value: ATC radar does not see turbulence
numbers.quote: ATC radar is not able to detect turbulence.

numbers.value: Center's display can be 6 minutes old
numbers.quote: the precipitation data on the ARTCC controller's display could be up to 6 minutes old
It is very important, therefore, that the request for deviation or radar vector be forwarded to ATC as far in advance as possible.

questions.q: How do I ask ATC to go around a cell?
questions.a: Request a deviation with a direction and amount ('request 20 degrees left for weather, about 15 miles') and tell them where you will rejoin; ask early because coordination takes time.

7-1-18.gist: Pilot weather reports: ATC must solicit them when ceilings are at or below 5,000 ft, visibility at or below 5 miles, thunderstorms, light or greater icing, moderate or greater turbulence, wind shear or volcanic ash are reported or forecast, and pilots are urged to volunteer them. Give them to whoever you are talking to. Format: UA routine or UUA urgent, then /OV location, /TM time, /FL altitude, /TP type, then sky, weather, temperature, wind, turbulence and icing; the altitude and type are essential for turbulence and icing reports.
7-1-18.why: Reading a coded PIREP is a knowledge-test skill and giving one is expected of a cross-country pilot.

numbers.quote: FAA air traffic facilities are required to solicit PIREPs when the following conditions are reported or forecast: ceilings at or below 5,000 feet; visibility at or below 5 miles (surface or aloft); thunderstorms and related phenomena; icing of light degree or greater; turbulence of moderate degree or greater; wind shear and reported or forecast volcanic ash clouds.
Routine or Urgent PIREP

numbers.value: Altitude and type are essential for turbulence and icing
numbers.quote: Essential for turbulence and icing reports

questions.q: Decode: KCMH UA /OV APE 230010/TM 1516/FL085/TP BE20/SK BKN065/TB LGT.
questions.a: Routine PIREP near Columbus: 10 miles southwest of Appleton VOR at 1516Z, 8,500 ft, a King Air 200, broken clouds with bases at 6,500 ft, light turbulence.

7-1-19.gist: Airframe icing: ice cuts thrust and lift, adds drag and weight, and raises stall speed; a half inch can cut lift by half. Expect icing in visible precipitation between +2 and -10 degrees C; if it starts, leave the precipitation or find warmer air. Intensities: trace, light, moderate and severe, defined by accretion rate and how the deice systems cope. Rime ice is rough and opaque from small droplets freezing instantly; clear ice is glossy from large droplets freezing slowly.
7-1-19.why: For a non-deiced trainer the only right answer is avoidance, and the examiner wants the temperature band and the rime-versus-clear distinction.

numbers.value: Icing between +2 and -10 degrees C in visible moisture
numbers.quote: A pilot can expect icing when flying in visible precipitation, such as rain or cloud droplets, and the temperature is between +02 and -10 degrees Celsius.

numbers.value: Half an inch can halve the lift
numbers.quote: It takes but 1/2 inch of ice to reduce the lifting power of some aircraft by 50 percent
Rime ice. Rough, milky, opaque ice formed by the instantaneous freezing of small supercooled water droplets.
Clear ice. A glossy, clear, or translucent ice formed by the relatively slow freezing of large supercooled water droplets.

questions.q: What conditions produce airframe ice?
questions.a: Visible moisture (cloud or precipitation) with the temperature between about +2 and -10 degrees C; freezing rain and drizzle are the worst because their large droplets form clear ice.

7-1-20.gist: The AIM's icing vocabulary: glaze (clear) ice, rime ice, mixed ice, intercycle, residual and runback ice; and the conditions: known icing (ice observed or detected in flight), forecast icing, potential icing (the manufacturer's temperature-and-moisture definition), freezing drizzle and freezing rain, supercooled drops and supercooled large drops.
7-1-20.why: The 'known icing conditions' definition is the one the FAA uses when deciding whether a flight was legal in an aircraft not approved for icing.

numbers.quote: Atmospheric conditions in which the formation of ice is observed or detected in flight.
Environmental conditions expected by a National Weather Service or an FAA-approved weather provider to be conducive to the formation of inflight icing on aircraft.
Water drops/droplets which remain unfrozen at temperatures below 0°C.

questions.q: What are 'known icing conditions'?
questions.a: Atmospheric conditions in which ice formation is observed or detected in flight; an AIRMET Zulu is forecast icing, and the POH's own limitation on flight into known icing is what makes it illegal for most trainers.

7-1-21.gist: Turbulence reporting: light (slight, erratic changes; slight strain on belts), moderate (definite changes, aircraft in positive control; definite strains, objects dislodged), severe (large abrupt changes, momentarily out of control; occupants forced violently against belts) and extreme (practically impossible to control, possible structural damage). 'Chop' is the rhythmic bumpiness without attitude change. Occasional is less than a third of the time, intermittent a third to two thirds, continuous more. Report location, time, intensity, in or near clouds, altitude, aircraft type and duration.
7-1-21.why: The examiner may ask how you would report the bumps you felt on the way to the checkride.

numbers.quote: Occupants may feel a slight strain against seat belts or shoulder straps. Unsecured objects may be displaced slightly.
Occupants feel definite strains against seat belts or shoulder straps. Unsecured objects are dislodged. Food service and walking are difficult.
Occupants are forced violently against seat belts or shoulder straps. Unsecured objects are tossed about. Food Service and walking are impossible.

numbers.value: Occasional: less than 1/3 of the time
numbers.quote: Occasional-Less than 1/3 of the time.
Continuous-More than 2/3.

questions.q: What is the difference between moderate turbulence and moderate chop?
questions.a: Moderate turbulence changes altitude or attitude and airspeed while the aircraft stays in positive control; moderate chop is rapid rhythmic jolts without appreciable altitude or attitude change.

7-1-22.gist: Report wind shear as the airspeed loss or gain and the altitudes where it happened ('loss of 20 knots at 400'), never as 'negative' or 'positive' wind shear, which has been misread as no shear. Tell ATC when you fly a wind shear escape maneuver and again when it is complete.
7-1-22.why: Low-level wind shear on final is a takeoff-and-landing risk element and this is how it is reported.

numbers.value: Report loss or gain and altitude
numbers.quote: The recommended method for wind shear reporting is to state the loss or gain of airspeed and the altitudes at which it was encountered.
Denver Tower, Cessna 1234 encountered wind shear, loss of 20 knots at 400.

questions.q: How do I report wind shear on final?
questions.a: State the airspeed change and where: 'encountered wind shear, loss of 15 knots at 300 feet on final'; avoid the words negative or positive wind shear.

7-1-23.gist: Clear air turbulence is a serious hazard mostly above 15,000 ft; the only source of information is pilots, so report the time, location and intensity of any CAT encounter.
7-1-23.why: Mostly a jet issue, but the knowledge test asks what CAT is and where it lives.

numbers.value: Report CAT with time, location and intensity
numbers.quote: All pilots encountering CAT conditions are urgently requested to report time, location, and intensity (light, moderate, severe, or extreme) of the element

questions.q: What is clear air turbulence?
questions.a: High-altitude turbulence, typically above 15,000 ft, not associated with clouds, often near the jet stream; it is reported as CAT with an intensity in a PIREP.

7-1-24.gist: Microbursts are intense small-scale downdrafts (up to 6,000 fpm) that spread out on reaching the ground, producing horizontal winds of 45 knots and a 90-knot headwind-to-tailwind shear across a diameter of under a mile (outflow about 2.5 miles). They intensify for about 5 minutes after touching down and seldom last more than 15. They occur in heavy rain and in benign-looking virga, where a ring of blowing dust may be the only clue. Airports with LLWAS, TDWR or WSP issue alerts such as 'microburst alert, 35 knot loss 2 mile final'.
7-1-24.why: Every number here is a knowledge-test question, and the 'virga with a dust ring' picture is what should make you delay a landing.

numbers.quote: The downdrafts can be as strong as 6,000 feet per minute. Horizontal winds near the surface can be as strong as 45 knots resulting in a 90 knot shear (headwind to tailwind change for a traversing aircraft) across the microburst.

numbers.value: Intensifies for 5 minutes after touching down
numbers.quote: An important consideration for pilots is the fact that the microburst intensifies for about 5 minutes after it strikes the ground.
An individual microburst will seldom last longer than 15 minutes from the time it strikes the ground until dissipation.

numbers.value: Blowing dust may be the only clue
numbers.quote: When there is little or no precipitation at the surface accompanying the microburst, a ring of blowing dust may be the only visual clue of its existence.
RUNWAY 27 ARRIVAL, MICROBURST ALERT, 35 KT LOSS 2 MILE FINAL, THRESHOLD WIND 250 AT 20.

questions.q: What happens to an airplane flying through a microburst on final?
questions.a: First a headwind and performance gain, then a downdraft and tailwind with a large performance loss, all within a mile or two and a few hundred feet of the ground; the AIM's answer is not to be there, and to go around at the first sign.

7-1-26.gist: Thunderstorms carry turbulence, hail, icing, lightning and up- and downdrafts, and the visible cloud is only part of the system: severe turbulence extends up to 20 miles from a severe storm and about 10 from a less severe one. Radar shows precipitation, not turbulence. Lightning strikes are most likely between -5 and +5 degrees C, even in clear air near the storm. A METAR has no 'severe' flag, but 50-knot winds or 3/4-inch hail in the report mean a severe storm.
7-1-26.why: The 20-mile clearance figure is the number the examiner wants when you say you would go around a storm.

numbers.value: Severe turbulence up to 20 miles from a severe storm
numbers.quote: Severe turbulence can be expected up to 20 miles from severe thunderstorms.

numbers.value: Lightning most likely between -5 and +5 degrees C
numbers.quote: The probability of lightning strikes occurring to aircraft is greatest when operating at altitudes where temperatures are between minus 5 degrees Celsius and plus 5 degrees Celsius.

numbers.value: Severe thunderstorm: 50 knots or 3/4 inch hail
numbers.quote: by understanding severe thunderstorm criteria, i.e., 50 knot winds or 3/4 inch hail

questions.q: How far should I stay from a thunderstorm?
questions.a: At least 20 miles from any storm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo; turbulence and hail extend well beyond the visible cloud.

7-1-27.gist: Thunderstorm do's and don'ts: never take off or land facing an approaching storm, never fly under one or under its anvil, never trust its appearance, never assume ATC will vector you around it, and never use data-linked NEXRAD (15 to 20 minutes old) for tactical maneuvering. Do avoid severe storms by 20 miles, circumnavigate an area with 6/10 coverage, treat tops of 35,000 ft or more as extremely hazardous, give a PIREP, and divert and wait it out if you cannot get around. If penetration is unavoidable: belts tight, hold course and a constant attitude, pick an altitude below the freezing level or above -15 C, pitot heat on, penetration speed set, lights up, autopilot altitude and speed hold off, and never turn back once inside.
7-1-27.why: It is the checklist the examiner expects when asking 'thunderstorms are forecast along your route; what is your plan?'

numbers.value: Do not take off or land in the face of a storm
numbers.quote: Don't land or takeoff in the face of an approaching thunderstorm. A sudden gust front of low level turbulence could cause loss of control.
Do avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo.
Do circumnavigate the entire area if the area has 6/10 thunderstorm coverage.

numbers.value: Tops 35,000 ft or higher: extremely hazardous
numbers.quote: Do regard as extremely hazardous any thunderstorm with tops 35,000 feet or higher whether the top is visually sighted or determined by radar.
The weather conditions depicted may be 15 to 20 minutes older than indicated on the display.

numbers.value: Inside: constant attitude, let altitude and airspeed vary
numbers.quote: Do maintain constant attitude. Allow the altitude and airspeed to fluctuate.

questions.q: Why can't I use the radar on my tablet to pick my way between cells?
questions.a: Because the NEXRAD mosaic shows where the weather was 15 to 20 minutes ago, not where it is; use it strategically to avoid the whole area, and use eyes and ATC for anything closer.

7-1-28.gist: The key to decoding TAFs and METARs: message type, station, issuance time in UTC, TAF valid period of 24 or 30 hours, wind as true direction and speed in knots with gusts and variability, visibility in statute miles (P6SM means more than six), runway visual range, present weather with intensity (- light, none moderate, + heavy) and proximity (VC means 5 to 10 miles away), sky cover in eighths (FEW 1 to 2, SCT 3 to 4, BKN 5 to 7, OVC 8) with heights in hundreds of feet, temperature and dew point in Celsius, altimeter in inches, and the TAF change groups FM, TEMPO, PROB30 and BECMG.
7-1-28.why: You will decode a METAR and a TAF on the knowledge test and read the real ones on the morning of the checkride.

numbers.value: Wind: true direction, knots, gusts, variability
numbers.quote: Wind: 3 digit true-north direction, nearest 10 degrees (or VaRiaBle); next 2-3 digits for speed and unit, KT (KMH or MPS); as needed, Gust and maximum speed; 00000KT for calm; for METAR, if direction varies 60 degrees or more, Variability appended, e.g., 180V260
Cloud amount, height and type: Sky Clear 0/8, FEW >0/8-2/8, ScaTtered 3/8-4/8, BroKeN 5/8-7/8, OverCast 8/8
Valid period, either 24 hours or 30 hours.

numbers.value: VC: 5 to 10 miles from the station
numbers.quote: “VC” = Vicinity, but not at aerodrome. In the US METAR, 5 to 10 SM from the point of observation.

traps: METAR and TAF winds are true; the ATIS and tower give magnetic winds. Both are in knots.
A ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer (or vertical visibility), not the lowest scattered layer.
