questions.a: Pittsburgh at 1955Z on the 9th: wind 220 true at 15 gusting 25, visibility 3/4 mile, RVR runway 28L 2,600 ft, thunderstorm with rain, overcast at 1,000 ft cumulonimbus, temperature 18 dew point 16, altimeter 29.92.

7-2-1.gist: Altimeters are subject to instrument error, static-system position error, nonstandard pressure and nonstandard temperature; the standard setting of 29.92 at high altitude removes the pressure-source errors between aircraft.
7-2-1.why: It is the list of altimeter errors the examiner asks you to name.

numbers.quote: Nonstandard atmospheric pressure.
Nonstandard temperatures.

questions.q: What errors affect the altimeter?
questions.a: Instrument error, static-port position error, nonstandard pressure (fixed by the current setting) and nonstandard temperature (not fixed by any setting: cold air puts you lower than indicated).

7-2-2.gist: Extreme pressure: many altimeters cannot be set above 31.00 inches, and when the pressure is higher your true altitude is higher than indicated. Below 28.00 inches flight is not recommended if the altimeter cannot be set that low, because true altitude is then lower than indicated, and cold temperatures make it worse.
7-2-2.why: It is the direction-of-error question: which way is the error when you cannot set the real pressure?

numbers.value: Above 31.00: true altitude higher than indicated
numbers.quote: When an aircraft's altimeter cannot be set to pressure settings above 31.00 “Hg, the aircraft's true altitude will be higher than the indicated altitude on the barometric altimeter.

numbers.value: Below 28.00: not recommended, true altitude lower
numbers.quote: Flight operations are not recommended when an aircraft's altimeter is unable to be set below 28.00 “Hg. In this situation, the aircraft's true altitude is lower than the indicated altitude.

questions.q: The altimeter setting is 31.20 but my altimeter only goes to 31.00. Where am I really?
questions.a: Higher than indicated, by about 200 ft; the AIM's high-pressure NOTAM procedures apply and VFR aircraft have no additional restrictions.

7-2-3.gist: Altimeter procedures: on the ground, a reading 75 ft or more off field elevation makes the altimeter questionable. Flying from high pressure into low without resetting puts you closer to the ground than indicated, about 1,000 ft per inch of error. Below 18,000 ft set a station within 100 nm; above 31.00 inches a NOTAM has everyone set 31.00 en route, with no extra restrictions on VFR aircraft; at 18,000 ft and above set 29.92, and the lowest usable flight level rises as pressure falls (FL180 at 29.92 or higher, FL190 down to 28.92, FL200 below that).
7-2-3.why: The 75 ft ground check and 'high to low, look out below' are checkride staples.

numbers.value: Ground check: 75 ft or more is questionable
numbers.quote: If the difference from the known field elevation and the altitude read from the altimeter is plus or minus 75 feet or greater, the accuracy of the altimeter is questionable

numbers.value: High to low, look out below
numbers.quote: If the altimeter is not set to the current altimeter setting when flying from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure, the aircraft will be closer to the surface than the altimeter indicates.
Set the altimeter to a current reported altimeter setting from a station along the route and within 100 NM of the aircraft, or;
VFR aircraft. VFR operating aircraft have no additional restrictions.

numbers.value: Lowest usable flight level at 29.92 or higher: 180
numbers.quote: 29.92 or higher

questions.q: On the ramp the altimeter reads 1,290 ft and field elevation is 1,200. Is that acceptable?
questions.a: No; a difference of 75 ft or more means the altimeter's accuracy is questionable and it should go to a repair station.

mnemonics: High to low, look out below (and hot to cold, look out below).

7-4-1.gist: Every aircraft producing lift trails two counter-rotating vortices, and a wake encounter can impose rolling moments beyond the roll control of the following aircraft, injuring occupants and damaging the airframe.
7-4-1.why: It is the physical basis for every wake-turbulence rule of thumb that follows.

numbers.quote: Wake turbulence is a function of an aircraft producing lift, resulting in the formation of two counter-rotating vortices trailing behind the aircraft.
Wake turbulence can impose rolling moments exceeding the roll-control authority of encountering aircraft

questions.q: When is wake turbulence worst?
questions.a: Behind a heavy, clean, slow aircraft, because vortex strength grows with weight and with the angle of attack needed at low speed in the clean configuration.

7-4-5.gist: Where wake bites: below and behind the generating aircraft, especially at low altitude. Be alert in calm wind when vortices linger in the touchdown zone, drift from a nearby runway, sink into a crossing runway's path, into the traffic pattern, or into the VFR hemispheric altitude 500 ft below an airliner; a visual approach behind landing traffic is a common scenario. Visualize the vortex trail and stay above it.
7-4-5.why: Calm-wind days are the trap: the vortices sit on the runway waiting for you.

numbers.quote: AVOID THE AREA BELOW AND BEHIND THE WAKE GENERATING AIRCRAFT, ESPECIALLY AT LOW ALTITUDE WHERE EVEN A MOMENTARY WAKE ENCOUNTER COULD BE CATASTROPHIC.
Pilots should be particularly alert in calm wind conditions and situations where the vortices could:

numbers.value: Vortices sink into the altitude 500 ft below
numbers.quote: Sink into the flight path of VFR aircraft operating on the hemispheric altitude 500 feet below.

questions.q: A light crosswind is blowing. Is wake turbulence on the runway a concern?
questions.a: Yes; a light quartering wind can hold one vortex over the runway or drift it onto a parallel runway, so it is among the worst cases, not the safest.

7-4-6.gist: The avoidance recipes. Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway: stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point; with a parallel runway closer than 2,500 ft, expect drift; on a crossing runway, cross above its path. Landing behind a departing large aircraft: land well before its rotation point. Departing behind one: rotate before its rotation point, climb above its path and turn away upwind. Be wary after a large aircraft's low approach or touch-and-go, and en route stay out from below and behind, moving laterally upwind.
7-4-6.why: The examiner will describe a heavy on the runway ahead and expect the specific plan for that case.

numbers.quote: Landing behind a larger aircraft- same runway. Stay at or above the larger aircraft's final approach flight path-note its touchdown point-land beyond it.
Landing behind a larger aircraft- when parallel runway is closer than 2,500 feet. Consider possible drift to your runway.

numbers.value: Departing behind: rotate before its rotation point
numbers.quote: Departing behind a larger aircraft. Note the larger aircraft's rotation point and rotate prior to the larger aircraft's rotation point.
If a larger aircraft is observed above on the same track (meeting or overtaking) adjust your position laterally, preferably upwind.

questions.q: A 737 just departed ahead of me. How do I take off safely?
questions.a: Wait for the interval (the tower will give 'caution wake turbulence' and usually 2 minutes if you ask), rotate before the point where the jet rotated, climb above its climb path and turn upwind away from it.

7-4-8.gist: Accepting traffic information, an instruction to follow an aircraft, or a visual approach clearance means you accept responsibility for wake separation. ATC says 'super' or 'heavy' when known. Lighter aircraft on a visual approach behind them should fly on or above the glidepath (the 3-to-1 rule: 3,000 ft at 10 miles), pick a landing point at least 1,000 ft down the runway and beyond the preceding aircraft's touchdown, keep the line of sight to it above and ahead of the heavier aircraft, ask ATC for separation updates, and report any wake encounter.
7-4-8.why: It closes the wake discussion: once you say 'traffic in sight, will follow', the separation is yours.

numbers.value: Following an aircraft transfers the responsibility
numbers.quote: Instructions to follow an aircraft; and

numbers.value: So does a visual approach clearance
numbers.quote: The acceptance of a visual approach clearance.

numbers.value: Fly on or above the glidepath
numbers.quote: Pilots of lighter aircraft should fly on or above the glidepath.

numbers.value: Land beyond the heavier aircraft's touchdown
numbers.quote: Land beyond the point of landing of the preceding heavier aircraft.

questions.q: Tower says 'follow the heavy Airbus on final, caution wake turbulence'. Who is responsible for separation?
questions.a: You are, once you accept the instruction: stay on or above its glidepath, note where it touches down, and land beyond that point.

7-6-7.gist: Mountain flying: file a flight plan and route over populated areas and known passes with altitude to glide clear; do not fly a light aircraft when winds aloft exceed 35 mph; expect downdrafts of 1,500 to 2,000 fpm on the lee side and add a thousand feet approaching from downwind; cross ridges at a 45-degree angle so you can turn away. Mountain obscuration is its own hazard. At high-elevation fields use the same indicated airspeed but expect a faster true airspeed and longer landing; performance charts assume 59 F and 29.92, and towers at airports of 2,000 ft or higher broadcast 'check density altitude' on hot days.
7-6-7.why: The 35 mph wind limit, the 45-degree ridge crossing and the density altitude advisory are all oral questions for anyone training near hills.

numbers.value: No light aircraft above 35 mph winds aloft
numbers.quote: Don't fly a light aircraft when the winds aloft, at your proposed altitude, exceed 35 miles per hour.
Downdrafts of from 1,500 to 2,000 feet per minute are not uncommon on the leeward side.
When approaching a mountain ridge from the downwind side, it is recommended that the ridge be approached at approximately a 45 degree angle to the horizontal direction of the ridge.

numbers.value: Same indicated airspeed at high-altitude fields
numbers.quote: When landing at a high altitude field, the same indicated airspeed should be used as at low elevation fields.

numbers.value: 'Check density altitude' at airports 2,000 ft and higher
numbers.quote: At airports with elevations of 2,000 feet and higher, control towers and FSSs will broadcast the advisory “Check Density Altitude” when the temperature reaches a predetermined level.

questions.q: Why cross a ridge at a 45-degree angle?
questions.a: So that if you meet a downdraft or turbulence you can turn away from the ridge with a small heading change instead of a 180, and with less stress on the airplane.

7-7-2.gist: NTSB notification: the operator must immediately notify the nearest NTSB office of an accident or of these incidents: flight control malfunction, a required crewmember unable to perform, turbine engine structural failure, in-flight fire, mid-air collision, property damage over $25,000, and an overdue aircraft believed in an accident (plus electrical, hydraulic and engine cases for large aircraft). A report on NTSB Form 6120.1 is due within 10 days of an accident or when an overdue aircraft is still missing after 7 days; an incident report only if the NTSB asks.
7-7-2.why: The oral asks what must be reported and when; the AIM's list is NTSB Part 830 in readable form.

numbers.quote: Flight control system malfunction or failure.
Inflight fire.
Aircraft collide in flight.
Damage to property, other than the aircraft, estimated to exceed $25,000 for repair (including materials and labor) or fair market value in the event of total loss, whichever is less.

numbers.value: Report within 10 days of an accident
numbers.quote: Within 10 days after an accident;

numbers.value: Overdue and still missing after 7 days
numbers.quote: When, after 7 days, an overdue aircraft is still missing;
A report on an incident for which notification is required as described in subparagraph a(1) must be filed only as requested by an authorized representative of the NTSB.

traps: Immediate notification and the written report are two different obligations with two different clocks.
Damage to the aircraft alone is not on the incident list; it is an accident only if it is substantial damage or someone is seriously injured.

questions.q: I had a gear-up landing with no injuries. What do I report and when?
questions.a: Notify the nearest NTSB office immediately if it meets the accident definition (substantial damage), then file Form 6120.1 within 10 days. A listed incident needs the immediate notification but a report only if the NTSB asks.

8-1-1.gist: Fitness for flight: a medical certificate, and the § 61.53 rule that a known disqualifying condition grounds you even with one. Do not fly with any illness; do not fly on medication unless the FAA approves it; alcohol impairs with as little as one drink and is detectable for at least 3 hours, the rule is 8 hours bottle to throttle and you may still be impaired after that; fatigue (acute and chronic), sleep apnea, stress and emotional upset each degrade judgment. The FAA's personal checklist: I'M SAFE, not impaired by Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
8-1-1.why: IMSAFE is the aeromedical part of every checkride oral and this paragraph is where it comes from.

numbers.quote: As little as one ounce of liquor, one bottle of beer or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills, with the alcohol consumed in these drinks being detectable in the breath and blood for at least 3 hours.
The CFRs prohibit pilots from performing crewmember duties within 8 hours after drinking any alcoholic beverage or while under the influence of alcohol.
The safest rule is not to fly while suffering from any illness.
The safest rule is not to fly as a crewmember while taking any medication, unless approved to do so by the FAA.
PERSONAL CHECKLIST. I'm physically and mentally safe to fly; not being impaired by:

traps: Eight hours is a floor, not a guarantee: the AIM says a pilot may still be under the influence 8 hours after moderate drinking, and § 91.17 also sets 0.04 percent blood alcohol.
Over-the-counter antihistamines and cold remedies count as medication that affects the faculties.

questions.q: What is IMSAFE?
questions.a: The FAA's personal preflight checklist: am I impaired by Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue or Emotion? Any yes means do not fly.

mnemonics: I'M SAFE: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.

8-1-2.gist: Effects of altitude. Hypoxia: night vision degrades from 5,000 ft; significant effects usually start above 12,000 ft (impaired judgment, memory, coordination, euphoria); above 15,000 ft tunnel vision and cyanosis; the ability to act is lost in 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 ft and 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000. Smoking, carbon monoxide, anemia and some medications lower the threshold. Use oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and 5,000 ft at night. Ear and sinus blocks come from flying with a cold and are not fixed by sprays. After scuba diving wait 12 hours (24 if a decompression stop was needed) before flying up to 8,000 ft and 24 hours before flying higher.
8-1-2.why: The oxygen recommendations, hypoxia symptoms and scuba wait times are all on the knowledge test.

numbers.value: Night vision from 5,000 ft; other effects above 12,000
numbers.quote: Although a deterioration in night vision occurs at a cabin pressure altitude as low as 5,000 feet, other significant effects of altitude hypoxia usually do not occur in the normal healthy pilot below 12,000 feet.
The ability to take corrective and protective action is lost in 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 feet and 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 feet, followed soon thereafter by unconsciousness.

numbers.value: Oxygen above 10,000 ft by day, 5,000 at night
numbers.quote: For optimum protection, pilots are encouraged to use supplemental oxygen above 10,000 feet during the day, and above 5,000 feet at night.

numbers.value: Do not fly with a cold
numbers.quote: An ear block is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergic condition.

The recommended wait time before going to flight altitudes up to 8,000 feet is at least 12 hours after diving that did not require a controlled ascent (i.e., non-decompression stop diving), and at least 24 hours after diving that required a controlled ascent (i.e., decompression stop diving). The recommended wait time before going to flight altitudes above 8,000 feet is at least 24 hours after any SCUBA dive.

traps: The regulatory oxygen requirement (§ 91.211) starts at 12,500 ft; the AIM's 10,000 by day and 5,000 at night are recommendations that are stricter.
Hypoxia symptoms do not vary in an individual, which is why altitude chamber training is valuable.

questions.q: I went scuba diving this morning. When can I fly?
questions.a: At least 12 hours after a no-decompression dive if staying at or below 8,000 ft, at least 24 hours after a decompression dive, and 24 hours after any dive if flying above 8,000 ft.

8-1-3.gist: Hyperventilation, rapid deep breathing under stress, blows off carbon dioxide and causes lightheadedness, tingling and a feeling of suffocation that can spiral. It clears in minutes when breathing is consciously slowed, or by breathing into a paper bag. Because early symptoms mimic hypoxia and both can occur together, if you are on oxygen go to 100 percent first and check the system before working on your breathing.
8-1-3.why: The hypoxia-or-hyperventilation question is a favorite because the first-aid steps differ.

numbers.quote: The buildup of carbon dioxide in the body can be hastened by controlled breathing in and out of a paper bag held over the nose and mouth.
Early symptoms of hyperventilation and hypoxia are similar.

questions.q: How do I tell hyperventilation from hypoxia?
questions.a: You may not be able to; if oxygen is available select 100 percent and check the system first, then slow and deepen your breathing. Hyperventilation clears within minutes of controlled breathing.

8-1-4.gist: Carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless and tasteless and comes from exhaust; cabin heaters that use air passed over the exhaust manifold leak it through cracks. If you smell exhaust or get a headache, drowsiness or dizziness with the heater on, suspect CO: shut off the heater, open the vents, and get medical help if symptoms persist.
8-1-4.why: Winter flying in a trainer with a muffler-shroud heater makes this a real preflight question.

numbers.quote: Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas contained in exhaust fumes.

A pilot who detects the odor of exhaust or experiences symptoms of headache, drowsiness, or dizziness while using the heater should suspect carbon monoxide poisoning, and immediately shut off the heater and open air vents.

questions.q: I get a headache with the cabin heat on. What do I do?
questions.a: Turn the heater off, open the vents and fresh-air sources, consider landing, and seek medical care if symptoms continue; CO poisoning produces hypoxia and can be fatal.

8-1-5.gist: Illusions leading to spatial disorientation: the leans, Coriolis, graveyard spin and spiral, somatogravic (acceleration feels like nose-up), inversion, elevator, false horizon and autokinesis; they are prevented only by reference to fixed ground points or the instruments. Illusions leading to landing errors: a narrow or upsloping runway, featureless terrain and rain or haze all make you feel high and fly a low approach; a wide or downsloping runway does the opposite; fog feels like pitching up; bright lights make the runway seem closer.
8-1-5.why: The ACS lists these by name and examiners ask which way each illusion pushes your approach.

numbers.quote: Spatial disorientation from these illusions can be prevented only by visual reference to reliable, fixed points on the ground or to flight instruments.

numbers.value: Somatogravic: acceleration feels like nose up
numbers.quote: Somatogravic illusion. A rapid acceleration during takeoff can create the illusion of being in a nose up attitude.

numbers.value: Narrow runway: feel high, fly low
numbers.quote: Runway width illusion. A narrower‐than‐usual runway can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it actually is.
An upsloping runway, upsloping terrain, or both, can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it actually is.
Autokinesis. In the dark, a static light will appear to move about when stared at for many seconds.

traps: Every 'feel high' illusion (narrow, upslope, featureless, rain, haze) ends in a low approach and a short landing; use the VASI or PAPI whenever it exists.

questions.q: Landing on a narrow upsloping runway at night, which way will I err?
questions.a: Both illusions make you feel higher than you are, so you will tend to fly a dangerously low approach; use the visual glide slope indicator and a normal aiming point.

mnemonics: ICEFLAGS: Inversion, Coriolis, Elevator, False horizon, Leans, Autokinesis, Graveyard spiral, Somatogravic.

8-1-6.gist: Vision: full dark adaptation takes 30 minutes, moderate adaptation 20 minutes under dim red light, and red light distorts chart colors; sunglasses should absorb 85 percent of light equally across colors. Scanning: only the fovea sees sharply, so scan in sectors, spend no more than a quarter to a third of the time inside (4 to 5 seconds on the panel per 16 outside), allow seconds to refocus between panel and horizon, and beware empty-field myopia above clouds or in haze, where the eyes relax to 10 to 30 ft.
8-1-6.why: Dark adaptation and the inside-outside scan ratio are the two numbers examiners pull from this paragraph.

numbers.value: Dark adaptation: 30 minutes, 20 under red light
numbers.quote: Although exposure to total darkness for at least 30 minutes is required for complete dark adaptation, a pilot can achieve a moderate degree of dark adaptation within 20 minutes under dim red cockpit lighting.
Sunglasses for protection from glare should absorb at least 85 percent of visible light (15 percent transmittance) and all colors equally (neutral transmittance)
no more than 4 to 5 seconds on the instrument panel for every 16 seconds outside

numbers.value: Empty-field myopia: eyes focus at 10 to 30 ft
numbers.quote: This causes the eyes to relax and seek a comfortable focal distance which may range from 10 to 30 feet.

questions.q: How long does it take to adapt to the dark before a night flight?
questions.a: About 30 minutes in full darkness, or a moderate adaptation in 20 minutes under dim red light; avoid bright lights (and the strobe reflections) once adapted.

8-1-8.gist: Collision-avoidance judgment: use the horizon to judge relative altitude (above the horizon means higher), know the right-of-way rules so you can act, expect the other pilot to maneuver too, and treat any target with no relative motion that grows in size as a collision course. High-hazard areas are airways near VORs and surface areas; most collisions happen in good weather; keep the windshield clean, cockpit organized, lights on, and use ATC advisories.
8-1-8.why: 'No relative motion means collision course' is the single most useful sentence for see-and-avoid.

numbers.quote: Any aircraft that appears to have no relative motion and stays in one scan quadrant is likely to be on a collision course.
If the other aircraft is above the horizon, it is probably on a higher flight path.
Remember, most collisions occur during days when the weather is good.
Day or night, use of exterior lights can greatly increase the conspicuity of any aircraft.

questions.q: How do I know if another aircraft is on a collision course with me?
questions.a: It stays in the same spot on your windshield with no relative motion and grows larger; take evasive action at once, preferably per the right-of-way rules, and keep scanning for others.

9-1-2.gist: Charts and publications are sold through FAA-approved print providers, and the Aeronautical Information Services website lists products, current edition dates and agents.
9-1-2.why: It tells you where a current paper chart comes from and where to check that yours is the latest edition.

numbers.quote: Public sales of charts and publications are available through a network of FAA approved print providers.

questions.q: How do I make sure my sectional is current?
questions.a: Compare its edition date with the AIS website listing of latest editions; sectionals are revised every 56 days and the next edition date is printed on the chart.

9-1-3.gist: Aeronautical Information Services publishes Safety Alerts for errors found in its digital products, Charting Notices for planned chart changes, and Data Product Notices for outages and upgrades, all listed on its website.
9-1-3.why: If a chart is wrong, this is where the FAA says so; a checkride briefing on current data can include it.

numbers.quote: Safety Alerts (SAs) are published to notify users of an error that was reported or discovered in one of our digital products.
Charting Notices (CNs) are published to notify users of a planned chart/publication enhancement

questions.q: Where would the FAA publish a known error on a sectional?
questions.a: As a Safety Alert on the Aeronautical Information Services website, alongside Charting Notices for coming changes.

9-1-4.gist: The FAA chart catalog: VFR navigation charts, IFR navigation charts, planning charts, supplementary charts and publications, and digital products, each described in 9-1-5.
9-1-4.why: It is the table of contents for the charts you carry on a VFR cross-country.

numbers.quote: VFR Navigation Charts

questions.q: What charts and publications do I need for a VFR cross-country?
questions.a: A current sectional (and terminal area chart near Class B), the Chart Supplement for airport data and frequencies, and optionally the VFR flyway planning chart on the back of the TAC.

9-1-5.gist: The chart series a VFR pilot uses: sectionals (1:500,000, for visual navigation of slow to medium speed aircraft, with topography, landmarks, airspace and airports), terminal area charts (larger scale around Class B, with VFR flyway planning charts on the back), the Grand Canyon and Gulf Coast specials, and the Chart Supplement (airport, NAVAID, frequency and weather-source data in seven volumes, revised every 56 days) plus airport diagrams. IFR en route and terminal procedure charts and the planning charts round out the catalog.
9-1-5.why: Knowing what each chart is for and how often it is revised is a chart-reading prerequisite on the checkride.

numbers.quote: Sectional Charts are designed for visual navigation of slow to medium speed aircraft.

numbers.value: Terminal area charts cover Class B at a larger scale
numbers.quote: TACs depict the airspace designated as Class B airspace. While similar to sectional charts, TACs have more detail because the scale is larger.

Chart Supplement refers to a series of civil/military flight information publications issued by FAA every 56 days consisting of the Chart Supplement U.S., Chart Supplement Alaska, and Chart Supplement Pacific.
Flyway planning charts depict flight paths and altitudes recommended for use to bypass high traffic areas.
Airport Diagrams. Full page airport diagrams are designed to assist in the movement of ground traffic at locations with complex runway/taxiway configurations

questions.q: When should I use a terminal area chart instead of a sectional?
questions.a: When operating to, from or near a Class B (or Class C) airport: the larger scale shows the shelves, VFR checkpoints, transition routes and frequencies in more detail.
